prompt: A developer builds a SaaS app, carbonops.cloud, registers it in their home tenant, and a customer tenant starts using it with Microsoft sign-in. A support engineer claims the app is 'the same object everywhere'. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The app registration and the enterprise application are the same object, with the same Object ID in every tenant

The app registration is the application object — the single blueprint in the home tenant. Each customer tenant gets its own enterprise application, which is a service principal. The Application (client) ID is the same everywhere; the Object ID is different in each tenant
Each customer tenant must create its own app registration with a new Application ID
Enterprise applications hold the app's secrets and redirect URIs; app registrations hold user assignments

explanation: Correct: app registration = application object, one global definition in the home tenant, holding the Application (client) ID, redirect URIs, secrets, and requested API permissions. Enterprise application = service principal, one per tenant that uses the app, holding consent, user assignment, and sign-in. Application ID is the same in every tenant; Object ID differs per tenant because each service principal is a different object. The first option reverses the IDs. The third is wrong — customers do not re-register the app. The fourth swaps the two objects' jobs.

prompt: A customer tenant uses the SaaS app, and the app requests OneDrive API access. The customer wants to limit the app to one folder, not the whole OneDrive account. Where is that governed?

options.text: Only in the developer's home tenant, by editing the app registration — customer tenants cannot limit it
In the customer tenant, on the enterprise application / service principal for that app — for example, by limiting its API permissions, assigning owners, and applying Conditional Access to it
By deleting the app registration in the home tenant
By assigning the app the Directory Reader role

explanation: Correct: governance happens in the customer tenant, on that tenant's enterprise application (service principal): limit API permissions / consent, assign owners, apply Conditional Access to the application, and monitor its sign-in and audit logs. The home-tenant app registration is the blueprint — it cannot enforce per-customer limits. Deleting the registration would break the app for everyone. A directory read role is not app governance.

prompt: An Azure Function needs to read secrets from Key Vault. A VM in another resource group also needs to read the same secrets. Which managed identity design is correct, and why?

options.text: System-assigned on the Function — it can be shared with the VM because both are in the same tenant
User-assigned — a standalone identity that can be assigned to both the Function and the VM; a system-assigned identity is tied to one resource and deleted with it
System-assigned on the VM — the Function can use the VM's identity over the network
Neither — managed identities cannot access Key Vault, you must store a client secret in code

explanation: Correct: a user-assigned managed identity is a standalone Azure resource that can be assigned to multiple resources. System-assigned is tied to one resource and deleted when that resource is deleted, so it cannot be shared with the VM. The first and third options assume sharing of a system-assigned identity. The fourth is false — managed identities are the recommended way to access Key Vault without stored credentials.

prompt: You enable a system-assigned managed identity on a VM. The VM still gets 'Forbidden' from Key Vault. What is the missing step?

options.text: Enable Conditional Access for the managed identity
Assign an Azure RBAC role (for example, Key Vault Secrets User) to the managed identity on the vault — the identity authenticates, but authorisation comes from RBAC
Register the managed identity as an app registration in the home tenant
Give the VM's user a Global Administrator role

explanation: Correct: a managed identity authenticates — it proves which identity is calling. Authorisation is separate: you must grant it an Azure RBAC role (or Key Vault access policy) on the target vault. Enabling Conditional Access does not grant vault access. App registration is a different identity type. Granting the human user a role does not grant the managed identity anything.

prompt: A user tries to connect a third-party AI meeting assistant that requests Mail.ReadWrite and Calendars.ReadWrite (delegated). Your tenant uses the Microsoft-managed consent policy. What is the expected behaviour, and where is it controlled?

options.text: The user can consent themselves — delegated permissions never need admin consent

The user is blocked from self-consent for those risky permissions and must request admin consent; this is controlled in Enterprise applications > Consent and permissions > User consent settings / Admin consent settings
The app is blocked tenant-wide automatically, with no request path
Only Global Administrators can use the app at all, even after admin consent

explanation: Correct: under the Microsoft-managed consent policy, risky delegated permissions such as Mail.ReadWrite and Calendars.ReadWrite are blocked for user self-consent and routed to admin consent. Control lives in Enterprise applications > Consent and permissions. The first option describes the old wide-open default. The third is wrong — there is a request path. The fourth is wrong — after admin consent, ordinary users can use the app.

prompt: You designate a help-desk lead as a reviewer in the admin consent workflow. A user requests consent for an app requesting Application.Read.All (application permission). Can the reviewer approve it?

options.text: Yes — being designated a reviewer automatically gives them permission to grant consent
No — designating someone as a reviewer does not elevate their privileges; they must separately hold the permissions required to grant that consent
Yes, but only for delegated permissions, not application permissions
No — only the user who requested consent can approve it

explanation: Correct: Learn is explicit — designating someone as a reviewer does not elevate their privileges. The reviewer must separately hold the permissions required to grant the requested consent — for Microsoft Graph application permissions, that is a highly privileged approval. The first option assumes the designation grants power. The third invents a delegated/application split for this rule. The fourth is wrong — the requester does not approve their own request.

prompt: An enterprise application is configured with 'Assignment required? Yes.' A user who is assigned to the app tries to sign in and is asked to request admin consent, even though the app only requests User.Read (a low-impact delegated permission). Why?

options.text: A bug — User.Read never needs admin consent
If an application requires assignment, its permissions require admin consent regardless of whether they would otherwise allow user consent
The user is a guest, and guests always need admin consent
The app registration is in another tenant, so all permissions need admin consent

explanation: Correct: if an application requires assignment, its permissions require admin consent regardless of whether they would otherwise allow user consent. The first option treats User.Read as always user-consentable, ignoring the assignment gate. The third and fourth invent other causes — the trigger is Assignment required = Yes.

prompt: A developer registers a new application in the Microsoft Entra admin center. What objects exist in the home tenant immediately after registration?

options.text: Both are created automatically in the home tenant when the app is registered
Only the application object is created; the service principal must be created manually in every tenant including the home tenant
Only the service principal is created; the application object is created when the first user signs in
Neither is created until an administrator grants admin consent

explanation: Correct: registering an app creates both an application object and a service principal object in the home tenant automatically (portal registration does both steps). The application object is the blueprint; the service principal is the local instance. The other options invent a manual second step or a missing object.

prompt: A SaaS vendor changes the redirect URIs on their application object in their home tenant. A customer tenant admin asks whether this changes the enterprise application in their tenant. What is the correct answer?

options.text: The change propagates to every customer tenant's service principal automatically
The change deletes all customer service principals and they must be recreated
The change applies to no service principal anywhere — app objects and service principals are unrelated
The change is reflected only in the home tenant's service principal; each customer tenant's service principal is governed locally by that tenant

explanation: Correct: changes to the application object are reflected in its service principal only in the home tenant; each customer tenant's service principal is its own object governed by that tenant's consent. The other options wrongly assume home-tenant edits propagate everywhere or that customers cannot govern the app locally.

prompt: A third-party app's service principal shows suspicious sign-ins. You need to stop it getting new tokens right now, but preserve everything for investigation and possible reactivation. What do you do?

options.text: Delete the application object immediately, because deletion is reversible with one click
Remove all user assignments and leave the app active — that stops token issuance
Deactivate the application, which prevents new token issuance while preserving the objects for investigation or future reactivation
Change the application's client secret, which immediately invalidates all existing tokens

explanation: Correct: deactivation prevents new token issuance while preserving the application object and service principal for investigation or future reactivation — the right move for a suspected compromise. Deletion is permanent and, if the app object is restored, its home service principal is not restored with it. Doing nothing or only removing user assignments leaves the app able to get tokens.

prompt: An auditor asks you to classify three service principals: one for a registered SaaS app, one for a managed identity on a VM, and one for an app created before app registrations existed. Which three types are these?

options.text: Application, Managed identity, and Legacy
Application and User only
Application, Guest, and Member only
There is only one type — every service principal is an application instance

explanation: Correct: there are three types of service principal — Application (the local instance of a global app object), Managed identity (representing a managed identity, with no associated app object), and Legacy (an app created before app registrations, with no associated app registration). The other options invent types or deny the managed identity type.

prompt: A developer tries to edit the service principal for a managed identity in App registrations and cannot find it. Why?

options.text: It has an app object that the developer can edit in App registrations
It can be updated directly like any other service principal
It is owned by the application developer and follows the app's lifecycle
It has no associated app object and cannot be updated or modified directly

explanation: Correct: a service principal representing a managed identity has no associated app object — unlike the Application type — and cannot be updated or modified directly. It is not an app registration, it is not owned by the developer, and it is not deletable through the app registrations blade.

prompt: You delete a VM that had a system-assigned managed identity with Key Vault access. What happens to the identity?

options.text: The identity survives and can be attached to a replacement VM
The identity survives but loses all role assignments
Azure automatically deletes the service principal when the resource is deleted
The identity is converted to a user-assigned managed identity automatically

explanation: Correct: the system-assigned service principal is tied to the resource's lifecycle — when the resource is deleted, Azure automatically deletes the service principal. The identity cannot outlive the resource, cannot be transferred, and does not need manual cleanup.

prompt: You enable a system-assigned managed identity on an App Service named invoicing-api. What is the managed identity's service principal called in Entra ID?

options.text: The service principal is named after the Azure resource it belongs to
The service principal gets a random GUID name unrelated to the resource
The service principal is named after the tenant
The administrator chooses the name at creation time

explanation: Correct: the system-assigned service principal's name is always the same as the Azure resource it was created for (and for a deployment slot, <app-name>/slots/<slot-name>). It is not a random GUID name, not the tenant name, and not chosen by the admin.

prompt: A scale set recycles VMs daily, and every VM needs the same Key Vault access with permissions that stay consistent across recycles. Which identity design fits?

options.text: A system-assigned identity on each VM, re-authorised every time a VM is recycled
A client secret stored in Key Vault and injected at startup
A user-assigned managed identity, pre-authorised on the vault and assigned to each VM as it is created — user-assigned is the recommended type for this pattern
A single service principal with a certificate that every VM shares

explanation: Correct: user-assigned managed identities are provisioned independently from compute, can be assigned to multiple resources, and are the recommended type for Microsoft services — exactly the pre-authorisation, frequent-recycling scenario. System-assigned identities cannot be shared and die with the resource; a stored secret reintroduces credential management.

prompt: A developer asks for the runbook on rotating a managed identity's credentials. What is the correct answer?

options.text: The developer must rotate the managed identity's secret every 90 days
The developer must store the managed identity's certificate in Key Vault
There are no credentials to manage or rotate — credentials are not even accessible to you
The developer must renew the managed identity's password annually

explanation: Correct: managed identities remove credential management entirely — credentials are not even accessible to you. There is no secret to rotate, no certificate to renew, and no password to store; the platform obtains tokens for the identity. The other options describe the old secret-based pattern that managed identities replace.

prompt: A workload running on Azure compute with a managed identity needs to act as an Entra ID application without storing any secret. What is the supported approach, and what is its limit?

options.text: A managed identity can be used as a federated identity credential on an Entra ID app, with a limit of 20 FICs — the recommended credential-free path
A managed identity can be used as a password on an app, with no limit
A managed identity cannot be used as a credential on an app at all
A managed identity replaces the app object, so no app registration is needed

explanation: Correct: workload identity federation lets a managed identity act as a credential on an Entra ID app — the recommended credential-free path — with a limit of 20 federated identity credentials when using managed identities as FIC. It is not a password, not unlimited, and not a replacement for the app object.

prompt: A backup service needs to read all mailboxes overnight with no user signed in, while a reporting add-in only reads the signed-in user's own mailbox. Which permission types do they need?

options.text: Delegated permissions let the app act on its own with no user signed in; application permissions require a user
Both types require a signed-in user at all times
Delegated permissions are only for Microsoft's own apps; third-party apps can only use application permissions
Delegated permissions let the app act on behalf of the signed-in user, limited to what that user can access; application permissions let the app act on its own with no user signed in

explanation: Correct: delegated permissions let an application act on behalf of the signed-in user, accessing only what that user can access. Application permissions let the app act on its own with no user signed in. The other options reverse the two or invent a user-presence requirement for application permissions.

prompt: Your tenant disables user consent entirely. A user tries to sign in to an app requesting only User.Read. What happens?

options.text: The user is prompted for consent anyway, because low-impact permissions always allow user consent
The app is blocked tenant-wide and can never be used
User consent is possible only where it is allowed for the application and the requested permissions — with user consent disabled, the user is not prompted and must request admin consent
The user can consent, but only if they are a guest user

explanation: Correct: user consent is possible only where it is allowed for the application and for the set of permissions requested — if user consent is disabled, or users are not allowed to consent for the requested permissions, they are not prompted for consent. The app is not blocked tenant-wide; it is routed to admin consent. And consent is not automatic for low-impact permissions when user consent is disabled.

prompt: An administrator is about to grant tenant-wide admin consent to a new SaaS app requesting Mail.ReadWrite for all mailboxes. What should they understand before clicking grant?

options.text: It is a sensitive operation that can give the application's publisher access to significant portions of the organisation's data or permission to do highly privileged operations
It only affects the administrator who grants it, not other users
It can be undone automatically after 30 days with no action needed
It only grants the permissions the first user requested, not the full set the app asks for

explanation: Correct: tenant-wide admin consent is a sensitive operation, potentially giving the publisher access to significant portions of the organisation's data or permission to do highly privileged operations — role management, full access to all mailboxes or all sites, full user impersonation. The other options understate the blast radius or invent a limitation that does not exist.

prompt: You grant tenant-wide admin consent for a reporting app. A month later a user is prompted for consent again when opening the same app. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: Users are prompted for consent on every sign-in, even after admin consent
Only administrators can use the app after admin consent; regular users still need to consent
Admin consent expires after 90 days and must be renewed
Users are not prompted for consent after admin consent — unless the app requests another permission the administrator has not granted

explanation: Correct: after admin consent is granted on behalf of the organisation, users are not prompted for consent for that application — unless the app later requests another permission the administrator has not granted, in which case the user may be prompted again. Consent is not per-session, not limited to admins, and not permanent for new permissions.

prompt: User consent is disabled in your tenant. A user tries to sign in to a new app and cannot consent. The admin consent workflow is enabled. What happens next?

options.text: The user is blocked permanently and must ask IT to register the app for them
The user can approve the request themselves by re-entering their password
The user sees an 'Approval required' window, submits a justification, and the designated reviewers are notified
The request is sent to Microsoft support for approval

explanation: Correct: the admin consent workflow gives users a way to request admin consent when they are not allowed to consent themselves — the user sees an 'Approval required' window, submits a justification, and the designated reviewers are notified. It is not automatic approval, not a block with no recourse, and not a self-approval path.

prompt: A user requests consent for an app that needs Microsoft Graph application permissions (app roles). The designated reviewer is a help-desk lead. Who can actually approve this request?

options.text: Only Global Administrators can approve admin consent requests for apps requesting Microsoft Graph app roles (application permissions)
Any designated reviewer can approve them
Any Application Administrator can approve them
The requesting user can approve them if no reviewer responds within 24 hours

explanation: Correct: only Global Administrators can approve admin consent requests for apps requesting Microsoft Graph app roles (application permissions) — a reviewer designated in the workflow cannot approve those, even if they can review the request. The other options give the reviewer power they do not have.

prompt: You configure the admin consent workflow at 9 a.m. At 9:15 a.m. a user still sees no 'Approval required' option. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: A Conditional Access Administrator can enable it instantly
Any designated reviewer can enable it for themselves
It is enabled automatically as soon as the first request is submitted
A Global Administrator must turn it on, and it can take up to an hour for the workflow to become enabled

explanation: Correct: enabling the workflow requires a Global Administrator to turn it on, and it can take up to an hour for the workflow to become enabled — the team should wait rather than re-creating it or assuming it failed. A Conditional Access Administrator cannot enable it, and reviewers cannot enable it for themselves.

prompt: How does the admin consent workflow actually move a request from a blocked user to a decision?

options.text: The application is granted consent automatically after 24 hours
The user grants consent to themselves by confirming twice
The user sends a request for admin approval, the designated reviewers receive it by email, a reviewer acts, and the user is notified
The request goes to the application's publisher for approval

explanation: Correct: the admin consent workflow gives admins a secure way to grant access to applications that require admin approval — when a user cannot provide consent, they send a request for admin approval, the request goes by email to the designated reviewers, a reviewer acts, and the user is notified. It is not an automatic grant, not a user self-approval, and not a block with no path.

prompt: You remove a help-desk lead from the admin consent reviewer list. A request they were already reviewing is still pending. What happens to that request?

options.text: A removed reviewer retains the ability to review requests made while they were designated, and keeps receiving expiration reminders for those requests
Removal is retroactive — all of the reviewer's pending requests are cancelled immediately
New reviewers are automatically assigned to all old requests
A removed reviewer can still approve new requests for 30 days

explanation: Correct: you can add or remove reviewers, but a reviewer retains the ability to review requests made while they were designated, and will keep receiving expiration reminders for those requests after removal; new reviewers are not assigned to requests created before they were set as reviewers. Removal is not retroactive.

prompt: One executive needs a niche app that requests a delegated permission. You do not want to grant tenant-wide admin consent for the whole organisation. What is the supported alternative?

options.text: It is impossible — consent is always tenant-wide or nothing
Disable user consent tenant-wide and the single user will be covered
Ask the user to consent themselves, which always works for any permission
Use the Microsoft Graph API to grant consent to delegated permissions on behalf of that single user

explanation: Correct: consent can be granted on behalf of a single user through the Microsoft Graph API instead of the whole organisation — the alternative to tenant-wide consent when only one person needs the app. It is not possible through the portal's tenant-wide grant alone, and it does not require disabling user consent tenant-wide.

prompt: You grant tenant-wide admin consent for an app that has 'Assignment required? Yes' with only the Finance group assigned. A user outside Finance tries to sign in. What happens?

options.text: Tenant-wide admin consent overrides assignment, so all users can sign in
User assignment is removed automatically once admin consent is granted
Requiring user assignment still limits access to assigned users only, even after tenant-wide admin consent
Only guest users are affected by assignment; members bypass it after admin consent

explanation: Correct: requiring user assignment limits who can use the app even after tenant-wide admin consent — consent and assignment are separate controls. Admin consent does not override assignment, assignment is not removed by consent, and guests are not automatically included.

prompt: A security analyst needs to see a SaaS app's permissions, who consented to them, and its sign-in activity in your tenant. Where do they look?

options.text: The Enterprise applications page, which lists and manages the service principals in the tenant
The App registrations page, which lists service principals
The Conditional Access policies page, which lists service principals
The Access reviews page, which lists service principals

explanation: Correct: the Enterprise applications page lists and manages the service principals in a tenant — permissions, user-consented permissions, who consented, and sign-in information. App registrations manages application objects, not service principals. The other options point at the wrong blades.

prompt: An administrator deletes an application object by mistake, then restores it from the app registrations UI. The app still does not work in the home tenant. Why?

options.text: Deleting the app object only deletes the customer service principals, not the home one
Restoring the app object restores its service principal automatically
Deleting the app object has no effect on any service principal
Deleting the app object also deletes its home tenant service principal, and restoring the app object will not restore that service principal

explanation: Correct: deleting an application object also deletes its home tenant service principal, but restoring the application object through the app registrations UI will not restore its corresponding service principal — the recovery is incomplete. The other options assume a clean restore that Learn explicitly rules out.

prompt: Two apps are registered: one single-tenant, one multitenant. A user in a customer tenant consents to the multitenant app. How many service principals exist for each app, and where?

options.text: A single-tenant app has a service principal in every tenant in the world
A multitenant app has only one service principal, in its home tenant
A single-tenant app has only one service principal, in its home tenant; a multitenant app has a service principal in each tenant where a user has consented to its use
Both models create a new application object in every customer tenant

explanation: Correct: a single-tenant application has only one service principal (in its home tenant), created and consented for use during registration. A multitenant application gets a service principal in each tenant where a user has consented to its use. The other options confuse the two models.

prompt: You find a service principal with credentials and reply URLs but no app registration behind it, usable only in your tenant. What is it?

options.text: It is a legacy service principal: it has no associated app registration and can only be used in the tenant where it was created
It is a managed identity that lost its Azure resource
It is an application-type service principal whose app object was deleted
It is a guest user account that was converted to an app

explanation: Correct: a legacy service principal represents a legacy app created before app registrations were introduced or through legacy experiences — it can have credentials, service principal names, and reply URLs, but has no associated app registration and can only be used in the tenant where it was created. It is not a managed identity and cannot be moved between tenants.

prompt: A developer asks what the application object actually defines about their app. Which three things does it describe?

options.text: The user assignments for the app in each tenant
The passwords of the users who sign in to the app
The billing information for the app's publisher
How the service can issue tokens, which resources the application might need to access, and the actions the application can take

explanation: Correct: the application object describes how the service can issue tokens to access the application, the resources the application might need to access, and the actions the application can take. It does not hold user assignments (those live on the service principal) and does not store user passwords.

prompt: A zero-trust review asks you to inventory workload identities in Entra ID. Which three identity types make up workload identities?

options.text: Users, groups, and devices
Guest users, members, and administrators
Applications, service principals, and managed identities
Devices, printers, and IoT hubs only

explanation: Correct: in Entra, workload identities are applications, service principals, and managed identities — the machine/non-human identities, alongside human identities. Devices are a separate identity type, and guest users are human identities, not workload identities.

prompt: An API you built accepts Microsoft Entra authentication. A Function with a managed identity needs to call it. Can the Function authenticate with its managed identity, or must it use a client secret?

options.text: Yes — managed identities can be used to authenticate to any resource that supports Microsoft Entra authentication, including your own applications
No — managed identities only work with Microsoft-owned services such as Key Vault and Storage
No — your own applications can only accept client secrets
Yes, but only if the application is registered in a different tenant

explanation: Correct: managed identities can authenticate to any resource that supports Microsoft Entra authentication, including your own applications — not just Microsoft services. They are not limited to Key Vault or storage, and they do not require a stored secret to call your own API.

prompt: A Function app tries to obtain a token using a VM's system-assigned managed identity. Will it work?

options.text: Yes — any resource in the same subscription can use it
Yes — any resource in the same resource group can use it
Yes — the Function can use it if it presents the VM's client secret
No — by design, only that Azure resource can use its system-assigned identity to request tokens

explanation: Correct: by design, only the Azure resource the system-assigned identity belongs to can use it to request tokens — the identity cannot be shared or borrowed by another resource. The other options wrongly assume sharing is possible or that a network call can transfer the identity.

prompt: A legacy service authenticates to Storage with a shared access key stored in its configuration. The key has leaked twice. What is the recommended identity fix?

options.text: Move the access key into Key Vault and keep using it
Rotate the access key more frequently and keep using it
Replace the access key with a managed identity, which replaces secrets such as access keys or passwords for service-to-service authentication
Keep the access key but restrict it by IP address only

explanation: Correct: a managed identity replaces secrets such as access keys or passwords, and can replace certificates or other forms of authentication for service-to-service dependencies. The migration removes the stored credential entirely rather than moving it to a safer store.

prompt: Your tenant wants users to be able to adopt low-risk apps themselves, but not to consent to risky permissions from unknown publishers. Which user consent setting fits?

options.text: Allow users to consent only to applications from verified publishers or your organisation, and only for permissions you select and classify as low impact
Allow users to consent to any application for any permission
Disable user consent entirely with no exceptions
Allow users to consent only to applications requesting application permissions

explanation: Correct: the user-consent settings offer built-in options including disabling user consent, allowing consent only to verified publishers or your organisation for selected low-impact permissions, or allowing consent to all applications. The 'verified publisher plus selected low-impact permissions' option is the middle control between disabling consent and allowing everything.

prompt: An app from an unknown publisher requests full access to all mailboxes and all SharePoint sites. What check must an administrator perform before granting tenant-wide admin consent?

options.text: The app has more than 10,000 users, so it must be safe
The publisher's website looks professional
The app was published recently, so it uses modern security
Ensure you trust the application and its publisher for the level of access requested — if you are not confident who controls the app and why it requests the permissions, do not grant consent

explanation: Correct: before granting tenant-wide admin consent, ensure you trust the application and its publisher for the level of access requested — if you are not confident who controls the app and why it requests the permissions, do not grant consent. The publisher's marketing, the user count, and the app's age are not the check.

prompt: A user signs in to a new app for the first time and sees a consent prompt. They accept. When will they see the prompt again for the same app and permissions?

options.text: The user must consent on every sign-in, even after granting it once
The user is never prompted if the app is from a verified publisher
The user is directed to the consent prompt when no previous record of user or admin consent exists for the required permissions, and usually does not have to consent again on future sign-ins
The user is prompted only if they are a guest; members are never prompted

explanation: Correct: when consent is required, the user is directed to the consent prompt if no previous record of user or admin consent exists for the required permissions — and once granted, the user usually does not have to consent again on future sign-ins. Consent is not per-session, not automatic, and not limited to the first tenant.

prompt: An auditor asks what your organisation gains by assigning an identity to every employee, partner, customer, device, and application — including cloud and on-premises apps — instead of managing access per system with shared credentials. Which answer is correct?

options.text: Every component gets the same password so sign-in is simpler across systems
Each component can be governed and monitored, and given credentials to authenticate
Role-based access control is no longer needed once every component has an identity
Each component automatically receives Global Administrator rights when it is given an identity

explanation: Correct: identity is a set of attributes for a person, device, or application/workload. Assigning an identity lets you govern behaviour, monitor sign-ins (when, from where, to what), and give the identity credentials to authenticate. The other options are wrong: identities do not share one password; RBAC is how you decide what an identity may do, so identity does not replace it; and an identity on its own grants no privilege — privilege comes from role assignment.

prompt: A user signs in to Microsoft Entra ID and then tries to open a storage account, but is denied even though sign-in succeeded. A colleague argues the sign-in itself should have decided everything. Which statement correctly separates the two steps?

options.text: Authorisation happens first, to prove who the user is; authentication happens second, to decide what they can do
Authentication answers 'who are you?'; authorisation answers 'what can you do?' and comes after authentication
Authentication and authorisation are the same step, performed by the same check at the same time
Authorisation is only needed for guest users; members are authorised by signing in

explanation: Correct: authentication proves who you are; authorisation decides what you may do, after authentication, by checking roles and permissions against the requested resource. The first option reverses the order. The third collapses two distinct steps. The fourth is wrong — members and guests both go through authorisation.

prompt: Your help desk is writing a guide on what counts as multi-factor authentication. Four users each present two proofs. Which combination is genuinely MFA?

options.text: A password plus a security question — two things the user knows
A password plus a push approval in Microsoft Authenticator — something you know plus something you have
A fingerprint plus facial recognition — two biometrics, so two factors
A password entered twice on two different devices

explanation: Correct: MFA needs two or more factors from different categories: something you know, something you have, something you are. Password plus Authenticator push is know plus have. A password plus a security question is two 'know' factors, not MFA. Fingerprint plus face is two 'are' factors from the same category. Entering the same password twice is the same factor twice.

prompt: A field engineer needs to sign in from a shared kiosk. Which passwordless option is hardware-based and resistant to phishing because its keys cannot be leaked in a phishing email?

options.text: SMS one-time code
Email one-time password
FIDO2 security key
A temporary access pass sent by email

explanation: Correct: FIDO2 is a hardware security key holding cryptographic keys, and Microsoft lists FIDO2 security keys among its phishing-resistant methods. Because authentication is hardware-backed, the keys cannot be phished out of an email the way a password or an emailed code can. SMS and email OTP are phishable and interceptable, and a temporary access pass is a short-lived credential for onboarding, not a phishing-resistant passwordless method.

prompt: A security architect challenges the claim that Windows Hello for Business is phishing-resistant, arguing that any biometric or PIN can be socially engineered. What actually makes it phishing-resistant?

options.text: It stores the password in the cloud, so the device never sees it
Its cryptographic keys are stored in a Trusted Platform Module (TPM), a hardware component on the device
It uses only facial recognition, which cannot be copied
It bypasses Conditional Access entirely

explanation: Correct: Windows Hello for Business stores its keys in the TPM, hardware on the device, and Microsoft lists it among the phishing-resistant methods. That is why it is phishing-resistant: there is no password to leak in a phishing email. The first option is wrong — keys are device-bound, not cloud-stored passwords. Biometrics alone are not the mechanism. And Windows Hello does not bypass Conditional Access.

prompt: Your tenant has Entra ID P1 only. A consultant proposes four controls in one project plan. Which one can you NOT do on P1 alone?

options.text: Require MFA with a Conditional Access policy
Use Conditional Access based on location and device state
Use Privileged Identity Management for just-in-time admin activation
Enable self-service password reset for a group of users

explanation: Correct: Conditional Access, MFA, and SSPR are P1 — Conditional Access requires P1 licences. PIM, just-in-time eligible activation with approval, requires P2 or Entra ID Governance. Risk-based Conditional Access using Identity Protection is also P2.

prompt: In the Entra admin centre, under Authentication methods, you want to enable FIDO2 security keys for one pilot group of users only, before a wider rollout. What is the correct approach?

options.text: Enable it tenant-wide; Entra does not support targeting authentication methods to a group
Open the FIDO2 security key method and include that group (or exclude others) in its targeting
Create a Conditional Access policy that enables FIDO2
Assign the group the Authentication Administrator role; methods follow the role

explanation: Correct: authentication methods are configured per method, with targeting to include or exclude users or groups — the Authentication methods policy lets administrators scope methods for specific users and groups. Tenant-wide enablement ignores the pilot scope. Conditional Access enforces access conditions; it does not enable authentication methods. A role does not enable a method.

prompt: Your tenant enables self-service password reset (SSPR). An administrator and a regular member both forget their passwords on the same day. Which statement about SSPR is correct?

options.text: SSPR is enabled for all users by default in every tenant, with no configuration needed
SSPR can be enabled for selected users or for all users, and accounts holding a Microsoft Entra administrator role face the strong two-gate password policy
SSPR replaces MFA — a user who can reset their password never needs MFA again
SSPR only works for guest users, not for members

explanation: Correct: SSPR can be scoped to selected users or to all users, and Microsoft enforces a strong two-gate policy for accounts assigned a Microsoft Entra administrator role. SSPR is not on for everyone by default. It is a recovery path, not a replacement for MFA. And SSPR applies to members as well as guests, subject to licensing and policy.

prompt: An attacker has a legitimate user's password after a phishing email. The user normally signs in from India during business hours. The attacker signs in from the United States at 2 a.m. India time, from an unfamiliar IP. Which Conditional Access idea does this test?

options.text: Conditional Access only checks the password, so the attacker will get in
Conditional Access evaluates signals — location, time, IP, device, and risk — after first-factor authentication, and can block or limit access even for a legitimate identity
Conditional Access blocks all sign-ins from the United States, regardless of policy
Conditional Access only applies before authentication, so it cannot help once the password is correct

explanation: Correct: Conditional Access is an if-then engine evaluated after first-factor authentication. It brings together signals — user/group, location, device, IP, application, and risk — and can grant, limit, or block access. A legitimate identity showing anomalous signals can be blocked. The first and fourth options misunderstand when Conditional Access runs. The third invents a blanket geo-block — the block comes from a policy, not from geography alone.

prompt: A new CISO wants every employee, for every cloud app, to be required to complete MFA — with the break-glass accounts excluded. In the policy, what do you set for users, target resources, and grant?

options.text: Users: All users (excluding the break-glass group); Target resources: All cloud apps; Grant: Require multifactor authentication
Users: All users; Target resources: All cloud apps; Grant: Block access
Users: Guest users only; Target resources: One app; Grant: Require compliant device only
Users: All users; Target resources: All cloud apps; Grant: No controls — MFA is automatic once a policy exists

explanation: Correct: the baseline MFA policy is Users = All users (with break-glass excluded), Target resources = All cloud apps, Grant = Require multifactor authentication, then enable the policy. Blocking everyone is not the goal. Narrowing the scope to guests and one app misses the requirement. And a policy with no grant control grants access without extra checks.

prompt: You create a Conditional Access policy for all admins. You want phishing-resistant MFA only — passkey or FIDO2, not Authenticator push. Which grant control do you use, and what must you NOT do in the same policy?

options.text: Grant: Require multifactor authentication; also add Require authentication strength (Phishing-resistant MFA) for defence in depth
Grant: Require authentication strength (Phishing-resistant MFA) only; do not also select Require multifactor authentication in the same policy
Grant: Require compliant device only; authentication strength is evaluated before first-factor authentication, so it replaces MFA
Grant: Block access for admins who do not have a passkey, and use a second policy for MFA

explanation: Correct: use Require authentication strength (Phishing-resistant MFA) as the grant control, alone. Learn is explicit: you cannot combine Require MFA and Require authentication strength in the same policy — they are alternative ways to express the grant. The first option tries to stack them. The third is wrong — strengths are evaluated after first-factor authentication, they do not replace it. The fourth splits the requirement across two policies in a way that does not enforce phishing-resistant MFA as a single grant.

prompt: A new hire has no registered methods yet. You give them a Temporary Access Pass (TAP) to register a passkey. A Conditional Access policy requires the Phishing-resistant MFA authentication strength. What happens when the hire signs in with the TAP?

options.text: The TAP satisfies Phishing-resistant MFA, so they get in
The TAP satisfies only the built-in MFA strength, not Phishing-resistant — the policy will not be satisfied by the TAP alone
The TAP bypasses Conditional Access entirely for 24 hours
The TAP satisfies Passwordless strength, but not Phishing-resistant

explanation: Correct: a TAP satisfies only the built-in MFA strength. It does not satisfy Passwordless or Phishing-resistant MFA strengths. So a policy requiring Phishing-resistant MFA will not be satisfied by a TAP sign-in alone — the user must complete a phishing-resistant method. The first and fourth options overstate TAP. The third is wrong — TAP does not bypass Conditional Access.

prompt: You have a new policy: require compliant device for all users accessing SharePoint Online. You have never tested it. What is the correct rollout order?

options.text: Enable the policy immediately, then check the sign-in logs tomorrow for lockouts

Put the policy in report-only mode, review Report-only: Success / Failure in the sign-in logs, use What If to simulate specific users/devices, then enable it — excluding break-glass accounts throughout
Use What If first, then enable the policy, then put it in report-only mode to confirm it works
Enable the policy in report-only mode for break-glass accounts only, and enforce it for everyone else at once

explanation: Correct order: report-only first, read Report-only: Success / Failure in sign-in logs, simulate with What If, then enable — with break-glass accounts excluded throughout. Enabling untested enforcement risks lockout. Reversing report-only and enable is backwards. And the exclusion is inverted in the fourth option — break-glass must be excluded from enforcement, not the only ones in report-only.

prompt: Your tenant has two emergency-access accounts. They are cloud-only Global Administrators with long random passwords stored offline and a phishing-resistant method registered. A new Conditional Access policy targets All users and All cloud apps and requires MFA. What must you do about the break-glass accounts?

options.text: Include them — MFA is required for everyone, with no exceptions, by Microsoft policy
Exclude them from every Conditional Access policy, and monitor their sign-ins; they must stay permanently active Global Administrators
Include them, but give them a 90-day exclusion that renews automatically
Delete them — Conditional Access replaces the need for break-glass accounts

explanation: Correct: break-glass accounts must be excluded from every Conditional Access policy, stay permanently active Global Administrators, be cloud-only, and be monitored. Including them risks locking yourself out of the tenant if Conditional Access or MFA fails. The other options all break that rule.

prompt: A user signs in from an unmanaged personal laptop and gets access to Exchange Online. You want to prevent them downloading, printing, or copying sensitive documents in that session, without blocking the sign-in outright. Which control does this?

options.text: A grant control: Require compliant device
A session control: Conditional Access App Control / app-enforced restrictions, applied after access is granted
A Conditional Access condition: block legacy authentication
A PIM activation requirement: require approval before the session starts

explanation: Correct: session controls shape the session after access is granted — Conditional Access App Control and app-enforced restrictions can block download, cut, copy, and print in web sessions. Grant controls decide whether access is granted at all. Blocking legacy authentication is a condition, not a session control. PIM activation is not a session control.

prompt: An attacker steals a session token from a user's laptop and tries to replay it from another machine. You have enabled 'Require token protection for sign-in sessions.' What should happen, and what licence is needed?

options.text: The token works on the other machine — token protection only logs the replay
The token is cryptographically bound to the original device, so replay from another machine is rejected; token protection requires Entra ID P1
The token is rejected only if the attacker is in a different country; same-country replay still works
Token protection requires Entra ID P2 and only applies to guest users

explanation: Correct: token protection cryptographically binds the sign-in token to the device, so replay from another machine is rejected, and as a Conditional Access session control it sits under Conditional Access, which requires Entra ID P1. The first option understates it — it enforces, not just logs. The third invents a geography rule. The fourth gets the licence and scope wrong.

prompt: Identity Protection flags two things: (1) a sign-in from an anonymous IP with impossible travel, (2) a user whose credentials were found in a leak. Which is sign-in risk and which is user risk, and what licence do you need to use either in Conditional Access?

options.text: (1) is user risk, (2) is sign-in risk; both need only P1
(1) is sign-in risk (this specific sign-in looks wrong), (2) is user risk (the account itself is likely compromised); using either in Conditional Access requires P2 / Identity Protection
Both are sign-in risk; user risk does not exist in Identity Protection
Both are user risk; sign-in risk is only for guest users

explanation: Correct: sign-in risk is about this sign-in (anonymous IP, impossible travel, malware-linked IP). User risk is about the account (leaked credentials, atypical behaviour over time). Both come from Identity Protection, and using either as a Conditional Access condition requires P2. The first option swaps the definitions and the licence. The other two deny one of the two risk types.

prompt: Your tenant still has the legacy MFA and SSPR policies enabled, and you now configure the Authentication methods policy to enable passkeys for a pilot group. What is the risk Microsoft warns about?

options.text: None — the legacy policies and the Authentication methods policy always agree

The policies can conflict — the migration guidance is to move to the Authentication methods policy as the single place to manage methods, and to retire the legacy MFA/SSPR controls, otherwise a method can be enabled in one place and blocked in another
The Authentication methods policy only applies to guests, so the pilot group will see no change
Passkeys cannot be enabled in the Authentication methods policy at all — they need a Conditional Access policy

explanation: Correct: the migration path is to use the Authentication methods policy as the single control for methods and to retire the legacy MFA and SSPR policies. Running both can leave a method enabled in one place and blocked in another, or vice versa. The first option assumes agreement. The other two misstate what the Authentication methods policy does.

prompt: A legacy line-of-business app uses IMAP with basic authentication. You have a Conditional Access policy requiring MFA for all users on all cloud apps. Why does the app still sign in without MFA?

options.text: Conditional Access does not apply to IMAP at all — it is out of scope

Legacy protocols such as IMAP / POP / SMTP AUTH bypass modern authentication and Conditional Access — you must block legacy authentication explicitly (for example, with a Conditional Access policy targeting legacy auth / Exchange Online, and by disabling basic auth), not rely on the MFA policy alone
The app is using a managed identity, which is exempt from Conditional Access
MFA policies only apply to interactive sign-ins from browsers, not to any app

explanation: Correct: legacy protocols (IMAP, POP, SMTP AUTH) use basic authentication and bypass modern authentication and Conditional Access MFA checks. You must block legacy authentication explicitly — for example, with a Conditional Access policy that blocks legacy auth, and by disabling basic auth for the protocols. Relying on an MFA policy alone does not stop a legacy client that never performs modern auth. The first option is too broad — Conditional Access can target legacy auth as a condition. The third confuses managed identities with legacy clients. The fourth is wrong — MFA policies apply to many interactive and non-interactive sign-ins, but legacy auth is the bypass.

prompt: An admin requires the Phishing-resistant MFA authentication strength for the finance portal. All finance users sign in with Microsoft Authenticator phone sign-in and assume they comply. What does the strength matrix actually say?

options.text: Both strengths accept Authenticator phone sign-in, so the policy is satisfied either way
Phone sign-in satisfies Phishing-resistant MFA but not Passwordless MFA
Phone sign-in satisfies Passwordless MFA but not Phishing-resistant MFA — the admin policy will fail until users register a FIDO2 key, Windows Hello, or multifactor CBA
Phone sign-in satisfies neither strength and can never satisfy a Conditional Access grant

explanation: Correct: Microsoft Authenticator phone sign-in satisfies the Passwordless MFA strength but is absent from the Phishing-resistant MFA strength, which accepts only FIDO2 security keys, Windows Hello for Business or platform credentials, and multifactor certificate-based authentication. The admin who configured phone sign-in believed it was phishing-resistant; it is passwordless, not phishing-resistant. The other options misread the strength matrix.

prompt: Two users access a resource protected by the built-in MFA authentication strength. One signs in with single-factor certificate-based authentication, the other with SMS sign-in. What happens?

options.text: Neither method satisfies any built-in authentication strength, so the policy will block both users
Single-factor CBA satisfies the MFA strength, but SMS satisfies none
SMS sign-in satisfies the MFA strength, but single-factor CBA satisfies none
Both satisfy the MFA strength, but neither satisfies Passwordless MFA

explanation: Correct: single-factor CBA and SMS sign-in satisfy no built-in strength at all — the strengths table leaves both blank across MFA, Passwordless, and Phishing-resistant. A policy requiring even the weakest built-in MFA strength will not be satisfied by either method alone. The other options invent partial credit that the matrix does not give.

prompt: A Conditional Access policy requires an authentication strength that includes Windows Hello for Business. A user signs in with a password as the primary method. What happens next?

options.text: Entra automatically re-prompts for Windows Hello for Business mid-session
The password sign-in is upgraded to phishing-resistant automatically
The policy is skipped because the user already authenticated
The user must restart the session, select Sign-in options, and select Windows Hello for Business — they are not prompted for it after a password sign-in

explanation: Correct: if a user signs in with another method (like a password) as the primary method and the strength requires Windows Hello for Business, the user is not prompted to sign in with Windows Hello — they must restart the session, select Sign-in options, and select the required method. The strength does not silently upgrade the session, does not auto-prompt, and does not fail the whole tenant.

prompt: A resource requires a passkey (FIDO2) authentication strength plus a 1-hour sign-in frequency. A user signed in with a passkey 24 hours ago, then unlocks their Windows device with Windows Hello for Business today and opens the resource. What happens?

options.text: Both requirements must be satisfied in the same sign-in, so access is denied
The user can access the resource: the passkey sign-in from yesterday satisfies the strength and today's device unlock satisfies the sign-in frequency
The sign-in frequency requirement overrides and cancels the authentication strength
The authentication strength requirement overrides and cancels the sign-in frequency

explanation: Correct: when a resource requires an authentication strength and a sign-in frequency, users can satisfy both requirements at two different times — yesterday's passkey sign-in satisfies the strength and today's device unlock satisfies the frequency. The requirements are not re-checked together at one moment, and neither requirement is waived.

prompt: During a credential-stuffing flood against the sign-in endpoint, a manager asks whether the Conditional Access MFA policy will act as the organisation's frontline defence against the denial-of-service volume. What is the correct answer?

options.text: Conditional Access runs before first-factor authentication, so it stops the flood at the edge
Conditional Access blocks the flood only if the policy targets All users and All cloud apps
Conditional Access is enforced after first-factor authentication and is not intended as a frontline defence for denial-of-service scenarios
Conditional Access automatically switches to block mode for all sign-ins during a denial-of-service attack

explanation: Correct: Conditional Access is enforced after first-factor authentication and is not intended as a frontline defence against denial-of-service attacks. The policy still uses signals from such events, but the team cannot present CA as the DoS control — that needs network and service-level protections. The other options misstate when CA runs or invent a pre-authentication enforcement point.

prompt: You create a Conditional Access policy scoped to User Actions to require MFA for security info registration, and put it in report-only mode to test it. A week later there is no report-only data at all. Why?

options.text: The registration policy cannot be evaluated in report-only mode, because report-only excludes the User Actions scope
The registration policy can be tested in report-only mode exactly like any other policy
Report-only works for User Actions policies only if the tenant has P2 licences
The policy must be created in report-only mode, then converted to audit mode for User Actions

explanation: Correct: administrators can evaluate Conditional Access policies in report-only mode, except for items included in the User Actions scope — report-only does not evaluate those, so no report-only data is produced for the registration policy. The policy can still be enforced, but it cannot be tested in report-only first. The other options invent report-only coverage or a licence workaround.

prompt: A new Conditional Access policy requiring a compliant device sits in report-only mode. Mac, iPhone, and Android users start getting repeated prompts to select a device certificate at sign-in, even though nothing is blocked. What is happening?

options.text: The policy was accidentally switched to On, so enforcement prompts are expected
The prompts mean the devices are non-compliant and must be wiped before they can sign in
The prompts only affect Windows devices, so the mobile users can be ignored

A report-only policy requiring a compliant device can still prompt macOS, iOS, and Android users to select a device certificate — exclude those platforms from the report-only policy to stop the prompts

explanation: Correct: policies in report-only mode that require a compliant device can prompt users on macOS, iOS, and Android to select a device certificate during evaluation, even though compliance is not enforced, and the prompts can repeat until the device is compliant. The fix is to exclude those device platforms from the report-only policy. The prompts are not a bug in enforcement, not a sign the policy is on, and not limited to Windows.

prompt: In the sign-in logs, a policy in report-only mode shows 'Report-only: Failure' for a user on an unmanaged device accessing SharePoint, where the policy requires a compliant device. What does this result mean for go-live?

options.text: Report-only: Success — the sign-in would have been allowed
Report-only: Failure — the conditions matched but the required grant or session controls were not satisfied, so enforcement would have blocked it
Report-only: Not applied — the user was excluded from the policy
Report-only: User action required — the user would have been prompted, so the policy cannot block

explanation: Correct: a Report-only: Failure result means all configured policy conditions were satisfied but not all required grant or session controls were satisfied — for example, a block control is configured or a device fails a compliant device policy. It is the signal that enforcement would have blocked the sign-in. Success means the controls were satisfied; Not applied means the conditions were not met; User action required means the user would have been prompted.

prompt: Before enforcing a new policy that requires compliant devices for Exchange Online, you want to check whether it would block a specific executive travelling with a personal iPad. Which tool simulates that sign-in?

options.text: Use What If on the Conditional Access Policies page to simulate that user, application, and device against the policies before enforcing
Enable the policy first, then use What If to roll it back if it blocks the executive
Read the Conditional Access insights workbook — What If only works after a policy has been enforced for 30 days
What If requires P2 licences and cannot simulate device state, so use the sign-in logs instead

explanation: Correct: the Policies page offers options to filter, view 'What if' scenarios, and create new policies — What If simulates a user, app, device, and location against the tenant's policies before enforcement. It is a simulation, not an enforcement switch, not a log, and not a report-only replacement; the results must still be confirmed with report-only data and sign-in logs.

prompt: A location-based Conditional Access policy blocks sign-ins from outside the country. The two break-glass accounts sign in from abroad during a test and are not blocked. An auditor flags this as a policy failure. What is the correct response?

options.text: Delete the break-glass exclusion — emergency accounts must obey the same location policy as everyone else
Recreate the break-glass accounts as federated users so the location policy applies to them
Nothing is wrong: the break-glass accounts are correctly excluded from the location block, and their sign-ins are monitored — the exclusion is the design
Convert the location policy to report-only so the break-glass sign-ins are blocked on the next attempt

explanation: Correct: the break-glass accounts are excluded from all Conditional Access, so the location block never touches them, and their sign-ins are monitored — the audit trail is the detection, not the block. A report-only location policy would not block anyone. Recreating the accounts or deleting the policy would destroy the emergency path; the exclusion is the design, not the flaw.

prompt: Your identity provider federation goes down and no administrator can sign in. The post-incident review finds the break-glass accounts were synchronised from on-premises Active Directory. What should they have been?

options.text: Make them federated accounts so they follow the same password policy as everyone else
Create them as cloud-only accounts using the .onmicrosoft.com domain, not federated or synchronised from on-premises
Synchronise them from on-premises Active Directory so their passwords rotate with the domain
Give them a personal employee mailbox so the credentials can be recovered by email

explanation: Correct: the accounts must be cloud-only using the .onmicrosoft.com domain, not federated or synchronised from on-premises, so that a federation or sync outage cannot take them down with everything else. The other options all reintroduce the dependency the break-glass account exists to survive.

prompt: Your normal administrators use Microsoft Authenticator for MFA. What authentication method should the two emergency-access accounts use, and why?

options.text: Register a FIDO2 security key for the emergency accounts, different from the Authenticator method the normal admins use
Register the same Authenticator method on the same phone the normal admins use, for consistency
Register SMS codes, because text messages work even when the Authenticator app is unavailable
Register no method at all, because emergency accounts are exempt from MFA by design

explanation: Correct: break-glass accounts must use a phishing-resistant method that is different from the normal admin accounts — if normal admins use Authenticator, the emergency accounts should use a FIDO2 key — so a compromise or outage affecting one method does not take out the other. Using the same method, SMS, or no method at all all defeat the purpose.

prompt: A tenant has no active Global Administrators — every admin role is eligible in PIM and requires approval, but the only approvers left the company. No administrator can activate any role. What has happened?

options.text: The Conditional Access policy has a corrupted assignment and must be deleted and recreated
The tenant needs a P2 licence before any admin can activate a role
An attacker has locked the tenant by enabling approval on all admin roles

All Global Administrator and Privileged Role Administrator assignments are eligible with approval required and no approvers available, so no one can approve activation — the tenant is effectively locked and only a break-glass account can recover it

explanation: Correct: when all Global Administrator and Privileged Role Administrator assignments are eligible, activation requires approval, and no approvers are selected (or all selected approvers were removed), no one can approve activation and tenant administration is effectively locked — which is exactly the scenario emergency access accounts exist for. The fix is a permanently active break-glass account excluded from the policy. The other options misdiagnose the lockout.

prompt: Your two break-glass accounts were created two years ago and have never been tested. The CISO asks how often they must be validated and what monitoring is required. What is the correct answer?

options.text: Validate them once a year during the annual audit; quarterly testing is excessive
Validate account functionality at least every 90 days, test sign-in, and monitor all sign-in and audit activity with alerts
Never test them — testing an emergency account consumes its one permitted sign-in
Rotate the password annually and assume the accounts work; monitoring is optional

explanation: Correct: emergency accounts must be validated regularly — Microsoft recommends at least every 90 days — including testing sign-in and administrative functionality, and every use must be monitored with alerts. Annual validation, trusting the accounts blindly, or rotating the password only are all insufficient.

prompt: An attacker steals a Primary Refresh Token from a registered Windows laptop and replays it from an unregistered machine in another country. Token protection is enforced. What stops the replay?

options.text: It forces a password reset on every sign-in from a new device
It adds a second MFA prompt whenever a token is presented twice
It binds the Primary Refresh Token cryptographically to the registered device, so a stolen token cannot be replayed from another device
It encrypts the token at rest on the user's laptop so it cannot be copied

explanation: Correct: when a user registers a supported device, a PRT is issued and cryptographically bound to that device, so even if a threat actor steals the token it cannot be used from another device. Token protection validates that only bound tokens are used. It is not a password reset, not a geo-check, and not a log-only control.

prompt: You plan to enforce token protection tenant-wide. Which resources and clients does it actually cover today?

options.text: Native applications on Exchange Online, SharePoint Online, and Microsoft Teams; browser-based enforcement is preview and limited to selected web apps accessing Azure Resource Manager
All browsers on all platforms, including Android and iOS web apps
Only third-party SaaS apps; Microsoft 365 apps are exempt from token protection
Only Azure Virtual Desktop; Exchange, SharePoint, and Teams are not supported resources

explanation: Correct: for native applications, token protection can be enforced on Exchange Online, SharePoint Online, and Microsoft Teams (plus Windows 365 and Azure Virtual Desktop on Windows). Browser-based enforcement is still preview, limited to selected web apps accessing Azure Resource Manager, and iOS browser apps are not supported. The other options overstate browser or Android coverage.

prompt: You are rolling out token protection. What deployment sequence does Microsoft recommend to avoid locking users out of incompatible apps?

options.text: Enforce it tenant-wide immediately; token protection is compatible with every client by design
Enforce it for admins only and skip report-only, since admins are the only token-theft targets
Collect one day of sign-in logs, then enforce for everyone
Start with a pilot group, run the policy in report-only mode, capture interactive and non-interactive sign-in logs, and analyse them long enough to cover normal application use before enforcing

explanation: Correct: the deployment guidance is to start with a pilot group, create the policy in report-only mode before enforcing, capture interactive and non-interactive sign-in logs, and analyse them long enough to cover normal application use. Enforcing tenant-wide on day one, skipping the pilot, or relying on a single day of logs all risk mass disruption from incompatible clients.

prompt: Your compliance team wants finance users re-authenticated every 8 hours when accessing SharePoint Online, without signing them out of every other app. Which session control does this, and how does it work?

options.text: It forces reauthentication on every single action inside the app
It specifies how long a user can stay signed in before being prompted again, and works with OAuth 2.0 and OIDC apps
It only applies to legacy authentication protocols such as IMAP and POP
It replaces token protection, so enabling one disables the other

explanation: Correct: sign-in frequency specifies how long a user can stay signed in before being prompted again, and it works with apps that use OAuth 2.0 or OIDC — most Microsoft native apps and web apps follow it. It does not re-authenticate the user on every action, does not apply to legacy protocol sign-ins in the same way, and does not replace token protection.

prompt: A user opens SharePoint Online from an unmanaged personal device and can view documents but cannot download them. A colleague on a compliant corporate laptop can download freely. Which control produces this difference?

options.text: The cloud app receives device information from Entra and gives a limited experience on unmanaged or non-compliant devices, and a full experience on managed or compliant ones
The device is blocked from the app entirely until Intune marks it compliant
A local agent is installed on the device to block downloads at the operating system level
The session is limited only for guest users; members always get the full experience

explanation: Correct: application enforced restrictions require Entra to pass device information to the selected cloud apps, and the cloud app then provides a limited experience if the device is not managed or compliant, and a full experience if it is. It is not a block, not a download agent, and not a device-compliance grant — the app itself limits the session based on the device signal.

prompt: You want to block downloads from a sanctioned SaaS app in real time, inside the browser session, for users on unmanaged devices. Which architecture enforces Conditional Access App Control?

options.text: It is a grant control that blocks the sign-in before any session starts
It is enforced only through Microsoft Purview DLP policies in Edge
It uses a reverse proxy architecture integrated with Conditional Access and is enforced with Defender for Cloud Apps access and session policies
It requires an agent installed on every user device and works offline

explanation: Correct: Conditional Access App Control uses a reverse proxy architecture integrated with Conditional Access and is enforced through Defender for Cloud Apps access and session policies, which monitor and control sessions in real time. It is not a CA grant control, not a Purview-only feature, and not an endpoint agent — the proxy is what inspects the session.

prompt: An app team asks you to disable continuous access evaluation for their service because it drops sessions too aggressively. What are the constraints on disabling it?

options.text: Disable it on a policy scoped to Exchange Online only
Disable it only when All resources are selected, no conditions are selected, and Disable is chosen under Session > Customize continuous access evaluation
Disable it on a policy with a trusted-location condition, so only office users lose continuous evaluation
Disable it for a single named user while keeping it enabled for everyone else

explanation: Correct: disabling continuous access evaluation works only when All resources are selected, no conditions are selected, and Disable is selected under Session > Customize continuous access evaluation. Scoping it to one app, adding a location condition, or applying it to a single user all violate the constraints, so the setting will not take effect as intended.

prompt: Your tenant disabled resilience defaults. During a Microsoft Entra outage, users whose sessions expire are denied access instead of being allowed to continue. Why?

options.text: Existing sessions are extended indefinitely until the outage ends
Only guest sessions are affected; member sessions continue normally
Sessions are converted to report-only mode so users keep access without enforcement
Access is denied when existing sessions expire, because the resilience default that extends access during an outage has been disabled

explanation: Correct: during an outage, Entra extends access to existing sessions while enforcing Conditional Access policies; if resilience defaults are disabled, access is denied when existing sessions expire. Disabling resilience defaults does not extend sessions, does not only affect guests, and does not convert sessions to report-only.

prompt: Identity Protection flags two users: one signed in from an anonymous IP with impossible travel, another whose credentials appeared in a public leak. Your risk-based Conditional Access policy must treat them differently. How?

options.text: The leaked-credentials user carries user risk and should be forced through a secure password reset, which remediates the risk; the anonymous-IP sign-in carries sign-in risk and can be challenged with strong authentication
Both users carry sign-in risk and both should simply be blocked by IP
Both users carry user risk and both must have their accounts deleted
The anonymous-IP user carries user risk and the leaked-credentials user carries sign-in risk

explanation: Correct: sign-in risk is the risk of the specific sign-in (anonymous IP, impossible travel), and user risk is the risk that the account itself is compromised (leaked credentials). A risk-based policy can require a secure password reset based on the detected risk level, and completing it remediates the risk automatically. Blocking the IP alone or resetting only the sign-in risk user misses the account-level compromise.

prompt: Your tenant has Entra ID P1 only. You build a Conditional Access policy that blocks sign-ins at medium or higher sign-in risk. Will it work?

options.text: Yes — risk-based policies are included in P1, so the policy will work as written
Yes — risk policies work on any licence once Conditional Access is enabled
No — risk policies require Microsoft Entra ID P2 licences; on P1 the risk condition is not available
No — risk policies require a separate Defender for Identity licence and P2 is irrelevant

explanation: Correct: ID Protection requires P2 licences, and the risk-policy capability (sign-in and user risk policies via ID Protection or Conditional Access) is available only on P2 / Entra Suite — not on Free or P1. A P1 tenant can use Conditional Access, but cannot use risk as a condition. Buying more P1 licences or enabling security defaults does not unlock risk-based policies.

prompt: A new hire's Temporary Access Pass expires before they register their passkey. The help desk wants to issue a fresh one. What is the correct action?

options.text: Create a second TAP for the same user so they have a backup, and keep the first one active
Create a new TAP, which overrides the existing valid TAP — each user can only have one TAP
Extend the existing TAP by 30 days from the user blade without creating a new one
Email the original TAP value again from the audit log, since TAP values are stored retrievably

explanation: Correct: a TAP is a time-limited passcode configurable for single use or multiple sign-ins, used to onboard other passwordless methods, and each user can only have one TAP — creating a new one overrides the existing pass. It is not a permanent password replacement, it cannot be shared across users, and it does not auto-extend.

prompt: An admin creates a Temporary Access Pass for a contractor, clicks OK without writing the code down, and now cannot find the value anywhere. What must they do?

options.text: Reopen the user's Authentication methods blade — the TAP value is shown there permanently
