explanation: Correct: once activated, the user can use the role for a preconfigured period before they need to activate again — the activation expires on its own and the user must re-activate. It does not stay active until sign-out, does not require re-approval to expire, and does not convert to permanent.

prompt: An auditor asks for proof of every Global Administrator activation in the last 90 days, including who approved each one. Where does that evidence come from in PIM?

options.text: Only denied activations are logged; approved ones are not recorded
Activations are logged only if the tenant has Microsoft Sentinel connected
The audit history is available only to Microsoft support on request
Every activation is recorded and the audit history can be downloaded for internal or external audit

explanation: Correct: the audit history is a PIM feature — you can download the audit history for internal or external audit, and every activation is recorded. PIM does not hide activations, does not only log denials, and does not require a separate SIEM to have a record.

prompt: What can a Privileged Role Administrator do in PIM that an ordinary eligible administrator cannot?

options.text: Enable approval for specific roles, specify approver users or groups, and view request and approval history for all privileged roles
Approve their own role activation without another approver
Delete the tenant's PIM configuration without confirmation
Bypass the MFA requirement on activation for themselves

explanation: Correct: a Privileged Role Administrator can enable approval for specific roles, specify approver users or groups, and view request and approval history for all privileged roles. They cannot approve their own activation, cannot delete the tenant, and cannot bypass MFA on activation.

prompt: A designated approver receives a PIM activation request for the Security Administrator role. What can they do with it?

options.text: The approver can grant the role permanently instead of time-limited
The approver can change the role's maximum activation duration
The approver can view pending approvals, approve or reject requests (single and bulk), and provide justification for the decision
The approver can activate the role on the requester's behalf

explanation: Correct: an approver can view pending approvals, approve or reject requests for role elevation (single and bulk), and provide justification for the approval or rejection. Approvers cannot grant the role permanently, cannot change the role settings, and cannot activate the role for the requester.

prompt: A board member asks what 'just-in-time access' actually means in PIM, in one sentence. Which definition is correct?

options.text: Permanent access that is logged more carefully
Access granted only after two approvers sign off, with no expiry
Access that is always active but hidden from the directory
Temporary permissions granted only when needed, expiring automatically so they cannot be used afterwards

explanation: Correct: just-in-time access is the model where users receive temporary permissions to perform privileged tasks, which prevents malicious or unauthorised users from gaining access after the permissions expire — access is granted only when needed. It is not permanent access with logging, not a synonym for approval, and not limited to groups.

prompt: A manager proposes giving every IT staff member Global Administrator 'to keep things simple'. Which principle does PIM's least-privilege model contradict, and what does it require instead?

options.text: Every user gets only the minimum privileges needed for the tasks they are authorised to perform, minimising Global Administrators in favour of specific roles
Every administrator gets Global Administrator so no task is ever blocked
Least privilege means access expires after 8 hours regardless of the task
Least privilege means no user may hold more than one role at a time

explanation: Correct: least privilege means every user is provided with only the minimum privileges needed to accomplish the tasks they are authorised to perform, minimising the number of Global Administrators and using specific roles instead. It is not about giving everyone the same role, not about time limits alone, and not about removing all admin roles.

prompt: What can an eligible role user do in PIM for themselves?

options.text: Approve their own activation request
Change the role's activation settings
Request activation of a role that requires approval, view the status of the request, and complete the task if activation was approved
View and approve other users' activation requests

explanation: Correct: an eligible role user can request activation of a role that requires approval, view the status of the request, and complete the task if activation was approved. They cannot approve their own request, cannot change the role settings, and cannot see other users' pending requests.

prompt: A role-assignable group has eligible members and an eligible owner. The owner needs to approve a membership change that only owners can make. What must the owner do first?

options.text: Only members can be eligible; owners are always permanent
Owners cannot activate anything — only members can
Ownership is inherited automatically by every member who activates
Both member and owner assignments can be eligible and activated just-in-time

explanation: Correct: the owner activates the owner assignment and the member activates the member assignment — PIM for Groups covers both membership and ownership as eligible assignments. Ownership is not automatically permanent, not shared with all members, and not excluded from PIM for Groups.

prompt: A delegated approver approves a pending request for the Contributor role on a resource group. What happens next for the requester?

options.text: After the request is approved, the member can start using the role
The member must activate a second time after approval before the role works
The member must wait for a second approver even when only one is configured
The approval expires immediately, so the member must request again within one minute

explanation: Correct: after the request is approved, the member can start using the role — approval is the gate, and the delegated approver's decision is what unlocks it. The member does not wait for a second approval, does not need to re-activate, and the approval does not expire instantly.

prompt: A Global Administrator activates their role at 3 a.m. without telling anyone. How does the Security team find out?

options.text: Nothing is recorded — PIM activations are private to the user
Only the approver is notified, and no record is kept
PIM sends notifications when privileged roles are activated and records every activation in the audit history
The activation is recorded only if the admin also files a change ticket

explanation: Correct: PIM sends notifications when privileged roles are activated, and the audit history records every activation — the Security team can review who activated what and when, and whether approval and MFA were satisfied. There is no silent activation path in PIM, and the admin cannot suppress the audit trail.

prompt: An auditor reviewing PIM activations asks why every activation carries a justification field. What is its purpose?

options.text: Justification is optional decoration that PIM discards after activation
Justification replaces approval — a good reason means no approver is needed
Justification is visible only to the user who entered it
Justification records the business reason for the activation and can be required by the role settings, so reviewers can understand why the role was used

explanation: Correct: use justification to understand why users activate — justification is a PIM feature that records the business reason for each activation, and it can be required by the role settings. It is not a free-text note that is discarded, not a replacement for approval, and not visible only to the user.

prompt: An on-call team of six engineers shares a security group. They need the Security Reader role just-in-time during incidents, without six separate permanent assignments. How can PIM handle this?

options.text: Assign the role to the group as eligible in PIM, so members of the group activate the role just-in-time when on call
Assign the role permanently to every member of the group individually
Make the group the approver for its own role activations
Delete the group and assign the role to a service principal instead

explanation: Correct: PIM can manage role assignments for a group — a group can be made eligible for a role, and members activate the role through the group — which is how you give a whole on-call team just-in-time access without assigning each person individually. The group itself is not the approver, the role is not automatically active for all members, and the group does not need to be deleted.

prompt: You invite a colleague's personal Outlook account to your tenant, getwings.co, to collaborate. What user type is created, and what happens next?

options.text: An internal member user with a getwings.co address; no invitation is needed
A guest user (B2B); the person receives an invitation email and accepts it to join the tenant
A service principal; it can sign in but cannot be assigned roles
A managed identity; Azure manages its credentials automatically

explanation: Correct: inviting an external user creates a guest (B2B) user, not an internal member. The person gets an invitation email, accepts it, and joins the tenant as a guest. The first option describes creating an internal user. The other two confuse user types with service principals and managed identities.

prompt: You assign Directory Reader to the new guest user. What can that user do in the Entra admin centre?

options.text: Read basic directory information, but not create users or edit user properties
Create new internal users and invite external users
Reset any user's password, including Global Administrators
Assign roles to other users

explanation: Correct: Directory Reader is read-only for basic directory information. The guest can see properties in the Entra admin centre but cannot create users or edit properties. The other options all require a more privileged role such as User Administrator.

prompt: You need a user to create users and edit user properties, but not to manage Azure subscriptions. Which Entra role fits, and where is it assigned?

options.text: Azure Owner at subscription scope
User Administrator in Microsoft Entra ID
Storage Account Contributor at resource-group scope
Global Reader in Microsoft 365

explanation: Correct: User Administrator is an Entra role for managing users in the directory — creating users, editing properties, resetting passwords. It does not grant Azure subscription access. Azure Owner is an Azure role, Storage Account Contributor is an Azure data-plane role, and Global Reader is a read-only Microsoft 365 role.

prompt: A user has the Entra role User Administrator. They switch to the Azure portal in the same tenant and see no subscriptions or resources. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: The user is signed in to the wrong tenant
Entra roles do not grant Azure resource access — Azure RBAC is separate, and the user has no Azure role (for example, Reader) on the subscription
User Administrator automatically includes Azure Owner, so the portal must be broken
The user needs a Conditional Access policy before Azure resources appear

explanation: Correct: this is the core Azure RBAC versus Entra RBAC distinction. An Entra role governs the directory and Microsoft 365. It does not give Azure Resource Manager permissions. Seeing no subscriptions in the Azure portal is the expected symptom of having no Azure role on that subscription — the fix is an Azure Reader assignment on the subscription. Signing in to the wrong tenant is possible in general, but the point here is the role-scope gap, and the user can see the tenant. User Administrator does not include Azure Owner. A Conditional Access policy does not grant authorisation.

prompt: You assign Reader on a pay-as-you-go subscription to a guest user, as an active, permanent assignment. What can that user do?

options.text: View all resources in the subscription, but not make changes
Create and delete storage accounts in the subscription
Assign roles to other users in the subscription
Upload blobs to any storage account in the subscription

explanation: Correct: Reader lets a user view all resources but not make changes. Creating and deleting storage accounts, assigning roles, and uploading blobs all require write or role-management permissions (Contributor, Owner, Role Based Access Control Administrator, or a data-plane role).

prompt: A guest user has Reader on a subscription but cannot upload a blob to a storage account. You want them to be able to do it only when needed, with approval. What is the correct PIM approach?

options.text: Give them Storage Account Contributor permanently as an active assignment

Make Storage Account Contributor an eligible assignment on that storage account / resource group, with activation requiring justification and approval; the user activates it in My Roles, the approver approves, and the role moves to Active for a limited time
Give them Global Administrator permanently — it is the only role that can upload blobs
Create a Conditional Access policy requiring MFA; that alone grants upload permission

explanation: Correct: PIM for Azure resources works the same way as PIM for Entra roles: make the role eligible, not standing. The user activates it from My Roles, provides a justification, the approver approves, and the role becomes Active for a limited window — after which the upload succeeds. A permanent active assignment keeps standing privilege, which PIM exists to remove. Global Administrator is excessive and still standing. A Conditional Access grant is not an RBAC permission.

prompt: You need a custom role that can reset passwords for users in the Finance administrative unit only, and a custom role that can manage VMs in one resource group only. Which is possible, and at what scope?

options.text: Both are Azure custom roles — Entra does not support custom roles

Entra custom role scoped to the Finance administrative unit; Azure custom role scoped to that resource group. Entra custom roles can be scoped to tenant, administrative unit, or a single object; Azure custom roles to management group / subscription / resource group / resource
Both must be scoped tenant-wide — custom roles cannot be scoped narrower
Entra custom roles can only be scoped to a resource group; Azure custom roles only to a tenant

explanation: Correct: Entra custom roles can be scoped to the tenant, an administrative unit, or a single object. Azure custom roles can be scoped to management group, subscription, resource group, or resource. The first option denies Entra custom roles. The other two get the scopes backwards or too narrow.

prompt: Defender for Cloud flags a user with Owner at subscription scope who only reads cost reports. What is the least-privilege fix?

options.text: Remove the user entirely — Owner cannot be reduced
Replace Owner with Reader at subscription scope (or a narrower scope), and review the assignment — this is 'Evaluate and remediate overprivileged access assignments by using Azure RBAC'
Make the Owner assignment eligible in PIM, but keep Owner at subscription scope permanently
Move the user to a different subscription — scope does not matter if the role is Owner

explanation: Correct: least privilege is to replace Owner with the smallest role that does the job — Reader at subscription scope, or narrower — and to review and remediate the assignment. That is exactly the skill 'Evaluate and remediate overprivileged access assignments by using Azure RBAC.' Removing the user entirely is excessive. Making the Owner assignment eligible in PIM keeps standing Owner, which eligibility alone does not fix. Moving subscriptions ignores scope — Owner at a narrower scope is still Owner, but scope is the point of right-sizing.

prompt: You need a rule that storage accounts must use private endpoints, applied to a whole management group, and a second rule that virtual machines must have disk encryption, applied with it as one bundle. Which Azure Policy concepts match the single rule and the bundle?

options.text: The single rule is a policy definition and the bundle is an initiative (a collection of policy definitions), both applied through a policy assignment at a scope such as a management group
The single rule is a policy assignment and the bundle is a policy definition
The single rule is a blueprint and the bundle is a resource lock
The single rule is an exemption and the bundle is a remediation task

explanation: Correct: a policy definition is a single rule; an initiative is a collection of policy definitions grouped for a goal such as a compliance standard; a policy assignment applies a definition or initiative at a scope — management group, subscription, resource group, or resource — and is inherited below that scope. An assignment is not the rule itself, an exemption is an exception, and blueprints and locks are different controls.

prompt: You want to roll out a new rule — virtual machines must not have a public IP — but you are not yet sure how many existing deployments it would break. What is the safe first effect to use, and what does it do?

options.text: DeployIfNotExists, which deletes the public IP automatically on existing VMs
Audit, which allows the request to proceed but records the resource as non-compliant so you can measure impact before enforcing
Deny, which blocks the deployment and deletes existing non-compliant VMs
Disabled, which enforces the rule silently without logging

explanation: Correct: Audit allows the request but logs a compliance warning and marks the resource non-compliant, giving visibility without blocking — the standard safe rollout before switching to Deny. Deny blocks matching create/update requests but does not delete existing resources. DeployIfNotExists deploys a missing related resource, it does not delete a public IP. Disabled means the rule is not evaluated at all.

prompt: A production resource group holds a storage account that must never be deleted, but engineers must still be able to update its configuration. A second, archived resource group must not be changed or deleted at all. Which locks fit?

options.text: ReadOnly on both; CanNotDelete still allows deletion by an Owner
ReadOnly on the production group and CanNotDelete on the archived group
CanNotDelete on the production group and ReadOnly on the archived group
CanNotDelete on both; ReadOnly and CanNotDelete do the same thing

explanation: Correct: CanNotDelete lets authorised users read and modify a resource but not delete it — right for production. ReadOnly lets users read but not delete or update, similar to restricting everyone to Reader permissions — right for the archive. The swapped answer would block production updates and allow archive changes. The two locks are not equivalent, and CanNotDelete does block deletion.

prompt: You assign a Deny policy that blocks storage accounts without private endpoints. A week later, 40 existing storage accounts still have public endpoints and are marked non-compliant. An engineer says the Deny policy will fix them automatically at the next evaluation cycle, about 24 hours later. Is that right, and what actually fixes them?

options.text: Yes — Deny remediates existing resources on the next compliance evaluation

No — Deny only blocks future create and update requests; existing non-compliant resources stay non-compliant until a remediation task runs, and only modify or deployIfNotExists policies support remediation tasks that change existing resources
No — Deny deletes the existing storage accounts at the next evaluation
Yes, but only if the policy is assigned at management group scope; at subscription scope Deny cannot remediate

explanation: Correct: Deny affects future requests — it rejects matching creates/updates and marks existing matches non-compliant, but it does not change them. Compliance evaluation alone never corrects existing resources; only a remediation task, for a modify or deployIfNotExists policy, changes what is already deployed. Deny never deletes resources, and scope does not change this behaviour.

prompt: You need a policy that adds a missing 'CostCenter' tag to resources at creation, and a second policy that deploys diagnostic settings where they are missing. Which effects do you use, and what does each assignment need that an audit policy does not?

options.text: Modify for the tag and deployIfNotExists for diagnostics; both need a managed identity on the assignment so the change or deployment can be performed, while audit needs no identity
Append for the tag and auditIfNotExists for diagnostics; neither needs anything extra
Audit for both; a remediation task supplies the managed identity automatically
Deny for the tag and modify for diagnostics; only Deny needs a managed identity

explanation: Correct: Modify adds, replaces, or removes tags and properties on create/update, and deployIfNotExists deploys a template when a related resource is missing — both are the effects that can remediate, and both require a managed identity on the assignment (the deployment or modification uses the assignment's identity). Audit and auditIfNotExists only report and need no identity. Append is the older, narrower option Microsoft recommends replacing with modify for tags, and Deny blocks rather than adding anything.

prompt: A hospital has a legacy VM that cannot meet the 'allowed VM SKUs' policy. The team wants a documented, time-limited exception for that one VM, after which the policy applies again — without changing the assignment for everyone else. A second team wants a whole resource group permanently left out of the policy. Which mechanisms fit each need?

options.text: A remediation task for the VM and a Deny policy for the resource group
Exclusion for the VM and exemption for the resource group — the two terms are interchangeable
Delete the policy assignment for both; exceptions cannot be scoped to a single resource
Exemption for the VM (time-bound, with an expiry date and a reason, scoped to that resource) and an exclusion on the assignment scope for the resource group

explanation: Correct: an exemption is a documented, time-limited exception for specific resources, with an expiry after which compliance evaluation resumes — the governed way to allow one legacy VM temporarily. An exclusion removes a scope (such as a resource group) from the assignment itself. The terms are not interchangeable: exemption is per-resource and expiring, exclusion is a scope carve-out on the assignment. Deleting the assignment removes the control for everyone, and a remediation task fixes resources rather than excepting them.

prompt: A new administrator assumes that assigning an Entra role and assigning an Azure role are two views of the same permission system. What is the correct model?

options.text: They are the same system with two names — a role in one is automatically a role in the other
Entra roles are a subset of Azure roles, stored in the same data store
Azure roles are evaluated by the Entra policy decision point, and Entra roles by Azure Resource Manager
They are separate RBAC systems with different data stores for role definitions and assignments and different policy decision points for access checks

explanation: Correct: Entra roles and Azure roles are separate RBAC systems — different data stores for role definitions and assignments, and different policy decision points for access checks. The other options wrongly merge the two systems or invent a sync that does not exist.

prompt: An architect is mapping which Entra roles can manage which services. How are Entra built-in roles categorised?

options.text: There is only one category — all Entra roles work the same way everywhere
Entra roles are divided into Reader and Writer only
Entra ID-specific roles, service-specific roles, and cross-service roles
Entra roles are divided by licence: P1 roles, P2 roles, and free roles

explanation: Correct: Entra built-in roles fall into three categories — Entra ID-specific roles (User Administrator, Application Administrator, Groups Administrator), service-specific roles (Exchange, Intune, SharePoint, Teams Administrators), and cross-service roles (Global Administrator, Global Reader, Security Administrator, Security Reader). The other options invent categories or deny the structure.

prompt: Which two Entra roles are the global cross-service roles that all Microsoft 365 services honour?

options.text: User Administrator and Helpdesk Administrator
Exchange Administrator and SharePoint Administrator
Security Administrator and Security Reader
Global Administrator and Global Reader

explanation: Correct: Global Administrator and Global Reader are the two global cross-service roles — all Microsoft 365 services honour them. Security Administrator and Security Reader are cross-service security roles, not global ones. User Administrator is Entra ID-specific, and Exchange Administrator is service-specific.

prompt: An auditor asks what an Azure role assignment is made of. Which three elements must it contain?

options.text: User, password, and subscription
Role definition and scope only — the principal is implied
Security principal, role definition, and scope
Security principal, Conditional Access policy, and licence

explanation: Correct: a role assignment consists of three elements — security principal, role definition, and scope. Without all three there is no assignment. The other options omit an element or add one that is not part of the assignment.

prompt: A runbook's managed identity needs Reader on a resource group. A colleague says only users and groups can be security principals. Is that right?

options.text: Only a human user can be a security principal
Only a group can be a security principal
A security principal is the role definition itself
A user, group, service principal, or managed identity requesting access to Azure resources

explanation: Correct: a security principal is a user, group, service principal, or managed identity requesting access — any of these can hold a role assignment. It is not limited to human users, and it is not the role definition or the scope.

prompt: You need to give a team Contributor on one resource group only, not the whole subscription. At how many levels can Azure RBAC scope be set, and which are they?

options.text: Three levels: subscription, resource group, or resource
Two levels: subscription or resource group
Four levels: management group, subscription, resource group, or resource
Five levels: tenant, management group, subscription, resource group, or resource

explanation: Correct: scope can be set at four levels — management group, subscription, resource group, or resource — in a parent-child structure, and roles can be assigned at any level. There is no tenant-wide Azure RBAC scope and no fifth level.

prompt: A user has Contributor at subscription scope and Reader on one resource group in that subscription. What are their effective permissions?

options.text: The Reader assignment overrides Contributor, so the user can only read
The two assignments cancel each other out and the user has no access
The narrower scope wins, so the user can only read inside the resource group
Effective permissions are the sum of the assignments, so the user effectively has Contributor across the subscription and the Reader assignment has no impact

explanation: Correct: Azure RBAC is an additive model — effective permissions are the sum of the assignments, so the Reader assignment adds nothing on top of Contributor at the subscription scope. There is no 'most restrictive wins' rule for overlapping allow assignments, and the narrower assignment does not cancel the broader one.

prompt: A user is a member of Group A. Group A is a member of Group B. Group B has Contributor on a resource group. Does the user have Contributor permissions?

options.text: The user has no permissions — only direct members of the assigned group count
The user has permissions only if they are also directly assigned the role
The user has the permissions, because role assignments are transitive for groups
The user has the permissions only during the first 24 hours after joining the nested group

explanation: Correct: role assignments are transitive for groups — if a user is in a group, and that group is in another group that has the role assignment, the user has the permissions. The other options deny transitivity or invent a direct-membership-only rule.

prompt: A custom role allows Microsoft.Storage/* but lists Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/delete in NotActions. What can a holder of this role do?

options.text: The wildcard grants everything, including the excluded actions — NotActions is only advisory
NotActions only applies to data actions, not management actions
The role grants nothing, because a wildcard and a NotActions entry cancel each other out
Effective permissions are Actions minus NotActions — the wildcard allows everything except the actions listed in NotActions

explanation: Correct: effective permissions are computed as Actions minus NotActions (and DataActions minus NotDataActions) — a wildcard allow with a subtraction for the excluded actions. The other options ignore NotActions, treat wildcards as unlimited, or invent a deny-by-default for data actions.

prompt: A user has Owner on a subscription, but a deny assignment applies to a storage account in that subscription. Can the user delete the storage account?

options.text: The Owner assignment wins, because Owner outranks deny assignments
The deny assignment is only advisory and is logged, not enforced
If a deny assignment applies, access is blocked — deny is evaluated before the allow assignments
The two assignments are summed, so the user keeps half their permissions

explanation: Correct: Azure RBAC checks deny assignments first — if a deny assignment applies, access is blocked, and evaluation does not continue to the allow assignments. A deny assignment is not outranked by Owner, not limited to one scope, and not advisory.

prompt: Finance asks whether the Azure RBAC rollout needs a new licence budget. What is the licensing position?

options.text: Azure RBAC requires Entra ID P1 for every user with a role assignment
Azure RBAC requires Entra ID P2 for every user with a role assignment
Azure RBAC is charged per role assignment per month
Azure RBAC is free and included in the Azure subscription

explanation: Correct: Azure RBAC is free and included in the Azure subscription — there is no per-user RBAC licence. The other options invent a P1/P2 requirement or a per-assignment charge.

prompt: An engineer with Contributor creates a storage account without a private endpoint, and the creation is blocked. They have the RBAC permission to create storage accounts. Which control blocked it, and why?

options.text: Azure Policy controls who can perform an action, and Azure RBAC checks the resulting resource state
Azure Policy and Azure RBAC do the same thing, so only one is needed
Azure Policy evaluates resource state against business rules without concern for who made the change; Azure RBAC focuses on managing user actions at different scopes
Azure Policy only works if the user has no RBAC role at all

explanation: Correct: Azure Policy evaluates resource state against business rules without concern for who made the change or who has permission to make it — that is the Policy versus RBAC distinction. RBAC manages user actions at scopes; Policy ensures the resulting resource state is compliant. The other options assign Policy the RBAC job or vice versa.

prompt: A Reader on a subscription wants to see which Azure Policy assignments apply to their resource group. Can they?

options.text: Policy objects are visible only to Owners
Policy objects are visible only to users with a P2 licence
Policy definitions are hidden from Readers by default
All Policy objects, including definitions, initiatives, and assignments, are readable to all roles over their scope

explanation: Correct: all Policy objects — definitions, initiatives, and assignments — are readable to all roles over their scope, by design, so everyone can see what rules are set. The other options invent a read restriction, a P2 requirement, or a hidden-by-default model.

prompt: A non-compliant storage account was created before a policy was assigned. When will Policy evaluate it?

options.text: Only when a resource is created — never again
Only when an administrator manually triggers an evaluation
At resource creation or update, when a scope gets a new assignment, when an assigned policy is updated, and in the standard 24-hour compliance evaluation cycle
Only once a week, on Sundays

explanation: Correct: Policy evaluates at resource creation or update, when a scope gets a new assignment, when an assigned policy or initiative is updated, and in the standard compliance evaluation cycle every 24 hours. It does not evaluate only at creation, only on demand, or only weekly.

prompt: A deployIfNotExists policy is assigned but its remediation tasks keep failing with authorisation errors. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: No identity is needed — remediation runs with the user's permissions
The assignment needs the Global Administrator role
The assignment needs a managed identity with Reader on the subscription only
The assignment's managed identity needs enough permissions to create or update the targeted resources

explanation: Correct: the managed identity of a deployIfNotExists or modify assignment needs enough permissions to create or update the targeted resources — without them the remediation cannot run. An audit assignment needs no identity, and the identity does not need Owner on everything, nor is the identity optional for these effects.

prompt: Who can create and manage Azure Policy definitions and assignments?

options.text: The Resource Policy Contributor role includes most Azure Policy operations, and Owner has full rights
Any Contributor can create and update policy definitions and assignments
Only Global Administrators can read policy assignments
The Reader role can create policy assignments but not definitions

explanation: Correct: the Resource Policy Contributor role includes most Azure Policy operations, and Owner has full rights; Contributor has read access but cannot create or update definitions and assignments, and Reader has read access only. User Access Administrator is needed to grant the managed identity on deployIfNotExists or modify assignments.

prompt: Your team is designing an Azure Policy hierarchy for 50 subscriptions. What structure does Microsoft recommend?

options.text: Create definitions at the resource level and assign them one resource at a time
Create one assignment per resource and never use initiatives
Create definitions at higher levels such as management group or subscription, assign at the next child level, and use initiative definitions even when starting with a single policy definition
Create definitions only at the tenant level and never assign below it

explanation: Correct: definitions at higher levels such as management group or subscription, with the assignment at the next child level, is the recommended pattern — and initiatives should be used even for a single definition so more can be added later without new assignments. Creating everything at the resource level, or one assignment per resource, is the anti-pattern.

prompt: A storage account has a CanNotDelete lock. An Owner tries to delete it. What happens?

options.text: The Owner can delete the storage account — locks do not apply to Owners
The Global Administrator can override any lock without removing it
The Contributor can delete it if they also hold Reader
No one can delete it while the lock is in place — the lock overrides any user permissions, including Owner

explanation: Correct: a lock overrides any user permissions — even an Owner cannot delete or modify past a lock they do not remove first. The lock applies across all users and roles, unlike RBAC which grants permissions per user. The other options wrongly assume Owner or Global Administrator bypasses locks.

prompt: A storage account has a ReadOnly lock. A user with Storage Blob Data Contributor deletes blobs through the storage data plane. Are the blobs protected by the lock?

options.text: The blobs are protected — a ReadOnly lock blocks all deletions everywhere
The blobs are protected only if the user is not an Owner
Locks only apply to control plane operations, not data plane operations, so blob data can still be deleted through the data plane
The lock protects data only for 24 hours, then expires

explanation: Correct: locks only apply to control plane operations, not data plane operations — a ReadOnly lock on a storage account does not protect blob, queue, table, or file data from deletion through the data plane. The control plane protects the resource itself; the data plane is a separate path. The other options confuse the two planes.

prompt: You apply a ReadOnly lock at the resource-group scope. A week later an engineer creates a new VM in that group. Is the VM locked?

options.text: All resources in the group inherit the lock, including resources added later, and the most restrictive lock in the chain takes precedence
Only resources that existed when the lock was created are locked; new resources are exempt
A lock on a child resource cancels the parent lock for that resource
Locks do not inherit — each resource must be locked individually

explanation: Correct: when a lock is applied at a parent scope, all resources within that scope inherit it — even resources added later — and the most restrictive lock in the inheritance chain takes precedence. A child lock does not cancel a parent lock, and new resources are not exempt.

prompt: A resource group contains a storage account with a Delete (CanNotDelete) lock. An Owner tries to delete the entire resource group. What happens?

options.text: The resource group is deleted except for the locked resource
The locked resource is deleted but the group remains
The deletion succeeds because the lock is on the resource, not the group
The whole delete operation is blocked — a partial deletion is not possible

explanation: Correct: if a Delete lock is on a resource and you attempt to delete its resource group, the feature blocks the whole delete operation — even if the group and other resources are unlocked, a partial deletion is not possible. The lock does not only protect the single resource, and it is not bypassed by deleting the group.

prompt: A Contributor tries to add a CanNotDelete lock to a production resource group and gets an authorisation error. Who can create or delete management locks?

options.text: Any Contributor can create or delete locks
Any Reader can create locks but not delete them
Owner and User Access Administrator have the required access (Microsoft.Authorization/locks/*); a Contributor does not
Only Global Administrators can create or delete locks

explanation: Correct: creating or deleting management locks needs Microsoft.Authorization/* or Microsoft.Authorization/locks/* — Owner and User Access Administrator have it. Contributor does not, Reader does not, and a custom role needs those actions explicitly.

prompt: A resource group has a ReadOnly lock. An engineer tries to start a stopped VM in that group. What happens?

options.text: Starting the VM works — ReadOnly locks only block deletions
Starting the VM works for Owners, who bypass ReadOnly locks
Starting the VM works if the VM is already running, but not if it is stopped
Starting or restarting the VM is blocked, because those operations require a POST request that a ReadOnly lock blocks

explanation: Correct: a ReadOnly lock on a resource group prevents starting or restarting a VM, because those operations require a POST to the Resource Manager API, which the lock blocks. The other options invent exceptions for Owners, for running VMs, or for stop operations.

prompt: A storage account has a ReadOnly lock. A user with Reader tries to list the account keys in the portal. What happens?

options.text: Listing the account keys is blocked, because it is a POST request the ReadOnly lock stops — users without the keys must use Microsoft Entra credentials to access the data
Listing the keys works — ReadOnly locks only block data plane operations
Listing the keys works for Owners, who bypass the lock
The keys are automatically rotated when a ReadOnly lock is applied

explanation: Correct: a ReadOnly lock on a storage account prevents listing the account keys, because List Keys is a POST to the Resource Manager API, and the keys give complete access to the data. Users without the keys must use Entra credentials to access blob or queue data. The lock does not hand out the keys, does not only block Owners, and does not expire.

prompt: Your governance team wants a ReadOnly lock on the top-level management group to freeze the whole hierarchy. Is that possible?

options.text: A management group can be locked with a ReadOnly lock
A management group can be locked with a CanNotDelete lock
You can't add a lock to management groups — locks apply to subscriptions, resource groups, and resources
A management group lock requires a P2 licence, but is otherwise supported

explanation: Correct: locks cannot be added to management groups — the portal and API do not support it. They can be applied to subscriptions, resource groups, and resources. The other options invent a management-group lock capability.

prompt: A junior admin asks how a resource lock differs from simply removing everyone's RBAC roles on the resource. What is the key difference?

options.text: Locks grant permissions to specific users, like RBAC roles do
Locks only apply to guest users, not members
Locks are the same as deny assignments in Azure RBAC
Unlike RBAC, management locks apply a restriction across all users and roles

explanation: Correct: unlike RBAC, management locks apply a restriction across all users and roles — that is the point of a lock versus a permission. RBAC grants per-user permissions; a lock restricts everyone, including Owners, until it is removed. The other options describe RBAC, not locks.

prompt: A virtual machine has a network security group on its subnet that allows inbound RDP, and a network security group on its NIC that denies inbound RDP. A user tries to connect over RDP. What happens?

options.text: The connection succeeds, because the subnet NSG is evaluated first and allows it
The connection is denied, because inbound traffic is evaluated by the subnet NSG first and then the NIC NSG, and the NIC NSG deny blocks it
The connection succeeds, because NIC NSGs are only evaluated for outbound traffic
The connection is denied, because subnet NSGs always override NIC NSGs

explanation: Correct: for inbound traffic, the subnet network security group is evaluated first, then the NIC network security group. The subnet rule allows RDP, but the NIC rule denies it, so the connection is denied. Both NSGs must allow the traffic for it to reach the VM. For outbound traffic the order is reversed: NIC first, then subnet.

prompt: A virtual machine sends outbound traffic to the internet. The NIC network security group allows it, but the subnet network security group denies it. What happens?

options.text: The traffic is allowed, because the NIC NSG is evaluated first and allows it
The traffic is denied, because outbound traffic is evaluated by the NIC NSG first and then the subnet NSG, and the subnet NSG deny blocks it
The traffic is allowed, because subnet NSGs only apply to inbound traffic
The traffic is denied, because NIC NSGs are not evaluated for outbound traffic

explanation: Correct: for outbound traffic, the NIC network security group is evaluated first, then the subnet network security group. The NIC rule allows the traffic, but the subnet rule denies it, so the traffic is blocked. Both NSGs must allow outbound traffic for it to leave the VM.

prompt: A network security group has two rules: priority 100 allows inbound traffic from 203.0.113.0/24 on port 443, and priority 200 denies inbound traffic from 203.0.113.5 on port 443. A client at 203.0.113.5 connects on port 443. What happens?

options.text: The connection is denied, because the deny rule matches the specific client

The connection is allowed, because rules are evaluated in priority order with the lowest number first and the first matching rule wins, so the priority 100 allow rule applies before the priority 200 deny
The connection is denied, because deny rules always take precedence over allow rules
The connection is allowed only if the client uses HTTPS

explanation: Correct: NSG rules are evaluated in priority order, lowest number first, and the first matching rule wins. The priority 100 allow rule matches the client's traffic, so it is applied before the priority 200 deny rule is ever evaluated. Specificity does not override priority; the lowest priority number wins.

prompt: A team removes a network security group rule that was allowing inbound traffic on port 3389. An existing RDP session that was established before the removal is still active. What happens to it?

options.text: The session is terminated immediately, because removing a rule drops existing connections
The session continues, because NSGs are stateful and removing a rule does not affect existing connections
The session is terminated after 5 minutes, because NSGs have a connection timeout
The session continues only if the VM is rebooted

explanation: Correct: network security groups are stateful, and removing a rule does not affect existing connections. An RDP session established before the rule was removed continues until it is closed by the user or the application. The rule change only affects new connections.

prompt: A network security group has only custom rules configured. A VM in the subnet tries to reach another VM in the same virtual network. What happens?

options.text: The traffic is blocked, because no custom rule allows it
The traffic is allowed, because the default rule 65000 AllowVNet permits traffic within the virtual network, and default rules cannot be removed, only overridden by a lower-priority custom rule
The traffic is blocked, because intra-VNet traffic requires an explicit allow rule
The traffic is allowed only if the VMs are in the same subnet

explanation: Correct: every NSG includes default rules that cannot be removed, including rule 65000 AllowVNet, which permits traffic within the virtual network. Custom rules can override the defaults only if they have a lower priority number. Without a custom deny rule, intra-VNet traffic is allowed by the default rule.

prompt: A team wants to block all internet-bound traffic from a subnet, but allow traffic to Azure services. They add a custom deny rule for the Internet service tag at priority 100. What happens to traffic destined for Azure Storage?

options.text: It is blocked, because the Internet service tag includes Azure Storage

It is allowed, because the Internet service tag does not include Azure service traffic, and the default rule 65001 AllowInternet is overridden by the custom deny, but traffic to Azure services uses the AzureCloud service tag rather than Internet
It is blocked, because all outbound traffic is blocked by the custom rule
It is allowed only if a private endpoint is used

explanation: Correct: the Internet service tag represents traffic to the public internet, and it does not include traffic to Azure services, which are covered by service tags such as AzureCloud and Storage. The custom deny for Internet blocks internet-bound traffic but does not block traffic to Azure services, which is evaluated against the relevant service tag rules.

prompt: A network security group rule uses the VirtualNetwork service tag as the source. The team asks what this covers. What is the answer?

options.text: Only the virtual network the NSG is attached to
All virtual networks in the subscription, including peered virtual networks, because the VirtualNetwork service tag represents the virtual network address space including peered VNets
Only the subnet the NSG is attached to
All IP addresses in the Azure region

explanation: Correct: the VirtualNetwork service tag represents the virtual network address space, including the VNet the NSG is attached to and any peered virtual networks. It is broader than a single subnet and narrower than the whole region, and it is the standard way to allow intra-VNet and peered-VNet traffic.

prompt: A team creates an NSG rule with multiple source IP addresses and multiple destination ports in a single rule. They then try to add two service tags and two application security groups to the same rule. What will they find?

options.text: All of these are supported in a single rule
Augmented security rules allow multiple IP addresses and ports in one rule, but a single rule cannot contain multiple service tags or multiple application security groups
Multiple service tags are allowed, but multiple ASGs are not
Multiple ASGs are allowed, but multiple service tags are not

explanation: Correct: augmented security rules allow multiple source or destination IP addresses and multiple ports in a single rule, but a single rule cannot contain multiple service tags or multiple application security groups. The team must create separate rules if they need to reference multiple service tags or ASGs.

prompt: A team uses application security groups to group VMs by role, and attaches an ASG to a VM's network interface. They then try to attach the same ASG to a subnet. What happens?

options.text: The ASG can be attached to the subnet, because ASGs work at both levels
An application security group is attached to a network interface, not to a subnet, so the team must attach it to the NICs of the VMs in that role
The ASG can be attached to the subnet, but only if no NSG is attached to the subnet
ASGs cannot be attached to anything; they are only used in Azure Policy

explanation: Correct: application security groups are attached to network interfaces, not to subnets. An NSG rule references an ASG as a source or destination, and the rule applies to the NICs that have that ASG attached. Attaching an ASG to a subnet is not supported.

prompt: A VM needs to reach the Azure Instance Metadata Service at 169.254.169.254 and the Azure platform DNS at 168.63.129.16. The team adds an NSG deny rule for all outbound traffic. Will these platform services still work?

options.text: No, because the deny rule blocks all outbound traffic including platform IPs

Yes, because the platform IP addresses 168.63.129.16 and 169.254.169.254 are not subject to NSG rules unless they are targeted by the AzurePlatformDNS, AzurePlatformIMDS, or AzurePlatformLKM service tags
No, because platform services require an explicit allow rule
Yes, but only if the VM has a public IP address

explanation: Correct: the Azure platform IP addresses 168.63.129.16 and 169.254.169.254 are not subject to NSG rules, unless they are targeted by the AzurePlatformDNS, AzurePlatformIMDS, or AzurePlatformLKM service tags. A broad deny rule does not block these platform services, which is why metadata and platform DNS continue to work.

prompt: A subscription created in 2024 has a VM that needs to send email directly over SMTP port 25 to an external mail server. The connection fails. What is the cause?

options.text: Port 25 is blocked by the NSG default rules
Outbound port 25 is blocked for subscriptions created after 15 November 2017, and the team must use an SMTP relay, typically on port 587, instead of direct SMTP delivery
Port 25 is blocked only for VMs without a public IP address
Port 25 requires an Azure Firewall, because NSGs cannot allow it

explanation: Correct: outbound SMTP on port 25 is blocked for Azure subscriptions created after 15 November 2017, as an anti-spam measure. The team must use an SMTP relay service, typically on port 587 with authentication, rather than sending email directly over port 25. This block is applied at the platform level, not by the NSG.

prompt: A team has been using NSG flow logs for traffic analysis. They receive a notice that NSG flow logs will retire. What should they migrate to, and when?

options.text: NSG flow logs retire on 30 September 2027, and the team should migrate to VNet flow logs, which replace NSG flow logs
NSG flow logs never retire, so no action is needed
NSG flow logs retire on 30 September 2027, and the team should migrate to Azure Firewall logs
NSG flow logs retire immediately, and there is no replacement

explanation: Correct: NSG flow logs retire on 30 September 2027, and Microsoft recommends migrating to VNet flow logs, which provide the same traffic analysis capability at the virtual network level. The team should plan the migration before the retirement date.

prompt: A security admin rule in Virtual Network Manager is configured as Allow with priority 100, and an NSG rule on the subnet denies the same traffic. What happens?

options.text: The traffic is denied, because the NSG rule overrides the security admin rule

The traffic is allowed through the security admin rule and then continues to NSG evaluation, where the NSG deny blocks it, because an Allow security admin rule continues to NSG evaluation while an Always Allow rule terminates evaluation
The traffic is allowed, because security admin rules always override NSGs
The traffic is denied, because security admin rules are evaluated after NSGs

explanation: Correct: security admin rules are evaluated before NSGs. An Allow rule permits the traffic to continue to NSG evaluation, where the NSG deny blocks it. An Always Allow rule would terminate evaluation and allow the traffic regardless of the NSG. The distinction between Allow and Always Allow is the key to this scenario.

prompt: A security admin rule in Virtual Network Manager is configured as Always Allow with priority 100, and an NSG rule denies the same traffic. What happens?

options.text: The traffic is denied, because the NSG rule overrides it
The traffic is allowed, because an Always Allow security admin rule terminates evaluation and the NSG is never consulted
The traffic is denied, because Always Allow only applies to inbound traffic
The traffic is allowed only if the NSG rule has a higher priority number

explanation: Correct: an Always Allow security admin rule terminates evaluation, so the traffic is allowed and the NSG is never consulted. This is the difference from a plain Allow rule, which continues to NSG evaluation. Always Allow and Deny are the terminating actions in security admin rules.

prompt: A security admin rule in Virtual Network Manager is configured as Deny with priority 100. An NSG rule allows the same traffic. What happens?

options.text: The traffic is allowed, because the NSG rule overrides the security admin rule
The traffic is denied, because security admin rules are evaluated before NSGs and a Deny rule terminates evaluation
The traffic is allowed, because Deny rules in Virtual Network Manager are advisory only
The traffic is denied only if the NSG rule has a lower priority number

explanation: Correct: security admin rules are evaluated before network security groups, and a Deny rule terminates evaluation. The traffic is denied regardless of the NSG allow rule. This is how central security policy can enforce a block that no local NSG can override.

prompt: A team creates a security admin configuration in Virtual Network Manager for the East US region. They try to create a second security admin configuration for the same region. What happens?

options.text: Both configurations apply, because multiple configurations per region are supported
Only one security admin configuration can be applied per region, so the second configuration cannot be created for East US
Multiple configurations are allowed, but only the first one is evaluated
Multiple configurations are allowed if they are in different resource groups

explanation: Correct: only one security admin configuration can be applied per region. The team cannot create a second security admin configuration for East US. They must add their rules to the existing configuration for that region.

prompt: A team applies a security admin rule and expects it to take effect immediately on all virtual networks. The rule does not appear to be enforced for several minutes. What explains the delay?

options.text: Security admin rules are applied with eventual consistency, so there is a delay before the rules are enforced on all virtual networks
Security admin rules are applied instantly, so the delay must be caused by something else
Security admin rules require a VM reboot to take effect
Security admin rules are only applied during maintenance windows

explanation: Correct: security admin rules are applied with eventual consistency, so there is a delay between configuring a rule and its enforcement on all virtual networks. The team should allow time for the rules to propagate before concluding the configuration failed.

prompt: A security admin rule targets a network group containing 50 virtual networks. A private endpoint in one of those VNets needs to be reached, but the rule blocks the traffic. What is the behaviour for private endpoints?

options.text: Security admin rules apply to private endpoints the same as any other resource
Security admin rules do not apply to private endpoints, so traffic to a private endpoint is not blocked by a security admin rule
Security admin rules apply to private endpoints only if the rule priority is below 100
Security admin rules block private endpoints only for inbound traffic

explanation: Correct: security admin rules do not apply to private endpoints. Traffic to a private endpoint is not evaluated against security admin rules, so the rule does not block it. This is a documented exception, and it means private endpoint traffic is governed by the private endpoint's own network policies rather than the security admin rules.

prompt: An Azure Firewall has a DNAT rule that forwards port 3389 to a VM, a network rule that allows outbound traffic on port 443, and an application rule that allows *.microsoft.com. A packet arrives for port 3389. Which rule type is evaluated first?

options.text: Application rules are evaluated first
Network rules are evaluated first
DNAT rules are evaluated first, then network rules, then application rules, and all rules are terminating
Rules are evaluated in parallel, so all three apply at once

explanation: Correct: Azure Firewall rules are processed in order: DNAT rules first, then network rules, then application rules, and all rules are terminating, meaning the first matching rule decides the outcome and evaluation stops. A packet for port 3389 is evaluated against the DNAT rules first.

prompt: A team configures an Azure Firewall network rule to allow outbound traffic on port 443 and an application rule to deny *.contoso.com. A user tries to reach https://www.contoso.com. What happens?

options.text: The traffic is allowed, because the network rule allows port 443

The traffic is denied, because the network rule allows the connection at the transport layer, but the application rule then evaluates the FQDN and denies it, since rules are processed DNAT, then network, then application
The traffic is allowed, because application rules are evaluated before network rules
The traffic is denied, because network rules cannot allow port 443 when an application rule exists

explanation: Correct: Azure Firewall evaluates rules in order: DNAT, then network, then application. The network rule allows the TCP connection on port 443, but the application rule then evaluates the HTTP request and denies the FQDN. The application rule is the one that blocks the request, because it is evaluated after the network rule.

prompt: A team deploys Azure Firewall in a virtual network and creates a subnet named AzureFirewallSubnet with a /28 prefix. The deployment fails. What is the minimum subnet size?

options.text: /28 is the minimum, so the failure must be caused by something else
AzureFirewallSubnet requires a minimum of /26, so a /28 is too small
AzureFirewallSubnet requires a minimum of /24
AzureFirewallSubnet requires a minimum of /27

explanation: Correct: the AzureFirewallSubnet requires a minimum of /26 address space. A /28 subnet is too small and the deployment fails. The team must use a /26 or larger subnet for the firewall.

prompt: A team attaches a network security group to the AzureFirewallSubnet to filter traffic to the firewall. What happens?

options.text: The NSG filters traffic normally, because NSGs work on any subnet
Network security groups are disabled on the AzureFirewallSubnet, so the NSG has no effect and the firewall manages its own traffic
The NSG blocks all traffic to the firewall, because the subnet does not allow NSGs
The NSG is required on the AzureFirewallSubnet for the firewall to work

explanation: Correct: network security groups are disabled on the AzureFirewallSubnet. An NSG attached to that subnet has no effect, because the firewall manages its own traffic and the subnet is reserved for the firewall. The team should not attach an NSG to the AzureFirewallSubnet.

prompt: A team deploys an Azure Firewall in a virtual network in resource group A, and wants to use a public IP address in resource group B. Is this supported?

options.text: No, the firewall and its public IP must be in the same resource group
The firewall and its virtual network must be in the same resource group, but the public IP address can be in a different resource group
The firewall, VNet, and public IP must all be in the same resource group
The public IP must be in the same region but can be in any resource group, while the firewall and VNet can be in different resource groups

explanation: Correct: the Azure Firewall and its virtual network must be in the same resource group, but the public IP address associated with the firewall can be in a different resource group. This is a common point of confusion, because the firewall and VNet are tightly coupled but the public IP is not.

prompt: A team enables forced tunneling on an Azure Firewall so that all internet-bound traffic goes through an on-premises firewall. They use the Basic SKU. Is forced tunneling supported?

options.text: No, forced tunneling is only supported on Premium
Yes, Azure Firewall Basic supports forced tunneling, so the configuration is valid
No, forced tunneling is not supported on any Azure Firewall SKU
Yes, but only if the firewall is deployed in a secured virtual hub

explanation: Correct: Azure Firewall Basic supports forced tunneling, which routes internet-bound traffic through an on-premises firewall or NVA. Forced tunneling is available on the Basic SKU, while IDPS and TLS inspection are Premium-only features.

prompt: A team wants intrusion detection and prevention and TLS inspection on their Azure Firewall. They deploy the Standard SKU. What will they find?

options.text: Both features are available on Standard
IDPS and TLS inspection are Premium-only features, so the Standard SKU does not provide them and the team must use Premium
IDPS is available on Standard but TLS inspection is Premium-only
TLS inspection is available on Standard but IDPS is Premium-only

explanation: Correct: intrusion detection and prevention (IDPS) and TLS inspection are Premium-only features of Azure Firewall. The Standard SKU does not provide them. The team must deploy the Premium SKU if they need IDPS or TLS inspection.

prompt: A team configures a threat intelligence allowlist on Azure Firewall to exclude a specific FQDN from threat intelligence blocking. What does the allowlist do?

options.text: It blocks the FQDN, because the allowlist is a block list
The threat intelligence allowlist can exclude an FQDN or IP address from threat intelligence blocking, so traffic to that destination is allowed even if threat intelligence would otherwise block it
The allowlist has no effect on threat intelligence, because threat intelligence cannot be overridden
The allowlist only applies to DNAT rules, not to threat intelligence

explanation: Correct: the threat intelligence allowlist can exclude an FQDN or IP address from threat intelligence blocking. Traffic to an allow-listed destination is permitted even if threat intelligence would otherwise block it. This is useful for destinations that are falsely flagged by threat intelligence.

prompt: A team pings a destination through Azure Firewall using TCP ping and receives a response. They assume the destination is reachable. What is the actual behaviour?

options.text: The response proves the destination is reachable, because TCP ping tests end-to-end connectivity
A TCP ping is answered by the firewall itself, not by the destination, so a response does not prove the destination is reachable
TCP ping is blocked by Azure Firewall, so no response should be received
TCP ping tests the firewall's public IP, not the destination

explanation: Correct: when a TCP ping is sent through Azure Firewall, the firewall itself answers the ping rather than forwarding it to the destination. A response therefore does not prove the destination is reachable. The team should test connectivity with an actual application request instead.

prompt: A team stops and starts an Azure Firewall and finds that its private IP address has changed. Is this expected?

options.text: No, the private IP address never changes
Yes, stopping and starting an Azure Firewall may change its private IP address, so the team should not rely on the private IP remaining stable across a stop and start
Yes, but only if the firewall is in a secured virtual hub
No, the private IP changes only when the firewall is deleted and recreated

explanation: Correct: stopping and starting an Azure Firewall may change its private IP address. The team should not hard-code the firewall's private IP address in their routing or configuration, because it can change across a stop and start. Use the firewall's name or a stable reference instead.

prompt: A team deploys Azure Firewall in a virtual network and later wants to enable availability zones. What is required?

options.text: Availability zones can be enabled on any existing firewall deployment

Availability zones are reconfigurable only if the firewall is deployed in a virtual network rather than a secured hub, and the region supports availability zones, and the public IP addresses share the same zones
Availability zones cannot be enabled after deployment under any circumstances
Availability zones require the Premium SKU

explanation: Correct: availability zones on Azure Firewall are reconfigurable only if the firewall is deployed in a virtual network rather than a secured hub, and the region supports availability zones, and the public IP addresses share the same zones. A firewall in a secured hub cannot have its zone configuration changed in the same way.

prompt: A team manages Azure Firewall rules across 10 subscriptions and wants a central place to define and enforce rules. What should they use?

options.text: A separate firewall in each subscription, because rules cannot be centralised
Firewall Policy, which centralises firewall rules across multiple subscriptions and supports a hierarchy of policies, so rules can be defined once and applied to many firewalls
Network security groups, because they centralise firewall rules
Azure Policy, because it replaces Firewall Policy

explanation: Correct: Azure Firewall Policy centralises firewall rules across multiple subscriptions and supports a hierarchy of policies. Rules can be defined in a parent policy and inherited by child policies, so the team can enforce consistent rules across many firewalls from one place.

prompt: A VM in a private subnet needs to reach the internet for patching. The team configures Azure Firewall as the default route and the VM's outbound traffic is translated to the firewall's public IP. What is this process called?

options.text: DNAT, because the firewall translates the destination address
SNAT, because the firewall translates the VM's private IP address to the firewall's public IP address for outbound traffic
Private Link, because the traffic stays on the backbone
Forced tunneling, because the traffic is forced through the firewall

explanation: Correct: source network address translation (SNAT) translates the VM's private IP address to the firewall's public IP address for outbound traffic. DNAT translates the destination address for inbound traffic. SNAT is what allows a VM in a private subnet to reach the internet through the firewall.

prompt: A team creates a Private Link service to expose their own service behind a Standard Load Balancer to consumers in other virtual networks. A consumer requests access. What must happen before the consumer can connect?

options.text: Nothing, because Private Link services are open to all consumers by default
The service owner must approve the private endpoint connection, because a private endpoint connection to a Private Link service requires owner approval before it becomes active
The consumer must create a public IP address, because Private Link requires one
The consumer must peer their VNet with the service VNet, because Private Link does not work without peering

explanation: Correct: a Private Link service exposes a service behind a Standard Load Balancer, and a consumer connects through a private endpoint. The private endpoint connection starts in a Pending state and requires the service owner to approve it before it becomes active. This approval step gives the owner control over who can consume the service.

prompt: A private endpoint connection shows a status of Pending. The consumer can see the endpoint but cannot reach the service. What does Pending mean?

options.text: The endpoint is ready and the consumer can connect, so the issue must be elsewhere
Pending means the connection is awaiting approval from the service owner, and the endpoint cannot be used until it is approved
Pending means the endpoint failed to deploy and must be recreated
Pending means the endpoint is approved but the DNS has not propagated yet

explanation: Correct: a private endpoint connection in Pending status is awaiting approval from the service owner. The endpoint cannot be used until the owner approves it. Once approved, the status changes to Approved and the endpoint becomes usable. Rejected means the owner declined the connection.

prompt: A private endpoint is created in a virtual network in East US for a storage account in West Europe. The deployment fails. What is the rule?

options.text: The private endpoint and the virtual network must be in the same region, so the endpoint must be created in a VNet in the same region as the resource it connects to
Private endpoints can be in any region, so the failure must be caused by something else
Private endpoints must be in the same resource group as the resource
Private endpoints must be in the same subscription as the resource

explanation: Correct: the private endpoint and the virtual network must be in the same region. A private endpoint in East US cannot connect to a resource in West Europe if the endpoint's VNet is in East US. The team must create the endpoint in a VNet in the same region as the resource, or use a different connectivity approach.

prompt: A team accesses a storage account from a virtual network through a service endpoint. The team asks whether the storage account is reached by its public IP address or a private IP address. What is the answer?

options.text: Service endpoints assign a private IP address to the storage account, so it is reached by private IP
Service endpoints still target the storage account's public IP address, but the traffic travels over the Azure backbone network rather than the public internet
Service endpoints require a VPN, because they do not use IP addresses at all
Service endpoints are the same as private endpoints, so the storage account is reached by private IP

explanation: Correct: service endpoints still target the resource's public IP address, but the traffic from the virtual network to the resource travels over the Azure backbone network rather than the public internet. This is the key difference from a private endpoint, which assigns a private IP address inside the virtual network.

prompt: A company enables DDoS Network Protection on a virtual network. They ask whether the free infrastructure protection is still active. What is the answer?

options.text: No, enabling Network Protection disables the free infrastructure protection

Yes, the free infrastructure protection is the baseline that is always active, and DDoS Network Protection is a paid plan that adds adaptive tuning, analytics, SLA, Rapid Response, and cost protection on top of it
No, because the two are mutually exclusive
Yes, but only for virtual machines, not for other resources

explanation: Correct: the free infrastructure protection is the baseline DDoS protection that is always active for Azure resources. DDoS Network Protection is a paid plan that adds adaptive tuning, analytics, a service level agreement, Rapid Response support, and cost protection on top of the baseline. Enabling Network Protection does not disable the baseline.

prompt: A team is hit by a layer 7 HTTP flood against a web application. They have DDoS Network Protection enabled. Why is the attack not mitigated?

options.text: DDoS Network Protection is disabled, because the attack is layer 7
DDoS Protection operates at layers 3 and 4, and layer 7 HTTP floods require a Web Application Firewall, which can rate-limit and block HTTP floods
DDoS Network Protection only protects virtual machines, not web applications
DDoS Network Protection requires an Azure Firewall to inspect HTTP traffic

explanation: Correct: Azure DDoS Protection protects at layer 3 (network) and layer 4 (transport). A layer 7 HTTP flood, which sends a high volume of apparently valid HTTP requests, requires a Web Application Firewall, which can rate-limit and block HTTP floods. DDoS Network Protection alone does not inspect HTTP request content.

prompt: A team wants to give a vendor RDP access to a VM without assigning a public IP address to the VM and without opening RDP to the internet. Which service provides this, and how?

options.text: Azure VPN Gateway, because it provides RDP over a VPN tunnel
Azure Bastion, which provides secure RDP and SSH connectivity to virtual machines over TLS on port 443, without requiring a public IP address on the virtual machines
Azure Firewall, because it provides RDP access to VMs
Just-in-time VM access, because it replaces Bastion entirely

explanation: Correct: Azure Bastion provides secure RDP and SSH connectivity to virtual machines over TLS on port 443, without requiring a public IP address on the VMs. The vendor connects through the Azure portal or a Bastion host, and the VM remains private. VPN Gateway requires a VPN client and tunnel, while Bastion works through the browser or a native client.

prompt: A team deploys Azure Bastion Developer SKU for a small test environment. They ask what the limitations are. What should they know?

options.text: The Developer SKU is a free tier that uses shared infrastructure, supports connecting to one virtual machine at a time, and is available in select regions, so it is suitable for testing but not for production use
The Developer SKU has no limitations and is identical to Standard
The Developer SKU requires a public IP on every VM
The Developer SKU supports session recording, which Standard does not

explanation: Correct: the Azure Bastion Developer SKU is a free tier that uses shared infrastructure, supports connecting to one virtual machine at a time, and is available in select regions. It is intended for testing and small environments, not for production. For production features such as native client support, file transfer, and session recording, the Standard or Premium SKU is required.

prompt: A team uses Azure Bastion Basic and wants to connect using their native RDP client and transfer files to the VM. What will they find?

options.text: Basic supports native client connections and file transfer
Basic supports only portal browser connections, while Standard adds native client support, shareable links, IP-based connections, custom ports, and file transfer, so the team must upgrade to Standard
Basic supports file transfer but not native client connections
Basic supports native client connections but not file transfer

explanation: Correct: Azure Bastion Basic supports only connections through the Azure portal browser. Standard adds native client support, shareable links, IP-based connections, custom ports, and file transfer. The team must upgrade to Standard for native client and file transfer capabilities.

prompt: A team needs session recording for compliance on their Bastion connections. Which SKU provides this, and what else does it add?

options.text: Standard, because it includes session recording
Premium, which adds session recording and private-only deployment on top of the Standard features
Basic, because session recording is a basic feature
Developer, because it is the only SKU with session recording

explanation: Correct: Azure Bastion Premium adds session recording and private-only deployment on top of the Standard features. Session recording captures the RDP or SSH session for compliance and auditing. Standard does not include session recording, so the team must use Premium.

prompt: A team deploys one Azure Bastion host in a hub virtual network and has virtual machines in peered spoke virtual networks. Can they use the single Bastion host to reach the spoke VMs?

options.text: No, each VNet needs its own Bastion host
Yes, one Bastion deployment can serve virtual machines in peered virtual networks, because Bastion works across VNet peering
No, because Bastion only works in the VNet where it is deployed
Yes, but only if the spoke VNets are in the same region and the Bastion is Premium

explanation: Correct: one Azure Bastion deployment can serve virtual machines in peered virtual networks. Bastion works across VNet peering, so a single Bastion host in a hub VNet can provide RDP and SSH access to VMs in spoke VNets. Each VNet does not need its own Bastion host.

prompt: A team configures a Firewall Policy with a parent policy and a child policy. A rule exists in both the parent and the child with conflicting actions. Which rule wins?

options.text: The child policy rule wins, because child policies override parent policies
The parent policy rule wins, because Firewall Policy supports a hierarchy where parent policies take precedence over child policies
Both rules apply, so the traffic is evaluated against both
Neither rule applies, because conflicting rules cancel each other out

explanation: Correct: Firewall Policy supports a hierarchy of policies, where a parent policy takes precedence over a child policy. If a rule exists in both with conflicting actions, the parent policy's rule wins. This lets central teams enforce rules that local teams cannot override.
