The registry runs the agents listed in it
The Entra Agent Registry inventories Microsoft and third-party agents in one place, with each agent holding an Agent ID, a sponsor and a registry entry
The registry is only a billing list with no governance use

explanation: Correct: the Entra Agent Registry inventories Microsoft and third-party agents in one place, and each agent gets an Agent ID, a sponsor and a registry entry. A is wrong: the registry covers third-party agents too. B is wrong: the registry is the inventory; it does not run agents. D is wrong: the registry is a governance record, not a billing list.

prompt: A team runs 50 agents, all acting on behalf of 10 licensed users. How many Agent 365 licences do the agents need?

options.text: Each agent needs its own Agent 365 licence, priced per agent
Agents acting on behalf of a licensed user are covered by that user Agent 365 licence, because Agent 365 is licensed per user
No licence is needed for any Agent 365 feature
Each agent needs a Microsoft 365 E7 licence of its own

explanation: Correct: agents acting on behalf of a licensed user are covered by that user Agent 365 licence; the licence is per user, not per agent. A is wrong: the licence is per user. C is wrong: a licence is required for the security features, but it is the user licence that covers the agent. D is wrong: the base identity is free, but the Agent 365 security features are licensed per user.

prompt: A CISO asks for a current inventory of AI apps and agents in use, with risk. Which DSPM view and time window provide it?

options.text: The current DSPM inventories AI apps and agents with activity in the last 30 days, showing how many are high risk and how many had sensitive interactions
The inventory covers all apps and agents ever created, with no time window
The inventory covers only Microsoft 365 Copilot, not other AI apps or agents
The inventory is in the classic DSPM for AI view

explanation: Correct: the current DSPM adds an inventory of AI apps and agents with activity in the last 30 days, how many are high risk, and how many had sensitive interactions. B is wrong: the inventory covers the last 30 days of activity, not all time. C is wrong: the inventory covers AI apps and agents, not only Copilot. D is wrong: the classic experience does not have this inventory.

prompt: A team is unsure whether to use DSPM for AI (classic) or the current DSPM. Which version should they use for new agent governance, and why?

options.text: The classic DSPM for AI is the current version and gets all new features
The current DSPM is a duplicate of classic with no new capabilities
The current DSPM is only for Copilot and does not cover agents
The current Data Security Posture Management under Solutions, DSPM covers AI apps and agents alongside the rest of the data, and most new features are added only there

explanation: Correct: the current DSPM covers AI apps and agents alongside the rest of the data, with security objectives and guided workflows, and most new features land only there. A is wrong: the classic experiences still work but get no new features. B is wrong: the current DSPM is the replacement. D is wrong: the current DSPM is under Solutions, DSPM in the Purview portal.

prompt: A pilot group of 50 users needs a custom data risk assessment before Copilot rolls out to them. How do default and custom assessments differ?

options.text: The default assessment runs monthly for every site in the tenant
The default assessment runs weekly for the top 100 SharePoint sites by usage, and custom assessments can target selected users or sites
Item-level scanning covers OneDrive the same as SharePoint
Custom assessments can scan unlimited sites with no limits

explanation: Correct: the default assessment runs weekly for the top 100 SharePoint sites, and custom assessments can target all users or a pilot group and selected sites. A is wrong: the default is weekly, not monthly. C is wrong: item-level scanning covers SharePoint only, not OneDrive. D is wrong: custom assessments are in preview for specific users and sites, not unlimited.

prompt: A team wants item-level scanning of overshared files in OneDrive and in 50 SharePoint sites. What are the actual limits?

options.text: Item-level scanning is restricted to SharePoint sites, up to 10 sites, with a maximum of 200,000 items per location, and OneDrive is not supported for item-level scanning
Item-level scanning covers OneDrive and SharePoint equally with no site limit
Item-level scanning has no item cap per location
Item-level scanning covers up to 100 sites

explanation: Correct: item-level scanning is restricted to SharePoint sites, up to 10 sites, with a maximum of 200,000 items per location, and OneDrive is not supported for item-level scanning. B is wrong: OneDrive is not supported. C is wrong: the cap is 200,000 items per location. D is wrong: the site limit is 10, not 100.

prompt: A team enables the DSPM one-click policy Detect sensitive info added to AI sites. Where does the enforcement policy live, and what does it do?

options.text: The one-click policies create Conditional Access policies in Entra
The one-click policies are only reports with no enforcement
DSPM one-click policies create enforcement policies in other Purview solutions, such as DLP for detecting and blocking sensitive info sent to AI sites, and Insider Risk Management for risky AI usage
The admin must write each policy from scratch; DSPM cannot create them

explanation: Correct: the one-click policies are named with a DSPM for AI prefix and create policies in DLP and Insider Risk Management, for example Detect sensitive info added to AI sites (DLP) and Detect risky AI usage (IRM). A is wrong: the policies are created in DLP and IRM, not in Entra. C is wrong: the policies are real enforcement policies, not reports. D is wrong: DSPM creates them; the admin does not write them from scratch.

prompt: A firm must stop Copilot from processing documents labelled Highly Confidential. Which DSPM one-click policy and enforcement mechanism do that?

options.text: Enable DSPM for AI and stop, because DSPM blocks Copilot from processing labelled items by itself

Enable the one-click policy Prevent data exposure in Microsoft 365 Copilot and Microsoft Copilot interactions, which creates a DLP policy that blocks Copilot and agents from summarising items with the selected labels
Write a Conditional Access policy, because DLP cannot target Copilot
Remove the labels, because labels prevent the policy from working

explanation: Correct: the DSPM one-click policy for Copilot is named Prevent data exposure in Microsoft 365 Copilot and Microsoft Copilot interactions, and it works with a DLP policy that blocks summarisation of labelled items. A is wrong: DSPM alone does not block; the DLP policy enforces. C is wrong: the policy targets Copilot interactions, not sign-ins. D is wrong: labels are the trigger for the block, not an irrelevance.

prompt: An investigator needs the full context of a suspicious agent interaction: what it accessed, which labels applied, which model ran, and whether a jailbreak was flagged. Where is that evidence?

options.text: Audit records carry metadata such as the resources accessed, sensitivity labels, the model and jailbreak flags, and prompt and response text is reviewed through DSPM for AI and eDiscovery
Audit records contain only a timestamp and nothing else
Audit must be enabled manually for every agent, or nothing is recorded
Prompt and response text is never available anywhere in Purview

explanation: Correct: Purview audit records for Copilot and agent interactions carry metadata such as the resources accessed, sensitivity labels, the model and detection flags, and prompt and response text is reviewed through DSPM for AI and eDiscovery. B is wrong: the records carry rich metadata. C is wrong: audit is auto-enabled for new agent instances. D is wrong: prompt text is available through DSPM for AI and eDiscovery.

prompt: A board asks what Agent 365 actually is in one sentence. Which description is correct?

options.text: Agent 365 replaces Entra Agent ID entirely
Agent 365 governs only Microsoft-built agents
Agent 365 hosts the models that agents run on
Agent 365 extends the infrastructure used to manage people (identity, access, data protection, threat defense) to AI agents, using Entra Agent ID, Purview and Defender

explanation: Correct: Agent 365 extends the infrastructure used to manage people to AI agents, with Entra Agent ID for identity, Purview for data security and Defender for runtime threat protection. A is wrong: Agent 365 does not replace Entra. B is wrong: it covers third-party agents too. D is wrong: it is a control plane, not a model host.

prompt: A compliance officer needs to manage DSPM for AI. Which role and portal are required?

options.text: Any user with a Microsoft 365 licence can manage DSPM for AI
An account with appropriate permissions for compliance management, such as membership of the Microsoft Entra Compliance Administrator group role, in the Microsoft Purview portal
Global Admin is the only role that can open DSPM for AI
A Security Reader can create and manage DSPM policies

explanation: Correct: to use DSPM for AI, an account needs appropriate permissions for compliance management, such as membership of the Microsoft Entra Compliance Administrator group role. A is wrong: Global Admin is not required; Compliance Administrator is the named role. C is wrong: a reader cannot manage DSPM. D is wrong: the Purview portal is the access point, not the Azure portal alone.

prompt: A company uses Copilot, a Foundry agent and a third-party generative AI app. Which Purview capability covers data security for all three?

options.text: Purview DSPM for AI provides a central location to secure data for AI apps and proactively monitor AI use, covering Copilots, agents and other AI apps including those using third-party large language models
DSPM for AI covers only Microsoft 365 Copilot and no other AI app
DSPM for AI is a Defender for Cloud plan, not a Purview capability
DSPM for AI trains the models that Copilot uses

explanation: Correct: DSPM for AI provides a central management location to secure data for AI apps and proactively monitor AI use, covering Copilots, agents and other AI apps that use third-party large language models. B is wrong: it covers third-party AI apps too. C is wrong: it is a Purview portal experience, not a Defender plan. D is wrong: it is a posture capability, not a model-training service.

prompt: A team argues oversharing is an old SharePoint problem that AI does not change. Why is that wrong?

options.text: Generative AI fixes oversharing automatically, so no assessment is needed
Generative AI has no effect on oversharing risk

Generative AI amplifies oversharing because it can proactively surface content that is obsolete, over-permissioned or lacks governance, so data risk assessments are needed to identify and remediate it
Data risk assessments only cover external sharing, not internal oversharing

explanation: Correct: generative AI amplifies oversharing because it can proactively surface content that is obsolete, over-permissioned or lacks governance, so data risk assessments identify and remediate it. A is wrong: AI does not fix oversharing by itself. B is wrong: AI amplifies the problem; it does not leave it unchanged. D is wrong: the assessments cover SharePoint and OneDrive oversharing insights, not only external sharing.

prompt: A Conditional Access policy targets all users with MFA. An agent with its own Agent ID signs in from an untrusted location and is not blocked. Why, and what is the fix?

options.text: Target the policy at the users, because that automatically covers agent identities

Create a separate Conditional Access policy targeting the agent identity with Block or Allow, because the agent identity and the user account are distinct objects and Conditional Access follows the token subject
Require MFA for the agent identity, because agents complete MFA like users
Target the policy at the human sponsor, because the sponsor is the subject of the agent token

explanation: Correct: the agent identity and the agent user account are distinct objects; Conditional Access follows the token subject, so a policy targeting users does not cover the agent identity, and the agent needs its own policy with Block or Allow. A is wrong: targeting users does not cover agent identities. C is wrong: MFA is not available for agent identities. D is wrong: the sponsor is not the subject of the agent token.

prompt: A Foundry agent must call tools over MCP. Which authentication options are supported, and what is explicitly blocked?

options.text: Authenticate MCP tools with key-based auth, Entra agent identity or project managed identity, or OAuth identity passthrough, and never forward a Microsoft-audience token to an untrusted third-party MCP endpoint
Forward the Microsoft-audience token to the third-party MCP endpoint, because that is the standard pattern
Use key-based auth only, because Entra identities cannot authenticate MCP tools
Use OAuth passthrough only, because key-based auth is forbidden for MCP tools

explanation: Correct: the Foundry Agent Service authenticates MCP tools with key-based, Entra agent identity or project managed identity, or OAuth identity passthrough, and explicitly blocks forwarding Microsoft-audience tokens to untrusted third-party MCP endpoints. B is wrong: forwarding a Microsoft-audience token is explicitly blocked. C is wrong: key-based auth is one of the supported methods. D is wrong: OAuth passthrough is a supported method, not a forbidden one.

prompt: A governance review finds a team using sponsor, agent identity and user account interchangeably. What is the correct separation?

options.text: The sponsor is the agent identity, so no separate identity is needed
The user account is the agent identity, so the agent needs no identity of its own

The agent identity, the human sponsor and the user account are three distinct objects: the identity acts, the sponsor is accountable for its lifecycle, and the user is the human the agent may act on behalf of
The three are interchangeable labels for the same Entra object

explanation: Correct: the agent identity is the non-human identity that acts, the sponsor is the person accountable for its lifecycle, and the user account is the human the agent may act on behalf of; conflating them breaks governance. A is wrong: the sponsor is not the agent identity. B is wrong: the user account is not the agent identity. D is wrong: the three are distinct objects with distinct roles.

prompt: A company has 40 agents built before Entra Agent ID existed, all using app registrations. What happens to them, and what must new agents use?

options.text: All old agents are automatically converted to Agent IDs by the platform
Existing agents created before Entra Agent ID keep their plain app registrations, and new agents should use the Agent ID framework and never use app-create commands to represent an agent
Old agents stop working immediately and must be rebuilt
New agents should also use plain app registrations, because Agent ID is only for Copilot Studio

explanation: Correct: the old agents keep their plain app registrations, and new agents should use the Agent ID framework, never app-create commands. A is wrong: existing agents are not forcibly migrated by the platform. C is wrong: the old agents keep working with app registrations. D is wrong: app registrations are the legacy pattern, not the recommended one for new agents.

prompt: A new agent is deployed with an Agent ID. How does the security team verify it is actually visible to governance and audited?

options.text: Verify on the DSPM AI observability page that the agent instance appears with its data risks, because new Agent 365 agent instances are auto-enabled for audit and sensitive-data detection
Assume the agent is governed because it has an Agent ID, with no verification needed
Enable audit manually for every agent, because auto-enablement does not exist
Check the Azure portal, because the observability page does not show per-agent detail

explanation: Correct: the AI observability page shows the agent instance and its data risks, and new agent instances are auto-enabled for audit and sensitive-data detection. B is wrong: audit is auto-enabled for new instances. C is wrong: the observability page is the verification surface. D is wrong: the observability page shows per-agent detail including Entra-enabled status and owner.

prompt: A team wants to score agents whose prompts and responses look risky, such as repeated attempts to access sensitive data. Which Purview capability does that, and how is it enabled?

options.text: Use Defender for Cloud, because Insider Risk Management is a Defender plan
Use DLP, because DLP scores risky behaviour
Use Purview Insider Risk Management, which scores risky prompts and responses, through the DSPM one-click policy Detect risky AI usage
Write a Sentinel rule from scratch, because DSPM cannot create an IRM policy

explanation: Correct: Insider Risk Management with a dedicated agent signal scores risky prompts and responses, and the DSPM one-click policy Detect risky AI usage creates that IRM policy. A is wrong: IRM is a Purview capability, not a Defender plan. C is wrong: DLP blocks sensitive data; IRM scores risky behaviour. D is wrong: the policy is created by DSPM one-click, not written from scratch in Sentinel.

prompt: A CISO asks which agents are actually active and risky right now, not which were created last year. Which DSPM inventory answers that?

options.text: The inventory lists every agent ever created, with no activity window
The current DSPM inventories AI apps and agents with activity in the last 30 days, and the AI observability page shows active agents with risk based on Insider Risk Management signals
The inventory covers only Microsoft-built agents
The inventory is in the classic DSPM for AI view

explanation: Correct: the current DSPM inventory covers AI apps and agents with activity in the last 30 days, and the AI observability page shows active agents with risk based on Insider Risk Management signals. A is wrong: the inventory is activity-based, not all-time. C is wrong: the inventory covers third-party agents too. D is wrong: the observability page is in the current DSPM, not classic.

prompt: A governance design must assign four jobs: agent inventory, agent identity, data protection, and runtime threat detection. Which product does each job?

options.text: Agent 365 alone does identity, audit, DLP and threat detection
Purview alone authenticates agents and blocks their tool calls
Defender alone inventories agents and manages their identities
Agent 365 as the registry and control point, Entra Agent ID for identity and Conditional Access, Purview for audit and data loss prevention, and Defender for runtime threat detection

explanation: Correct: the four products work together: Agent 365 as registry and control point, Entra Agent ID for identity and Conditional Access, Purview for audit and data loss prevention, and Defender for runtime threat detection. A is wrong: no single product does all four jobs. B is wrong: Purview does not authenticate agents. D is wrong: Defender does not inventory agents; Agent 365 does.

prompt: An App Service apps contributors can see a database secret stored as a plain app setting. The team moves the secret to Key Vault, but a developer argues anyone who is a Contributor on the app can still read it, so Key Vault changes nothing. Which design proves that argument wrong?

options.text: Use the Functions master key as the Key Vault secret, so the app and the developers share one credential
Grant the developers Key Vault Secrets Officer through access policies and let the app read the secret with the developers credentials
Enable the apps system-assigned managed identity, grant it Key Vault Secrets User on the vault, and consume the secret as a Key Vault reference, so app Contributors still cannot read the vault secret
Disable the managed identity and store the secret in an app setting, because only app settings are hidden from Contributors

explanation: Correct: the Learn pattern is system-assigned managed identity plus Key Vault Secrets User on the vault, with the secret consumed as a Key Vault reference (@Microsoft.KeyVault(...)); the app identity reads the secret at runtime while human contributors have no vault access. A is wrong: Key Vault access policies are the legacy model and granting Secrets Officer to humans gives them the secret. C is wrong: disabling the identity removes the only secretless path and forces secrets back into app settings. D is wrong: the master key is for Functions ADMIN authorisation, not Key Vault access.

prompt: A team wants users to sign in to an App Service web app with Microsoft Entra ID without writing authentication code in the application, and the app must reject unauthenticated requests before any app code executes. Which built-in capability does this?

options.text: A Key Vault reference, which authenticates users against the secrets stored in the vault
An NSG rule that only allows traffic from the companys office IP range
Azure Bastion, which authenticates web users before they reach the app
App Service Authentication (Easy Auth), the platforms built-in authentication that validates sign-in with federated identity providers before app code runs

explanation: Correct: App Service Authentication (Easy Auth) is built into the platform, requires little or no code, and integrates federated providers such as Microsoft Entra ID, validating sign-in before app code runs. A is wrong: Bastion is RDP and SSH access to VMs, not web-app user sign-in. C is wrong: Key Vault references supply app secrets, not user authentication. D is wrong: an NSG restricts network source; it does not authenticate individual users.

prompt: An Azure Functions HTTP trigger is set to authorisation level FUNCTION (the default). A partner system calls it and gets a 401. The partner argues the function should accept its Entra token. Which key must the caller present at this level?

options.text: The users Microsoft Entra ID token, because function keys are not used at FUNCTION level
No key, because FUNCTION level means anonymous access
Any function key for that function, or any host key
Only the master (admin) key, which also unlocks the host admin APIs

explanation: Correct: at FUNCTION level the caller must present a function key for that function or a host key. A is wrong: that describes ANONYMOUS level. C is wrong: the master key is required only at ADMIN level. D is wrong: Entra user authentication is a separate layer (App Service Authentication); the FUNCTION authorisation level itself is a shared-key check.

prompt: A public App Service web app is receiving SQL injection attempts. The team adds Azure Web Application Firewall (WAF). A developer claims the WAF now authenticates users and encrypts the database. What does the WAF actually do?

options.text: It provides RDP access to the App Service workers
It authenticates users with Microsoft Entra ID so the app needs no sign-in code
It encrypts the App Service disks so the database cannot be read if stolen
It inspects inbound HTTP traffic and blocks common web attacks such as SQL injection and cross-site scripting, typically in front of the app via Application Gateway or Front Door

explanation: Correct: WAF inspects HTTP traffic and blocks common web attacks; it is deployed with Application Gateway or Azure Front Door in front of App Service. A is wrong: WAF is not a disk-encryption feature. C is wrong: Bastion is RDP and SSH to VMs. D is wrong: a WAF does not replace the apps authentication; it protects the HTTP layer.

prompt: A Functions HTTP trigger at FUNCTION level is called by several employees scripts, all sharing one function key. An incident requires knowing which employee called the function, but the logs only show the shared key. What is the correct fix?

options.text: Add the partners origin to the CORS allowed origins list, because CORS authenticates the caller
Rotate the function key weekly and log which key was used, because that identifies the employee
Keep FUNCTION level and enable App Service Authentication with the Microsoft Entra provider, so the platform validates the users token before code runs
Change the trigger to ANONYMOUS and rely on the function key being secret

explanation: Correct: FUNCTION keys are shared secrets for service-to-service callers and cannot identify which employee called; only App Service Authentication (Easy Auth) with an Entra provider validates the users token before code runs and identifies the caller. A is wrong: rotating the function key does not add user identity. C is wrong: ANONYMOUS removes even the shared-key check. D is wrong: CORS is a browser-origin control, not authentication; non-browser callers bypass it entirely.

prompt: A back-end API is exposed through Azure API Management. Calls are unauthenticated, one subscriber is burning the token budget, and SQL injection attempts reach the API. Which layered design addresses all three?

options.text: Replace API Management with a WAF, because WAF policies are the back-end API protection mechanism
Add a private endpoint to the API and stop; network isolation is the same as API authentication and rate limiting
Add a WAF in front of the API; a WAF authenticates callers and enforces per-subscriber token limits
Put Azure API Management in front of the API as the back-end gateway (authentication, token-limit and logging policies) and keep WAF for HTTP attack inspection

explanation: Correct: API Management is the back-end API protection layer (authentication, token limits, policies at the gateway), while WAF inspects HTTP traffic for web attacks. A is wrong: WAF alone does not authenticate API callers or enforce per-subscriber token limits. C is wrong: that inverts the two; APIM governs the API, WAF inspects HTTP. D is wrong: a private endpoint secures network access to a PaaS resource; it does not authenticate callers or rate-limit tokens.

prompt: An App Service app must be reachable only privately AND must reach Key Vault and Azure SQL without going over the public internet. The team adds a private endpoint for the app and declares the work done. What is missing?

options.text: Leave the app public and put a firewall on Key Vault; the app can then reach Key Vault privately
Add a private endpoint for the web app; that also gives the app private outbound access to Key Vault and SQL
Add a private endpoint for inbound traffic to the app AND enable VNet integration for the apps outbound calls to Key Vault and SQL, with private endpoints on those services too
Add a service endpoint on the web apps subnet; service endpoints are the same as VNet integration for outbound calls

explanation: Correct: a private endpoint gives the app a private inbound address, while VNet integration gives the app private outbound connectivity from the VNet to PaaS services; they are opposite directions and both are needed. A is wrong: a private endpoint alone does not give the app outbound private access to Key Vault or SQL. C is wrong: service endpoints are a different subnet-level mechanism, not the apps outbound integration. D is wrong: exposing the app publicly and relying on a firewall on the vault does not give the app a private path.

prompt: Three App Service apps must all authenticate to the same Key Vault and SQL Database with one identity, and the identity must survive any single app being deleted and recreated. Which managed identity type fits?

options.text: Use a user-assigned managed identity, because it survives the app, can be shared across the three apps, and is deleted only when explicitly removed
Use a system-assigned managed identity, because it survives app deletion and can be shared across apps
Use a user-assigned managed identity, because it can only ever be attached to one app
Use a service principal with a client secret, because managed identities cannot be shared across apps

explanation: Correct: a user-assigned identity survives the app being deleted and can be shared by several apps, while a system-assigned identity is tied to the app lifecycle and is deleted with it. A is wrong: system-assigned identities are deleted with the app. C is wrong: user-assigned identities are not per-app only; they can be assigned to multiple resources. D is wrong: both identity types authenticate to Azure services without stored credentials.

prompt: A Functions app connects to Azure SQL, Storage and a third-party API that has no Entra support. The team must rank the connection methods by security. Which design is correct?

options.text: Store the connection string with its password in app settings, because that is the most secure option
Use Key Vault references, because they are more secure than managed identities
Use a managed identity with the least-privilege RBAC role on the target service, because that eliminates secrets entirely; use Key Vault only when the target does not support Entra authentication
Embed the connection string in the function code, because code is not visible to app contributors

explanation: Correct: managed identities are the highest-security connection method because they eliminate secrets entirely; Key Vault is the fallback when the target does not support Entra authentication, and shared secrets in app settings are the last resort. A is wrong: shared secrets are the lowest-security method. B is wrong: Key Vault is high security but still involves a secret; managed identity eliminates secrets. D is wrong: connection strings in code are the failure being fixed.

prompt: A partner must call exactly one HTTP function in an app that has twelve functions. A developer suggests sharing the master key for simplicity. Which key design is least privilege, and why is the master key wrong?

options.text: Change the trigger to ANONYMOUS so no key management is needed
Give the partner a host key, because host keys are scoped to a single function
Give the partner the master key, because it is the standard key for external callers
Give the partner a function key scoped to that one function, and never share the master key, which also unlocks the host admin APIs

explanation: Correct: the master key is a host key with admin reach, so it must never be given to a partner; the partner gets a function key scoped to the one function it calls. A is wrong: the master key unlocks host admin APIs. C is wrong: ANONYMOUS removes the key check entirely. D is wrong: a host key works for every function in the app, which is broader than one function key.

prompt: A team shares one host key across ten partner integrations calling different functions in one Function app. The key leaks and must be rotated. What is the blast radius, and what should the design have been?

options.text: Nothing changes, because host keys are scoped to the function they were created for
Only the new function is affected, because host keys do not apply to functions added later
Only the master key is affected, because host keys are per-function
Every function caller using that host key is affected, because a host key works for every function in the app, including functions added later

explanation: Correct: a host key works for every function in the app at FUNCTION level, including functions added later, so rotating one host key breaks all callers; per-function keys limit the blast radius. A is wrong: host keys are app-wide. B is wrong: function keys are per-function, not per-app. C is wrong: the master key is a host key with admin reach, broader still.

prompt: A function is set to authorisation level ADMIN. A partner presents a valid function key and gets a 401. Which key does ADMIN level require, and what is the risk of sharing it?

options.text: Only the master key, which also unlocks the host admin APIs, so it must never be shared with ordinary callers
Any function key for that function, because ADMIN is the same as FUNCTION level
No key, because ADMIN means the platform trusts the caller automatically
The callers Entra ID token only, because ADMIN level disables key checks

explanation: Correct: ADMIN level requires the master key only, and the master key also unlocks the host admin APIs, so it must never be used for ordinary callers. B is wrong: ADMIN does not accept any function key. C is wrong: ADMIN is not anonymous. D is wrong: Entra authentication is a separate layer; ADMIN level itself is a master-key check.

prompt: A team wants to expose an HTTP function directly to the internet and proposes ANONYMOUS level because the function only reads public data. What is the correct design, and what is wrong with the proposal?

options.text: Set the trigger to ANONYMOUS, because anonymous functions are still protected by the Functions runtime
Keep ANONYMOUS and add a CORS rule, because CORS authenticates callers
Put the function behind a gateway that authenticates callers, or enable App Service Authentication, and only then use ANONYMOUS for the trigger itself
Set the trigger to ANONYMOUS and rely on the function key, because anonymous level still requires a key

explanation: Correct: ANONYMOUS is reserved for endpoints protected by an upstream gateway that authenticates callers, or with App Service Authentication in front; on its own it means anyone can call. A is wrong: ANONYMOUS is not safe for an internet-facing function with no gateway. B is wrong: ANONYMOUS does not check any key. D is wrong: CORS is a browser control, not authentication.

prompt: A Logic App workflow has a managed identity with write access to a production SQL database. A contractor is granted Contributor on the workflow to fix a bug. What is the identity risk, and how long is the token involved valid?

options.text: Nothing, because Contributors cannot use the workflows managed identities
Treat Contributor on the workflow as equivalent to holding every permission of its managed identities, because a contributor can request an identity bearer token for any audience
Nothing, because identity tokens are always scoped to the workflow itself and expire in one minute
Rely on the platform to block token requests to destinations outside the workflow

explanation: Correct: Contributor or workflow-editing permission equates to holding the permissions of every managed identity assigned to that workflow, because a contributor can add an HTTP action that requests an identity bearer token for any audience, valid for one hour. A is wrong: Contributor is not read-only for identities. C is wrong: the token is not scoped to the workflow audience; it can be requested for any audience. D is wrong: the platform does not restrict the destination of those requests.

prompt: A Logic App passes a database password through several actions, and the password is visible in run history to anyone who can view runs. Which setting fixes this?

options.text: Enable secure inputs and secure outputs on the actions that handle the secret, so sensitive data does not appear in run history
Rely on the default run history, because Logic Apps encrypts all action inputs and outputs automatically
Delete the run history after each run, because that is the only way to hide secrets
Restrict RBAC on the logic app, because that hides action inputs from anyone who can view runs

explanation: Correct: secure inputs and secure outputs on individual Logic App actions protect sensitive data from appearing in run history. A is wrong: run history is not encrypted per-action by default; the secure settings are the control. C is wrong: deleting history after the fact does not prevent exposure in the first place. D is wrong: RBAC on the logic app does not hide action inputs and outputs from people who can view runs.

prompt: A Logic App on the Consumption plan must call an internal API over a private network and must not share a multi-tenant runtime with other customers. The team tries to add VNet integration and a private endpoint, but the options are missing. What is the fix?

options.text: Stay on Consumption and add VNet integration, because all plans support it
Stay on Consumption and add IP restrictions only, because that is equivalent to private endpoints
Move to the Standard plan, which provides virtual network integration, private endpoints and single-tenant isolation that the Consumption plan does not support
Stay on Consumption and enable a private endpoint through the portal, because private endpoints are plan-independent

explanation: Correct: the Standard plan provides VNet integration, private endpoints and single-tenant isolation that the Consumption plan does not support, so network isolation requires Standard. A is wrong: Consumption has no VNet integration or private endpoints. B is wrong: IP restrictions alone do not give private endpoints or single-tenant isolation. D is wrong: the plan is the constraint; no setting on Consumption adds VNet integration.

prompt: An internal App Service app must be reachable only from inside the VNet, and must call a SQL database inside the same VNet. The team enables VNet integration and declares the app private. What is wrong, and what is the correct pair of controls?

options.text: Enable VNet integration, because it grants inbound private access to the app from the VNet
Add a private endpoint for inbound private access, and use VNet integration only for the apps outbound calls into the VNet
Block inbound traffic with an NSG on the integration subnet, because NSG inbound rules control VNet integration access
Enable VNet integration on the Basic tier, because VNet integration works on every pricing tier

explanation: Correct: private endpoints give inbound private access, VNet integration gives outbound calls from the app into the VNet, and NSG inbound rules do not apply to VNet integration because it cannot provide inbound access. A is wrong: VNet integration is outbound only. C is wrong: NSG inbound rules do not apply to the integration subnet for this purpose. D is wrong: a private endpoint is the inbound mechanism, not VNet integration.

prompt: An App Service app on the Free tier must call a database in a VNet in another region. The team enables VNet integration and it fails. Which two constraints explain the failure?

options.text: Move the app to at least the Basic tier and integrate with a VNet in the same region, because VNet integration requires a dedicated-compute tier and same-region networking
Keep the Free tier and enable VNet integration, because it works on every tier
Integrate with a VNet in a different region, because VNet integration is region-independent
Enable VNet integration to give the app a private inbound address for users

explanation: Correct: VNet integration requires a Basic, Standard, Premium or Elastic Premium tier; it is not available on Free or Shared, and it supports connecting to a VNet in the same region. B is wrong: VNet integration does not work on the Free tier. C is wrong: cross-region VNet integration is not supported; the VNet must be in the same region. D is wrong: VNet integration is outbound only, so it does not give the app a private inbound address.

prompt: A team replaces a plain-text database password in App Service app settings with a Key Vault reference. A reviewer asks whether the secret is still visible in the settings. How does the reference actually work?

options.text: The secret value is embedded in the app setting, just in encoded form
The app no longer needs any Key Vault permission, because the reference bypasses RBAC
The app setting holds a reference such as @Microsoft.KeyVault(...), the platform resolves it at runtime using the apps managed identity, and the plain secret never appears in app settings
The application code must be changed to call the Key Vault SDK directly, because references do not work in app settings

explanation: Correct: Key Vault references resolve the secret at runtime through the apps managed identity, so the plain secret never appears in app settings; the reference value itself is not the secret. A is wrong: the reference does not embed the secret value. B is wrong: the app still needs Key Vault Secrets User on the vault through its identity. D is wrong: a Key Vault reference is a platform-resolved setting, not a code change.

prompt: A Functions app on runtime 3.x must stop using connection strings and switch to managed identity connections to Azure Storage. The change fails. What is the cause?

options.text: Enable managed identity connections on the 3.x runtime, because all versions support them
Upgrade the Functions runtime to 4.x or later, because identity-based connections are only supported on version 4.x and later
Keep the connection string in app settings, because managed identity is less secure than a connection string
Change the hosting plan, because the runtime version does not matter for managed identity

explanation: Correct: managed identity is the highest-security method for Functions connections, and identity-based connections require Functions runtime 4.x or later, so a 3.x runtime cannot use them. A is wrong: 3.x does not support identity-based connections. C is wrong: managed identity eliminates secrets; a connection string is the fallback. D is wrong: the runtime version is the blocker, not the plan.

prompt: A Functions app on the Consumption plan must use managed identity everywhere, but the storage connection string for the content share cannot be converted. What is the correct handling?

options.text: Use a managed identity for AzureWebJobsStorage on every plan, because it works identically everywhere
Delete the WEBSITE_CONTENTAZUREFILECONNECTIONSTRING setting, because it is optional on Consumption and Premium plans
Use a managed identity where the plan supports it, and secure the WEBSITE_CONTENTAZUREFILECONNECTIONSTRING in Key Vault, because Azure Files does not currently support managed identity connections
Leave the connection string in plain app settings, because Key Vault references do not work for this setting

explanation: Correct: managed identity support for AzureWebJobsStorage varies by hosting plan, and Azure Files does not currently support managed identity connections, so the WEBSITE_CONTENTAZUREFILECONNECTIONSTRING must be secured in Key Vault. A is wrong: managed identity does not work for every setting on every plan. B is wrong: the setting is required for dynamic scaling on Consumption and Premium plans. D is wrong: a plain connection string is the last resort, not the recommended approach.

prompt: A compliance review asks how Logic Apps protects workflow data at rest and what else is needed. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Logic Apps stores workflow data in Azure Storage encrypted at rest with Microsoft-managed keys by default, and the team adds authentication, access controls and connector blocking on top
Logic Apps stores workflow data unencrypted unless the team enables encryption themselves
Logic Apps requires a customer-managed key for all workflow data, or it is stored in plain text
Encryption at rest also hides secrets from run history, so no secure inputs or outputs setting is needed

explanation: Correct: Logic Apps relies on Azure Storage to store and automatically encrypt data at rest with Microsoft-managed keys, and the security guidance adds authentication types, inbound and outbound access controls and connector blocking on top. B is wrong: data at rest is encrypted by default; the team does not need to encrypt it themselves. C is wrong: Logic Apps storage encryption is platform-managed, not customer-key by default. D is wrong: encryption at rest does not protect run history contents; secure inputs and outputs do that.

prompt: A consumer web app must let users sign in with Entra ID or Google, with no auth code in the app. Which Easy Auth statement is correct?

options.text: Only Microsoft Entra ID is supported, so social providers need custom code
Microsoft Entra ID, Microsoft accounts, Facebook, Google and X are supported, and the built-in authentication module handles requests before passing them to application code
Only one provider can be configured per app, and it must be Entra ID
Easy Auth handles authorisation but not authentication, so the app must still validate tokens itself

explanation: Correct: App Service Authentication supports multiple providers including Microsoft Entra ID, Microsoft accounts, Facebook, Google and X, and the built-in module handles requests before passing them to application code. A is wrong: Easy Auth is not Entra-only. C is wrong: the identity provider is configured in the platform, not in code. D is wrong: Easy Auth does not replace the need for authorisation logic in the app; it handles authentication.

prompt: An App Service app must be reachable only from the corporate network and must have no public endpoint at all. The team proposes IP restrictions alone. What is the correct design?

options.text: Use inbound IP restrictions to filter which sources can reach the app, and use a private endpoint to remove public internet exposure entirely, because the two controls do different jobs
Use inbound IP restrictions alone, because they are the same as a private endpoint
Use inbound IP restrictions for the apps outbound calls to Key Vault
Replace the private endpoint with a service endpoint, because they are identical

explanation: Correct: inbound IP restrictions filter who can reach the app, while private endpoints remove public exposure entirely; IP restrictions are a filter, not private connectivity. B is wrong: IP restrictions do not give private endpoints. C is wrong: IP restrictions apply to inbound traffic; they are not the outbound mechanism. D is wrong: service endpoints and IP restrictions are different controls.

prompt: A baseline highly available App Service architecture must be zone-redundant, publicly reachable only through a WAF, and privately connected to Key Vault and SQL. Which architecture is correct?

options.text: Expose App Service directly to the internet and put a firewall on Key Vault only
Use Application Gateway with WAF as the public endpoint, route to App Service through Private Link, and connect the app to Key Vault and SQL through VNet integration and Private Link
Replace Application Gateway with a WAF alone, because a WAF routes traffic to App Service
Keep Key Vault and SQL on public endpoints, because the app reaches them through Private Link anyway

explanation: Correct: the baseline architecture uses Application Gateway with WAF as the public endpoint, routing to App Service through Private Link, while the app uses VNet integration and Private Link for Key Vault and SQL. A is wrong: exposing App Service directly is not the baseline. C is wrong: WAF is on the gateway, not a replacement for the gateway. D is wrong: public endpoints on Key Vault and SQL defeat the private design.

prompt: A Function app orchestrates Azure OpenAI calls and reads from Azure SQL. Both connections currently use secrets in app settings. Which passwordless design is correct?

options.text: Rotate the SQL password monthly and keep it in app settings

Use the system-assigned managed identity with the appropriate RBAC role, so connection strings are no longer stored in application settings, and use the Cognitive Services OpenAI User role instead of an API key for Azure OpenAI
Store the password in Key Vault and keep the API key in code, because managed identity cannot replace both
Keep the connection string and add a firewall rule, because managed identity does not work for SQL

explanation: Correct: managed identity authentication for the SQL connection replaces the password entirely, and the Cognitive Services OpenAI User role replaces API key storage for AI orchestration. A is wrong: the password is removed, not rotated. C is wrong: a connection string with a password is the pattern being removed. D is wrong: Key Vault references are for secrets that must still exist; the managed identity removes the secret.

prompt: A Function app endpoint must be reachable only from the corporate network and must call Key Vault privately. Which network design is correct, and which plan constraint applies?

options.text: Use inbound IP restrictions and private endpoints on the Elastic Premium or Dedicated plan, with virtual network integration for outbound traffic
Use private endpoints on the Consumption plan, because all plans support them
Use VNet integration for inbound traffic and IP restrictions for outbound traffic
Use three layers of IP restrictions, because authentication and identity are the same layer

explanation: Correct: inbound controls are IP restrictions and private endpoints on Elastic Premium or Dedicated plans, and outbound control is VNet integration; the same three-layer model applies to Logic Apps. B is wrong: private endpoints for Functions need Elastic Premium or Dedicated, not Consumption. C is wrong: IP restrictions are inbound, VNet integration is outbound. D is wrong: the three layers are authentication, identity and network isolation, not three copies of the same layer.

prompt: A Logic App connects to Blob Storage, Cosmos DB and an HTTP API. The team wants managed identity everywhere. Which statement about connector authentication is correct?

options.text: Use Basic authentication for all connectors, because it is the most secure option
Managed identity is not available for managed connectors, only for built-in connectors
Use any user-assigned managed identity for every built-in service-provider connector, because all of them support it
Use managed identity for the connectors that support it, noting that most built-in, service provider-based connectors do not support selecting user-assigned managed identities

explanation: Correct: managed identity is available for built-in connectors in Consumption and Standard, and for managed connectors including Blob Storage, Cosmos DB and others; most built-in service-provider connectors do not support user-assigned managed identities. A is wrong: Basic authentication is the weakest option, not the recommended one. B is wrong: managed connectors do support managed identity. D is wrong: user-assigned managed identity support is limited for built-in service-provider connectors.

prompt: A company forbids the use of a specific third-party file-sharing connector in any Logic App because it exfiltrates data. Which control enforces that ban?

options.text: Connector blocking is not possible in Logic Apps, so any connector can be used
Block creating connections for specific connectors, using the connector-blocking control alongside authentication and access controls
Rely on RBAC on the logic app, because that blocks specific connectors
Enable secure outputs, because that blocks connectors from being created

explanation: Correct: blocking connections for specific connectors is a documented control, alongside authentication types and inbound and outbound access controls. A is wrong: connector blocking is a real control. C is wrong: RBAC on the logic app does not block a connector from being used inside a workflow. D is wrong: secure outputs hide data; they do not block connectors.

prompt: A Logic App HTTP connector must authenticate to an API with a Microsoft Entra ID token using OAuth 2.0. Which authentication type is that?

options.text: Active Directory OAuth (OAuth 2.0 with Microsoft Entra ID), which is the Entra-based authentication type for supported connectors
Basic authentication, because it uses Entra tokens
Raw authentication, because it is the OAuth option
Managed identity, because that is the only Entra-based option and OAuth does not exist for connectors

explanation: Correct: Logic Apps supports Active Directory OAuth (OAuth 2.0 with Microsoft Entra ID) for connectors, alongside Basic, Raw and managed identity, so OAuth is the Entra-based option. B is wrong: Basic sends a username and password, not an Entra token. C is wrong: Raw is not the OAuth option. D is wrong: managed identity is a separate option from Active Directory OAuth.

prompt: A Logic App has a request trigger whose URL was posted in a public chat. The team says the workflow is still safe because the URL is long. What is the correct response?

options.text: Publish the trigger URL publicly, because it is safe to share
Rely on the trigger URL being secret and add no other control, because the URL cannot be guessed
Secure inbound calls to the request trigger with access controls, because anyone holding the trigger URL and signature can invoke the workflow
Enable App Service Authentication on the Logic App, because that is how request triggers are secured

explanation: Correct: request-based triggers can be secured with inbound access controls, and the trigger URL contains a shared signature that must be protected; anyone with the URL can invoke the workflow. A is wrong: the trigger URL is not public-safe; it is a capability URL. C is wrong: IP restrictions and authentication apply to inbound calls. D is wrong: Easy Auth is for App Service apps, not Logic App request triggers.

prompt: An App Service app needs TLS with a certificate the team already manages in Key Vault. Which certificate option is correct?

options.text: Buy an App Service certificate, because that is the only supported certificate type
Use a certificate imported from Key Vault, because App Service supports free managed certificates, App Service certificates, third-party certificates and certificates imported from Key Vault
Use a self-signed certificate in code, because App Service does not support Key Vault certificates
Rely on the WAF certificate, because App Service needs no certificate of its own

explanation: Correct: App Service supports free managed certificates, App Service certificates, third-party certificates and certificates imported from Key Vault, so the team can use a Key Vault certificate without buying an App Service certificate. B is wrong: a Key Vault certificate is a supported option. C is wrong: a free managed certificate is also supported for eligible domains. D is wrong: TLS is not provided by the WAF alone.

prompt: A Logic App managed identity needs to read one Blob container and write to one queue. What permission principle applies?

options.text: Assign only the minimum necessary permissions for the managed identity, following least privilege
Assign Owner to the managed identity so the workflow never fails with a permission error
Assign the same permissions the developer has, because the identity acts as the developer
Assign no permissions and let the identity inherit the workflow owners permissions automatically

explanation: Correct: the least-privilege rule applies to the identity itself; only the minimum necessary permissions should be assigned to managed identities on workflows. B is wrong: least privilege is the rule, not broad permissions. C is wrong: the identity needs only what the workflow does. D is wrong: managed identity permissions are not inherited from the workflow owner.

prompt: A security review asks whether database credentials ever cross the public internet between App Service, Key Vault and SQL in the baseline architecture. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Secrets travel over the public internet between App Service and Key Vault
Key Vault, SQL and Storage keep public endpoints open so the app can reach them
A single firewall rule is the only network control in the baseline
Communication of secrets between apps and Azure resources occurs only within Azure, and Key Vault, SQL Database and Storage have public endpoints blocked with Private Link access only

explanation: Correct: communication of secrets and connection strings between apps and other Azure resources occurs only within Azure, without crossing network boundaries, and the architecture keeps Key Vault, SQL and Storage behind private endpoints with public endpoints blocked. A is wrong: the baseline blocks public endpoints on those services. B is wrong: secrets do not traverse the public internet in this design. D is wrong: the firewall is not the only control; private endpoints and identity are the layers.

prompt: An App Service app with VNet integration must send ALL outbound traffic through a firewall in the VNet, including internet traffic. The team enables VNet integration but internet calls still bypass the firewall. What is missing?

options.text: All outbound traffic always goes through the VNet, whether or not all-traffic routing is enabled

With all-traffic routing enabled, all outbound traffic is sent into the VNet; without it, only private traffic and service endpoints on the integration subnet go into the VNet, and internet traffic leaves directly from the app
All-traffic routing only changes DNS resolution, not traffic routing
An NSG on the integration subnet cannot block outbound traffic from the app

explanation: Correct: when all traffic routing is enabled, all outbound traffic is sent into the VNet; without it, only private (RFC1918) traffic and service endpoints on the integration subnet go into the VNet, and internet traffic leaves directly from the app. A is wrong: without all-traffic routing, internet traffic does not go through the VNet. C is wrong: the setting controls routing, not DNS. D is wrong: the integration subnet NSG can block outbound traffic.

prompt: A firewall log shows an App Service app reaching a Key Vault private endpoint from an unexpected IP. How does VNet integration assign the source address for private-endpoint calls, and where is it visible?

options.text: Calls to a private endpoint in the integration VNet use an address from the integration subnet, exposed through the WEBSITE_PRIVATE_IP environment variable
The app has no private IP at all when VNet integration is enabled
Calls to private endpoints always use the public outbound addresses listed in app properties
WEBSITE_PRIVATE_IP is the public IP of the app

explanation: Correct: outbound addresses in app properties are still used, but calls to a VM or private endpoint in the integration VNet use an address from the integration subnet, exposed as WEBSITE_PRIVATE_IP. B is wrong: the private IP is exposed through that variable. C is wrong: outbound calls to private endpoints do use the integration subnet address. D is wrong: the outbound address list is not the address used for private-endpoint calls.

prompt: A web app sits behind Application Gateway and uses Easy Auth with Entra ID. After deployment, sign-in fails with a reply URL mismatch. What is the correct configuration?

options.text: Write custom authentication code in the app, because Easy Auth cannot be used behind a gateway
Set the reply URL to the app direct URL, because the gateway is irrelevant to authentication
Use EasyAuth, the integrated authentication mechanism, and configure the reply URL for the custom domain as the gateway endpoint with the provider callback path
Set the callback path without a provider segment, because the provider is inferred automatically

explanation: Correct: EasyAuth is the integrated authentication mechanism, also called App Service Authentication, that simplifies identity provider integration without significant code changes, and the reply URL must be the gateway endpoint with the provider callback path. A is wrong: the reply URL is the gateway, not the app direct URL, when a gateway fronts the app. C is wrong: Easy Auth is the mechanism; there is no separate custom code requirement. D is wrong: the callback path includes the provider, such as aad.

prompt: A Functions app must call Office 365, Teams and SharePoint. The team proposes storing a service account password in app settings for each. What is the correct connection design?

options.text: Store a shared secret for each service in app settings, because that is the recommended pattern
Use managed connectors with built-in OAuth through a Connector Namespace where available, and otherwise use managed identity or Key Vault, never a shared secret in app settings as a first choice
Use anonymous connections, because Functions connectors do not need authentication
Store the credentials in the function code, because connectors cannot use managed identity

explanation: Correct: Functions supports managed connectors in preview for Office 365, Teams and SharePoint with built-in OAuth and webhook handling through a Connector Namespace, and the general rule is to use managed identities where possible and Key Vault where Entra is not supported. A is wrong: shared secrets in app settings are the last resort. C is wrong: managed connectors exist for those services. D is wrong: the connection must still be authenticated; it is not anonymous.

prompt: A Function app with a system-assigned managed identity gets 403 errors calling Azure Storage, even though the identity exists and the token is issued. What is missing?

options.text: Assign the identity a least-privilege RBAC role on the target service, because the identities used for connections must have permissions to perform the intended actions
Do nothing, because a managed identity token automatically grants access to every Azure service
Grant the developer Contributor on the app, because that grants the app identity access to the target
Assign Owner on the subscription to the identity, because least privilege does not apply to managed identities

explanation: Correct: the identities used for connections must have permissions on the target, normally through Azure RBAC with least privilege, and a managed identity token alone does not grant access. B is wrong: the token is authentication, not authorisation. C is wrong: the app Contributor role does not grant the identity data-plane access. D is wrong: roles must be assigned to the identity; there is no automatic grant.

prompt: A serverless review finds four gaps: unauthenticated HTTP triggers, plain-text connection strings, no inbound network restrictions, and hardcoded credentials in shared Logic App connections. Which remediation model closes all four?

options.text: Enable Easy Auth only, because authentication covers identity and network isolation too
Enable VNet integration only, because network isolation covers authentication too
Enable a managed identity only, because identity covers authentication and network isolation too

Apply all three layers: App Service Authentication for who can invoke, a system-assigned managed identity for what the app acts as downstream, and IP restrictions with private endpoints and VNet integration for network isolation

explanation: Correct: the three-layer model is authentication (who can invoke), identity (what the app acts as downstream) and network isolation (what can reach the endpoint), and the same model applies to Logic Apps. A is wrong: authentication alone does not cover identity or network. B is wrong: network isolation alone does not authenticate callers. D is wrong: the layers are distinct; identity is not the same as authentication.

prompt: A browser single-page app on another origin cannot call a Function app, but the same call works from curl. The team concludes the function is down. What is actually happening?

options.text: CORS blocks all callers from other origins, including curl and server-side code
CORS is enforced by browsers, so a browser app on another origin is blocked while curl and server-side calls succeed; add the origin to the apps CORS allowed origins
CORS authenticates the caller, so an allowed origin is proof of identity
Remove CORS entirely, because it is a security risk to have it enabled

explanation: Correct: CORS is enforced by browsers, so a browser single-page app on another origin is blocked while curl and server-side calls succeed; the fix is to add the origin to the app CORS allowed origins. A is wrong: CORS does not block server-side callers. C is wrong: CORS is not authentication; an allowed origin does not prove the caller identity. D is wrong: removing CORS does not add security; it removes a browser protection.

prompt: A database password is visible to every App Service Contributor as a plain app setting. Which design hides it from contributors while the app can still read it?

options.text: Move the secret to Key Vault, grant the apps managed identity Key Vault Secrets User, and consume it as a Key Vault reference, so contributors see only the reference, not the secret
Keep the secret in a plain app setting but rename it, because contributors cannot read app settings
Store the secret in the application code repository with a password, because code is not visible to contributors
Grant every contributor Key Vault Secrets User, because that is the only way the app can read the secret

explanation: Correct: the managed identity eliminates secrets, and the Key Vault reference resolves the secret at runtime; a plain app setting is visible to app Contributors. B is wrong: a Key Vault reference is not the same as a plain setting. C is wrong: the secret is not in code. D is wrong: the vault secret is read by the app identity, not by contributors.

prompt: A Logic App handles payroll data. The auditor asks how the workflow data is protected at rest and what else is required. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Encryption at rest must be enabled manually or data is stored in plain text
A customer-managed key is required for all Logic Apps data
Logic Apps data is encrypted at rest by default with Microsoft-managed keys, and the team adds authentication, access controls and connector blocking on top
Encryption at rest hides secrets from run history, so secure inputs and outputs are unnecessary

explanation: Correct: Logic Apps stores data encrypted at rest with Microsoft-managed keys, and the team should also configure authentication types, inbound and outbound access, and connector blocking. A is wrong: encryption at rest is automatic. C is wrong: a customer-managed key is not required for Logic Apps data. D is wrong: secure inputs and outputs are still needed for run history.

prompt: Application Gateway must reach an App Service app through its private endpoint, but name resolution returns the public IP. What is missing?

options.text: Use public DNS, because it resolves the app to its private endpoint automatically
Link the private DNS zone privatelink.azurewebsites.net to the virtual network, so the App Service default domain resolves to the private IP of the private endpoint
Do not link any DNS zone, because private endpoints work without DNS
Route the gateway to the public endpoint of App Service, because the private endpoint is only for outbound traffic

explanation: Correct: the private DNS zone privatelink.azurewebsites.net links to the VNet and maps the App Service default domain to the private IP of the private endpoint, so the gateway resolves the app privately. A is wrong: public DNS would resolve the public IP. C is wrong: the zone must be linked to the VNet for private resolution. D is wrong: the gateway routes through the private endpoint, not the public endpoint.

prompt: A company enables Defender for Containers for its AKS cluster. The team assumes scanning happens only when someone clicks Scan. What does Defender for Containers actually scan, and when?

options.text: Only images that are already running, and only when an administrator clicks Scan
Only the AKS control plane, once a month, on a manual schedule
Container images in Azure Container Registry automatically when pushed and continually thereafter, plus runtime and posture assessment of the cluster
Only the host operating system of the developer laptops that build the images

explanation: Correct: Defender for Containers scans ACR images automatically on push and continually thereafter, and provides vulnerability assessment, runtime threat detection and posture management for AKS. A is wrong: scanning is not control-plane-only or monthly-manual. C is wrong: developer laptops are not the protected workload. D is wrong: registry scanning is push-triggered and periodic, not manual-only or runtime-only.

prompt: An AKS cluster needs to pull container images from Azure Container Registry using Microsoft Entra ID authentication. A developer suggests enabling the registry admin user for simplicity. Which role should the cluster identity have, and why not the admin user?

options.text: Owner on the registry, so the cluster can manage all registry settings
The registry admin user credentials, shared with the cluster as a secret
AcrPush, because the cluster must be able to write images back to the registry
AcrPull, the read role that lets the cluster pull images from the registry

explanation: Correct: AcrPull is the read role the cluster identity needs to pull images; AcrPush grants push. A is wrong: AcrPush is a write role the cluster does not need. C is wrong: Owner on the registry is far broader than pulling images. D is wrong: using the registry admin user, a shared username and password, bypasses Entra authentication instead of using it.

prompt: A pod in AKS must read secrets from Key Vault without any long-lived credential stored in the cluster. Which mechanism does Microsoft recommend for the pod identity?

options.text: Use the kubelets identity on each node, which automatically grants the pod access to Key Vault
Store a service principal client secret in the pods environment variables
Use workload identity: the pod presents a federated token from the clusters OIDC issuer and exchanges it for a managed-identity token
Copy the clusters admin kubeconfig into the pod so it can authenticate as the cluster administrator

explanation: Correct: workload identity lets a pod authenticate as a managed identity via the cluster OIDC issuer and a federated identity credential, so no secret is stored in the pod. A is wrong: that is the shared-secret pattern workload identity replaces. C is wrong: copying the admin kubeconfig into a pod gives it cluster-admin access. D is wrong: the kubelet identity is not the pod workload identity.

prompt: A team wants AKS to refuse to admit a pod whose image has a critical vulnerability, before the pod starts. Registry scanning is already on. What else must be in place for this gated deployment to work?

options.text: Enable ACR image scanning on push and rely on developers to check the scan results before deploying
Install the Azure Policy for Kubernetes add-on only; policy alone performs image vulnerability gating
Enable agentless discovery for Kubernetes only; that automatically blocks vulnerable images at deploy time

Enable the Defender sensor with Security Gating and registry access with security findings, enable the cluster OIDC issuer and workload identity, and give a user-assigned managed identity AcrPull on the ACRs so the admission controller can read vulnerability findings

explanation: Correct: gated deployment needs the Defender sensor with Security Gating, registry access with security findings, an OIDC issuer and workload identity on the cluster, and a user-assigned managed identity with AcrPull on the ACRs. A is wrong: agentless discovery alone gives posture and visibility, not admission gating. C is wrong: gated deployment is an admission controller evaluating images before admission, not a post-deploy scan. D is wrong: registry scanning alone does not block a deployment.

prompt: A team enables Defender for Containers with agentless discovery only and expects real-time alerts when a running container spawns an unexpected shell or makes an unusual network connection. No such alerts appear. Why?

options.text: Rely on Kubernetes audit logs alone; they provide the same runtime process and network telemetry as the sensor
Enable agentless discovery only; it collects runtime process and network telemetry from running containers

Deploy the Defender sensor (DaemonSet, eBPF telemetry) as part of Defender for Containers, because runtime threat detection requires in-cluster components, while image and posture assessment can be agentless
Enable ACR image scanning only; scanning a pushed image is the same as monitoring its runtime behaviour

explanation: Correct: the capability model is explicit: image vulnerability assessment and posture assessment are agentless, but runtime threat detection requires in-cluster components, the Defender sensor DaemonSet collecting eBPF telemetry. A is wrong: agentless discovery gives posture and visibility, not live process and network telemetry. C is wrong: ACR scanning does not watch running containers. D is wrong: audit logs are one signal, but runtime threat protection needs the sensor telemetry as well.

prompt: A pod must pull images from a private ACR, but the team is forbidden from storing any long-lived credential in the cluster. The cluster OIDC issuer and workload identity are already enabled. Which design pulls images with no stored secret and least privilege?

options.text: Enable the registry admin user and put its password in a Kubernetes Secret for the pod to use
Use Azure Workload Identity: the pods service account federates via the cluster OIDC issuer to a user-assigned managed identity that has AcrPull on the registry
Grant the kubelet identity AcrPush on the registry so any pod on the node can pull and push images
Store a service principal client secret in the pods ConfigMap and rotate it manually each month

explanation: Correct: workload identity uses the cluster OIDC issuer and a federated identity credential on the managed identity, so no stored secret; the pod service account is the federated subject. A is wrong: the admin user is a shared credential that bypasses Entra authentication. C is wrong: AcrPush is a write role, and the pod needs to pull. D is wrong: the kubelet identity is not the pod workload identity and granting it AcrPush would be over-privileged.

prompt: A team enables Defender for Containers on an old AKS cluster whose nodes run on availability sets, not Virtual Machine Scale Sets. The sensor never deploys. What is the cause?

options.text: Rebuild the cluster with Virtual Machine Scale Sets for the nodes, because Defender for Containers only supports AKS clusters that use scale sets
Upgrade the Kubernetes version only, because the node pool type does not matter
Convert the cluster to Arc-enabled Kubernetes, because Defender for Containers does not support AKS at all
Keep the availability-set node pool and install the sensor manually, because the sensor works on any node pool

explanation: Correct: Defender for Containers supports only AKS clusters that use Virtual Machine Scale Sets for the nodes; a cluster without scale sets is not supported. B is wrong: the limitation is about the node pool type, not the Kubernetes version alone. C is wrong: Arc-enabled Kubernetes is a supported path, not a blocker. D is wrong: the sensor needs scale-set nodes; availability sets do not satisfy the requirement.

prompt: A developer asks how Defender for Containers actually scans an image without running it in production. Which description is correct?

options.text: It runs the image in the production cluster and watches what it does
It reads only the image tag and trusts the registry metadata
It pulls the image and runs it in an isolated sandbox with Defender Vulnerability Management, which extracts known vulnerabilities, and it generates recommendations only for images with issues
It generates a recommendation for every image it scans, healthy or not

explanation: Correct: Defender for Containers pulls the image from the registry and runs it in an isolated sandbox with Defender Vulnerability Management, which extracts the list of known vulnerabilities; findings are classified and recommendations are generated only for images with issues. A is wrong: the scanner does not execute the image in production. B is wrong: the scan analyses image layers and metadata in a sandbox, not just the tag. D is wrong: healthy images are marked healthy with no recommendation.

prompt: A running container image came from Docker Hub, not ACR. The team assumes Defender for Containers cannot assess it. How does agentless scanning of running containers actually work?

options.text: It monitors running containers in real time with no delay
It takes snapshots of VM disks every 24 hours for out-of-band analysis, and assesses data-plane containers in those snapshots regardless of their source registry
It only scans containers whose images came from Azure Container Registry
It scans running containers continuously with no snapshot involved

explanation: Correct: agentless scanning takes snapshots of VM disks every 24 hours for out-of-band analysis, and data-plane containers in those snapshots are assessed regardless of which registry the image came from. A is wrong: running-container scanning is not real-time process monitoring; that needs the sensor. C is wrong: the snapshot cadence is 24 hours, not continuous. D is wrong: agentless scanning is registry-agnostic for running containers in snapshots.

prompt: A team stores base images in Microsoft Container Registry and expects Defender for Containers to scan them. Will it, and which registries are actually supported?

options.text: Yes, Microsoft Container Registry is fully supported for scanning
No, only Azure Container Registry is supported and no other registry can be scanned
Yes, but only if the images are first copied into ACR
No, Defender for Containers cannot scan images in Microsoft Container Registry or the Azure Red Hat OpenShift built-in registry, although it can scan ACR, ECR, GCR and GAR

explanation: Correct: Defender for Containers can scan ACR, ECR, GCR, GAR and supported external registries, but not Microsoft Container Registry or the ARO built-in registry. A is wrong: MCR is explicitly not supported. B is wrong: ECR and GCR are supported. D is wrong: the limitation is about the registry type, not about whether the cluster is in Azure.

prompt: A network team refuses to open any inbound firewall rule to the AKS cluster. Can Defender for Containers still work, and what connectivity does it need?

options.text: No inbound connections are needed; all Defender for Containers components use outbound-only connectivity
The firewall must allow inbound connections from Defender for Cloud to every node
The sensor must be exposed through a public load balancer so Defender for Cloud can reach it
The registry must allow inbound connections from the sensor on every node

explanation: Correct: Defender for Containers components require no inbound connections to clusters and use outbound-only connectivity through Azure native security infrastructure. B is wrong: no inbound firewall opening is needed. C is wrong: the sensor is a DaemonSet on the nodes, not a public endpoint. D is wrong: the ACR integration is push-triggered and periodic, not a polling agent inside the registry.

prompt: A team must stop pods running as root, images from unknown registries, and containers with no resource limits. Which combination of controls enforces this, and what does each control actually do?

options.text: Enable Defender for Containers only, because scanning alone enforces configuration compliance
Use Azure Policy only to scan images for vulnerabilities, because Policy replaces Defender scanning
Apply Azure Policy to ACR and AKS to enforce policy compliance with built-in security policies, and use Defender for Containers to scan images and monitor runtime
Grant Owner on the registry to every developer, because RBAC enforces pod security standards
