explanation: Correct: the DevSecOps guidance is to apply Azure Policy to ACR and AKS to enforce policy compliance, with built-in policies for both, while Defender scans images and clusters. A is wrong: Policy enforces configuration; it does not scan images for CVEs. B is wrong: Defender scanning alone does not block non-compliant configuration at admission. D is wrong: RBAC on the registry does not enforce pod security configuration.

prompt: A container estate has three gaps: a registry using shared admin credentials, container workloads passing secrets as plain-text environment variables, and a Container Apps environment with unrestricted public ingress on every service. Which remediation closes all three?

options.text: Keep the ACR admin account enabled and keep secrets in plain-text environment variables

Disable the ACR admin account and replace it with RBAC and scope-map tokens, replace plain-text environment variables with Key Vault references retrieved by a managed identity, and use internal ingress for backend Container Apps services
Enable anonymous pull on the registry and give every container group a shared admin password
Put every Container Apps service on public ingress, because internal ingress breaks service-to-service calls

explanation: Correct: the training summary records the three container gaps closed together: disabling the ACR admin account in favour of RBAC and scope-map tokens, replacing plain-text environment variables in Container Instances with managed-identity Key Vault references, and using internal ingress in Container Apps. A is wrong: the admin account is disabled, not kept. C is wrong: secrets become Key Vault references, not plain environment variables. D is wrong: backend APIs move to internal ingress, not unrestricted public ingress.

prompt: A CI/CD pipeline must push images to exactly one repository in a shared ACR and must not be able to push or pull any other repository. Which credential design gives that least privilege?

options.text: Use a scope-map token scoped to that one repository, because it gives the pipeline the minimum permissions for its repository without granting access to the rest of the registry
Grant AcrPush on the whole registry, because that is the only way a pipeline can push
Enable the registry admin account for the pipeline, because it is scoped per repository
Enable anonymous pull, because that limits the pipeline to one repository

explanation: Correct: scope-map tokens give a pipeline the minimum permissions for one repository without granting access to the rest of the registry, while RBAC roles are registry-wide. A is wrong: AcrPush is registry-wide for that role. B is wrong: the admin account is a shared credential with full access. D is wrong: anonymous pull removes authentication entirely.

prompt: An Azure Container Instances group must call a private API and read a secret, with no public exposure. Which hardening set is correct?

options.text: Run as root with a writable root filesystem and pass the secret as a plain-text environment variable
Run as root but store the secret in a Kubernetes Secret, because that is the same as Key Vault
Give the container group a public IP so it can reach Key Vault over the internet
Run as a non-root user with a read-only root filesystem in a virtual network with private IPs, and retrieve the secret from Key Vault with a managed identity

explanation: Correct: containers should run as non-root users with read-only root filesystems, in a virtual network with private IPs, and secrets should come from Key Vault through a managed identity, not plain environment variables. A is wrong: running as root with a writable filesystem is the risk, not the fix. B is wrong: plain-text environment variables expose secrets to anyone who can inspect the container group. D is wrong: a public IP is not needed for the container to call Key Vault privately.

prompt: A Container Apps environment hosts a public front end and a backend API that handles payment data. Both are on public ingress and share one registry password. What is the correct redesign?

options.text: Put every service on public ingress with a shared registry password in environment variables
Separate services by trust level across environments, assign managed identities for image pull and Key Vault access, and configure internal ingress for backend APIs
Use one environment for all trust levels, because separation adds no security value
Give backend APIs public ingress and protect them only with a shared API key in code

explanation: Correct: separate services by trust level across environments, assign managed identities for image pull and Key Vault access, and configure internal ingress so backend APIs are not on the public internet. A is wrong: public ingress on every service is the gap, not the fix. C is wrong: a shared admin credential for image pull bypasses Entra authentication. D is wrong: secrets in environment variables are the plain-text gap.

prompt: A runbook still references Microsoft Defender for Kubernetes for AKS protection. What is the current state of that plan, and what must the team do?

options.text: Migrate to Microsoft Defender for Containers, because Microsoft Defender for Kubernetes has been deprecated and replaced with it
Keep Microsoft Defender for Kubernetes, because it is still the supported plan for AKS
Enable Defender for Servers instead, because it covers container scanning
Rename the existing plan in the portal, because the change is only a name

explanation: Correct: Microsoft Defender for Kubernetes has been deprecated and replaced with Microsoft Defender for Containers, so the team must move to the Defender for Containers plan. B is wrong: the old plan is not still supported alongside. C is wrong: Defender for Servers is for machines, not container posture. D is wrong: there is no in-place rename; it is a plan migration.

prompt: A DevSecOps team wants image scanning at three points: when the image is pushed, in the CI/CD pipeline, and at runtime. Which Defender for Containers statement covers all three?

options.text: Defender for Containers scans only images in the registry, never in pipelines or at runtime
Defender for Containers has no pipeline integration, so scanning must be manual in CI/CD
Defender for Containers scans images throughout their lifecycle: registry push and periodic scans, runtime agentless scanning, and a CLI tool for pipeline integration, for Linux and Windows images
Defender for Containers supports Linux images only

explanation: Correct: Defender for Containers provides vulnerability assessment across the lifecycle, in registries, runtime environments and CI/CD pipelines, with registry push and periodic scanning, runtime agentless scanning and a CLI tool for pipelines. A is wrong: scanning is not registry-only. B is wrong: the CLI tool exists precisely for pipeline integration. D is wrong: Windows images are supported alongside Linux.

prompt: A team runs AKS clusters on Kubernetes 1.30 and 1.31 and asks whether Defender for Containers supports them and how the sensor is deployed. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Only clusters on exactly Kubernetes 1.19 are supported
AKS clusters running Kubernetes 1.19 or later are supported, with the Defender sensor natively integrated in the AKS resource provider
The team must install a third-party sensor, because Defender provides no in-cluster component
Each cluster must be manually registered, because Defender cannot discover AKS clusters

explanation: Correct: AKS clusters running Kubernetes 1.19 or later are supported, and the sensor is natively integrated in the AKS resource provider. A is wrong: 1.19 is the floor, not the ceiling. C is wrong: the sensor is Azure-managed, not a third-party install. D is wrong: Defender for Containers discovers clusters automatically; manual registration is not required.

prompt: A new CVE is disclosed for a library in an image that was clean when it was built three months ago and is still running in production. Which scanning design catches it?

options.text: Scan the image once at build time and never again
Scan only after a security incident is declared
Rely on developers to check scan results manually with no Defender alerts
Enable Defender for Containers so images are scanned on upload to Container Registry and the AKS environment is scanned continuously, with alerts on vulnerabilities found

explanation: Correct: the DevSecOps guidance is to scan with Defender for Containers when the image is uploaded to Container Registry and to scan the AKS environment continuously, with alerts on vulnerabilities found in images. A is wrong: a one-time scan at build misses vulnerabilities disclosed later. B is wrong: scanning must be continuous, not only after an incident. C is wrong: the recommendation is to enable Defender for Containers, not to rely on developers checking manually.

prompt: An architect must document which Defender for Containers capabilities work without anything installed in the cluster and which need the sensor. Which split is correct?

options.text: Image vulnerability assessment and posture assessment are agentless, while runtime threat detection requires in-cluster components
Runtime threat detection is agentless and image assessment requires the sensor
All Defender for Containers capabilities require the sensor DaemonSet
All Defender for Containers capabilities are agentless and the sensor is optional

explanation: Correct: the capability model separates agentless capabilities, image vulnerability assessment and posture, from capabilities that require in-cluster components, namely runtime threat detection via the sensor. A is wrong: runtime threat detection is not agentless. B is wrong: image assessment does not need the sensor. D is wrong: posture assessment is agentless; the sensor is for runtime detection.

prompt: A team wants ACR image scanning but cannot deploy anything into the cluster yet. Does registry scanning work, and does it alter the images?

options.text: ACR scanning requires the Defender sensor on every node before it works
ACR scanning requires a sidecar in every pod
ACR scanning is push-triggered and periodic with no extra components, and findings can be published back to the registry without modifying the original image
ACR scanning modifies the original image to add the scan results

explanation: Correct: the ACR integration gives push-triggered and periodic image scanning without extra components, while the sensor is a separate DaemonSet for runtime protection. A is wrong: ACR scanning needs no in-cluster component. B is wrong: the sensor is not required for registry scanning. D is wrong: findings can be published back to the registry without modifying the original image.

prompt: A new AKS cluster is created in a subscription with Defender for Containers enabled. The team expects to register it manually. What actually happens?

options.text: Defender for Containers automatically discovers AKS clusters and container registries in the subscription, so the new cluster appears without manual registration, though the sensor still requires scale-set nodes
Each new cluster must be manually registered before Defender can see it
Automatic discovery installs the sensor even on availability-set node pools
Discovery only covers registries, not clusters

explanation: Correct: Defender for Containers automatically discovers all AKS clusters and container registries in subscriptions, so a new cluster is discovered without manual registration, but the sensor still needs scale-set nodes. B is wrong: discovery is automatic. C is wrong: discovery does not install the sensor on unsupported node pools. D is wrong: discovery covers AKS and ACR in the subscription.

prompt: A team asks what the Defender sensor actually is and what telemetry it collects. Which description is correct?

options.text: The sensor is a sidecar injected into every pod to scan its image
The sensor is a lightweight DaemonSet on AKS nodes collecting runtime telemetry (Kubernetes events, process and network data) using eBPF technology
The sensor scans images in ACR when they are pushed
The sensor is a third-party agent the team must install and maintain

explanation: Correct: the sensor is a lightweight DaemonSet on AKS nodes collecting Kubernetes events, process and network data with eBPF, which is the runtime telemetry that agentless scanning cannot provide. A is wrong: the sensor is a DaemonSet, not a sidecar per pod. C is wrong: the sensor collects runtime telemetry; it does not scan registry images. D is wrong: the sensor is Azure-managed and natively integrated in the AKS resource provider.

prompt: A registry team wants image scanning with no agents in the cluster and no changes to the images. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Registry scanning requires the sensor DaemonSet on every node
Registry scanning only runs when an administrator clicks Scan
Registry scanning modifies the image to embed the findings
Registry scanning is push-triggered and periodic with no in-cluster components required, and findings can be published back without modifying the image

explanation: Correct: the ACR integration is push-triggered and periodic, and image vulnerability assessment does not require any components deployed in the clusters. A is wrong: the sensor is for runtime protection, not registry scanning. B is wrong: scanning is push-triggered and periodic, not manual-only. D is wrong: findings are published back without modifying the image.

prompt: A GitHub Actions workflow builds an image and uploads it to Container Registry. When does Defender for Containers scan it, and what else does Defender scan in that pipeline?

options.text: Microsoft Defender scans Container Registry, the AKS cluster and Azure Key Vault, and Defender for Containers scans the container image when the CI workflow uploads it to Container Registry
The CI pipeline must call a manual scan API, because Defender never scans on upload
Images are scanned only when a pod starts, never in the registry
Defender for Key Vault scans the container images, and Defender for Containers scans the vault

explanation: Correct: the DevSecOps guidance is that Defender scans Container Registry, the AKS cluster and Key Vault for vulnerabilities, and Defender for Containers scans the image when the CI workflow uploads it to Container Registry. B is wrong: scanning is automatic on upload, not manual. C is wrong: the scan happens at upload, not only at deployment. D is wrong: Defender for Key Vault is a separate capability for the vault, not the image scan.

prompt: A team must run a baseline scan of an AKS cluster configuration. Where do the Defender for Cloud container recommendations live?

options.text: Under the Container Registry blade, because recommendations are registry-scoped
Under Azure Policy only, because Defender for Cloud has no container recommendations
Under Compute and apps in Defender for Cloud, where the container recommendations are used for baseline scans of AKS clusters
In kubectl, because baseline scans run as a Kubernetes plugin

explanation: Correct: the recommendations sit under Compute and apps in Defender for Cloud, and the guidance is to use them for baseline scans of AKS clusters. A is wrong: the recommendations are not under the registry blade. C is wrong: baseline scans are a Defender for Cloud capability, not a kubectl plugin. D is wrong: the recommendations are in Defender for Cloud, not in Azure Policy alone.

prompt: A production AKS cluster runs images that were clean at build time. Which continuous control catches vulnerabilities disclosed after deployment?

options.text: Scan images once before production and never again
Use Defender for Cloud to automatically scan and monitor production configurations, and conduct vulnerability assessments for images stored in Container Registry
Scan only after an incident is declared
Rely on manual review of Dockerfiles, because Defender cannot scan production configurations

explanation: Correct: the guidance is to use Defender for Cloud to automatically scan and monitor production configurations, and to conduct vulnerability assessments for images stored in Container Registry. A is wrong: a one-time pre-production scan misses later disclosures. C is wrong: scanning must be continuous, not incident-triggered. D is wrong: Defender for Cloud is the scanning tool; manual review is not the control.

prompt: A team enables the ACR admin account for the CI pipeline because it is simple. What is wrong with that design, and what is the default state of the account?

options.text: Keep the admin account disabled and use Microsoft Entra ID identities with RBAC roles, because the admin account is a shared credential with broad access
Enable the admin account for production, because it is enabled by default and is the recommended path
Enable the admin account but scope it to one repository, because it supports per-repository scoping
Use the admin account for the CI pipeline, because it provides a full audit trail

explanation: Correct: the registry admin account provides broad shared credentials and is disabled by default, and the secure baseline is to keep it disabled and use Entra ID identities and RBAC. B is wrong: the admin account is disabled by default, not enabled. C is wrong: the admin account cannot be scoped per repository; scope-map tokens do that. D is wrong: the admin account is a shared credential with no audit trail, not the recommended production path.

prompt: An AKS cluster must pull images from a private ACR. The team proposes the admin user, a service principal secret, or anonymous pull. Which design is correct?

options.text: Enable the registry admin user and store its password in a Kubernetes Secret
Store a service principal client secret in the cluster as an image pull secret
Use anonymous pull so no credential is needed
Attach the ACR to the AKS cluster with a managed identity granted AcrPull, so the cluster pulls images with Entra authentication and no stored secret

explanation: Correct: the admin account is a shared credential that bypasses Entra authentication, while managed identity via attach-acr grants AcrPull with RBAC and no secret. A is wrong: the admin account is the insecure option. B is wrong: a service principal secret in a Kubernetes Secret is a stored long-lived credential. D is wrong: anonymous pull removes authentication entirely.

prompt: A Container Instances workload handles payment tokens and must have no public IP, no root execution and no writable filesystem. Which hardening set is correct?

options.text: Give the container group a public IP and run as root with a writable filesystem
Run the containers in a virtual network with private IP addresses, as non-root users, with read-only root filesystems, and retrieve secrets from Key Vault with a managed identity
Store the secret as a plain-text environment variable, because Key Vault references do not work in Container Instances
Run as root, because non-root users cannot call private APIs

explanation: Correct: containers run in a VNet with private IPs, as non-root users, with read-only root filesystems, and the managed identity retrieves secrets from Key Vault. A is wrong: a public IP is not needed. B is wrong: running as root is the risk. D is wrong: a writable root filesystem is the risk.

prompt: A container that passed image scanning starts a crypto miner at runtime. Which Defender for Containers component detects it, and why do the other controls not?

options.text: ACR image scanning, because it watches running containers
Azure Policy, because it monitors runtime processes

The Defender sensor DaemonSet, because it collects runtime telemetry (Kubernetes events, process and network data) with eBPF, which detects runtime threats such as a crypto miner starting unexpectedly
Kubernetes audit logs alone, because they provide the same runtime telemetry as the sensor

explanation: Correct: the sensor collects Kubernetes events, process and network data with eBPF, which is how runtime threats such as a crypto miner are detected; image scanning alone cannot see runtime behaviour. A is wrong: image scanning finds known vulnerabilities, not runtime miners. B is wrong: Azure Policy enforces configuration at admission; it does not watch runtime processes. D is wrong: audit logs alone do not provide the process and network telemetry the sensor collects.

prompt: A CISO asks what Defender for Containers actually covers across the container lifecycle. Which scope statement is correct?

options.text: Defender for Containers provides vulnerability scanning, runtime threat detection, software supply chain capabilities and security posture management, natively integrated with Azure services
Defender for Containers only scans registry images and does nothing else
Defender for Containers is a deployment tool that builds and pushes images
Defender for Containers is a SIEM that replaces Microsoft Sentinel

explanation: Correct: Defender for Containers provides vulnerability assessment, runtime threat detection, software supply chain capabilities and security posture management, natively integrated with Azure services. B is wrong: it is not a registry-only scanner. C is wrong: it is not a deployment tool. D is wrong: it is a cloud-native security solution, not a SIEM.

prompt: A team worries Defender for Containers needs a separate third-party platform and manual onboarding of every cluster. What is the actual integration model?

options.text: It requires a third-party security tool to be installed first
It requires manual registration of every cluster and registry
It only works with on-premises registries, not ACR
It leverages native Azure integrations, automatically discovers AKS clusters and container registries, and needs no complex third-party configuration

explanation: Correct: Defender for Containers leverages native Azure integrations and automatically discovers clusters and registries, so no complex third-party configuration is needed. A is wrong: it is native, not third-party. B is wrong: discovery is automatic. D is wrong: it integrates with ACR and AKS, not only with on-premises registries.

prompt: A network-isolated cluster cannot have the sensor deployed yet. Which Defender for Containers capabilities still work, and which do not?

options.text: Both image assessment and runtime detection are agentless
Image vulnerability assessment is agentless, while runtime threat detection requires in-cluster components
Image assessment requires the sensor and runtime detection is agentless
Posture assessment requires the sensor and image assessment requires the sensor too

explanation: Correct: image vulnerability assessment can be agentless, while runtime threat detection needs the sensor; the architecture documents which capabilities need in-cluster components. A is wrong: runtime detection is not agentless. C is wrong: image assessment is agentless. D is wrong: posture assessment is agentless.

prompt: A scan returns no recommendations for an image. Does that mean the image is certified vulnerability-free, and how are findings handled?

options.text: Every scanned image generates a security recommendation, healthy or not
Findings are passed through raw with no filtering or classification
Defender for Cloud filters and classifies findings from the scanner, marks healthy images as healthy, and generates recommendations only for images that have issues
A clean scan certifies the image as free of all vulnerabilities, including unknown ones

explanation: Correct: Defender for Cloud filters and classifies findings from the scanner, and generates security recommendations only for images that have issues; healthy images are marked healthy. A is wrong: healthy images do not generate recommendations. B is wrong: findings are filtered and classified, not passed through raw. D is wrong: the scanner extracts known vulnerabilities; it does not certify an image as vulnerability-free.

prompt: A team asks whether their AKS cluster is eligible for Defender for Containers. Which support statement is correct?

options.text: Yes, Defender for Containers supports AKS clusters with Virtual Machine Scale Sets, and only clusters that use scale sets for the nodes are supported
Yes, any AKS cluster is supported regardless of node pool type
No, Defender for Containers does not support any AKS cluster
Yes, but only clusters on Kubernetes 1.19 exactly

explanation: Correct: the FAQ states Defender for Containers supports AKS clusters with Virtual Machine Scale Sets, and only those; a cluster without scale sets is not supported. B is wrong: the node pool type is the requirement. C is wrong: the requirement is about scale sets, not about the Kubernetes version. D is wrong: the sensor cannot be installed manually to bypass the requirement.

prompt: A team enables Defender for Containers but the sensor rollout is delayed by a month. What scanning still works in the meantime?

options.text: The sensor must be deployed before any registry scanning works
ACR scanning is push-triggered and periodic with no in-cluster components, while the sensor DaemonSet provides runtime threat protection separately
Registry scanning only runs manually
Registry scanning rewrites the image to add the findings

explanation: Correct: the ACR integration is push-triggered and periodic, and the sensor is a separate DaemonSet for runtime protection; registry scanning needs no in-cluster component. A is wrong: ACR scanning needs no sensor. C is wrong: scanning is push-triggered and periodic, not manual-only. D is wrong: findings are published back without modifying the image.

prompt: A cluster must refuse pods running as root and images with critical CVEs. Which control does which job, and why is one control not enough?

options.text: Azure Policy scans images for CVEs, so Defender is unnecessary
Defender for Containers blocks non-compliant pods at admission, so Policy is unnecessary
RBAC on the cluster enforces pod security standards, so neither Policy nor Defender is needed
Azure Policy enforces configuration at admission while Defender for Containers scans images for vulnerabilities and monitors runtime, so both are needed

explanation: Correct: Azure Policy enforces configuration at admission, such as refusing root containers or images from unknown registries, while Defender for Containers scans images and monitors runtime; the two are complementary. A is wrong: Policy does not scan images for CVEs. B is wrong: Defender scanning alone does not block a non-compliant pod at admission. D is wrong: RBAC does not enforce pod security configuration.

prompt: A critical CVE is published at 09:00. Agentless scanning shows no finding for a running container until the next day. Why is that expected behaviour?

options.text: Agentless scanning takes disk snapshots every 24 hours, so a vulnerability disclosed after the last snapshot appears only at the next snapshot
Agentless scanning is real-time, so the delay must be a portal bug
The sensor provides the vulnerability data in real time, so agentless scanning is irrelevant
Snapshots are weekly, so the delay is expected to be seven days

explanation: Correct: agentless scanning takes snapshots every 24 hours, so a vulnerability disclosed after the last snapshot is not visible until the next snapshot, while the sensor gives runtime telemetry but not vulnerability data. B is wrong: agentless scanning is not real-time. C is wrong: the sensor does not provide vulnerability assessment. D is wrong: the snapshot cadence is 24 hours, not weekly.

prompt: A container review finds shared admin credentials, secrets in plain-text environment variables, and public ingress on every Container Apps service. Which single remediation set closes all three gaps?

options.text: Keep the admin account and plain-text environment variables, and put everything on public ingress
Disable the admin account but keep plain-text environment variables

Disable the ACR admin account for RBAC and scope-map tokens, replace plain-text environment variables with Key Vault references retrieved by a managed identity, and use internal ingress for backend Container Apps services
Use internal ingress for the front end and public ingress for the backend API

explanation: Correct: the three container gaps closed together are disabling the ACR admin account for RBAC and scope-map tokens, replacing plain-text environment variables with Key Vault references, and using internal ingress in Container Apps. A is wrong: the admin account is disabled, not kept. B is wrong: secrets become Key Vault references, not environment variables. D is wrong: backend APIs move to internal ingress.

prompt: A team wants to fail the build if an image has a critical vulnerability, before the image is pushed to ACR. Which Defender for Containers capability does that?

options.text: There is no pipeline scanning option; images can only be scanned after they reach the registry
Use the Defender for Containers CLI tool for pipeline integration to scan the image in the CI/CD pipeline before it is pushed
Use the CLI tool to deploy the image, because it is a deployment tool
Use the CLI tool as a replacement for the registry, because it stores images

explanation: Correct: the CLI tool is for pipeline integration, so the pipeline can scan the image before it is pushed, while registry scanning happens on push and periodically. A is wrong: the CLI tool exists for pipelines. B is wrong: the CLI scans the image in the pipeline; it does not deploy it. D is wrong: the CLI is a scanning tool, not a registry replacement.

prompt: A new engineer confuses the ACR integration with the Defender sensor. What is the correct distinction?

options.text: ACR scanning is push-triggered and periodic, and the sensor DaemonSet provides runtime threat protection; they are separate components
The sensor scans registry images on push, and ACR scanning monitors runtime behaviour
Registry scanning only runs when a developer triggers it manually
The sensor must be installed manually from a third-party marketplace

explanation: Correct: the ACR integration scans images on push and periodically, and the sensor provides runtime protection; the two are separate components with separate jobs. B is wrong: the sensor does not scan registry images. C is wrong: registry scanning is automatic on push. D is wrong: the sensor is Azure-managed and natively integrated, not a manual install.

prompt: A runbook lists three different Defender plans for AKS: Defender for Kubernetes, Defender for Servers, and Defender for AKS. Which plan is actually correct for AKS container protection?

options.text: Enable Microsoft Defender for Kubernetes, because it is the current plan for AKS
Enable Defender for Servers, because it covers container image scanning
Enable a separate Defender for AKS plan, because Defender for Containers does not cover AKS
Enable Microsoft Defender for Containers, because Microsoft Defender for Kubernetes has been deprecated and replaced with it

explanation: Correct: Defender for Containers is the current plan, Microsoft Defender for Kubernetes is deprecated, and Defender for Servers is for machines, not containers. A is wrong: the Kubernetes plan is deprecated. B is wrong: Defender for Servers does not cover container scanning. D is wrong: there is no separate Defender for AKS plan; it is Defender for Containers.

prompt: A regulated workload runs on Windows VMs. The auditor asks how the OS disks, data disks and temporary disks are protected at rest, and the platform team proposes standardising on Azure Disk Encryption for every new VM. Which statement correctly describes the default, the temporary-disk gap, and the retirement trap?

options.text: Azure Disk Encryption replaces server-side encryption and remains the recommended design for all new VMs
Managed disks are unencrypted by default, so Azure Disk Encryption is the only way to get any at-rest protection

Managed disks are encrypted at rest by default with platform-managed keys; encryption at host extends protection to temporary disks and caches, while in-guest Azure Disk Encryption is retiring on 15 September 2028
Server-side encryption only protects data in transit, so Azure Disk Encryption is required for any at-rest protection

explanation: Correct: server-side encryption encrypts every managed disk at rest by default with platform-managed keys, and encryption at host extends that to temporary disks and disk caches. Azure Disk Encryption is in-guest BitLocker or DM-Crypt with keys in Key Vault, but it is scheduled for retirement on 15 September 2028, so it is not the design for new VMs. A is wrong: disks are encrypted by default. C is wrong: server-side encryption is at-rest protection, not transit-only. D is wrong: Azure Disk Encryption is retiring and is not recommended for new builds.

prompt: Administrators need RDP access to Azure VMs that have no public IP addresses, from laptops with no VPN client installed. The security team wants browser-based RDP and SSH without exposing any management port to the internet. Which service meets this requirement, and why do the alternatives fail?

options.text: Azure Bastion, which provides secure browser-based RDP and SSH over TLS without a public IP or exposed management ports on the VMs
A network security group rule opening port 3389 to the internet, restricted to the administrators office IP range
Azure Disk Encryption, which encrypts the RDP session as well as the disk
Just-in-time VM access on its own, which replaces the need for any RDP connectivity method

explanation: Correct: Bastion is a fully managed PaaS service giving RDP and SSH over TLS on port 443 from the portal or a native client, and VMs need no public IP, agent or special client software. B is wrong: opening 3389 to the internet, even to one office range, is the exposure Bastion removes. C is wrong: disk encryption protects data at rest, not remote-access connectivity. D is wrong: JIT only time-bounds when a port is open; it does not carry the RDP or SSH session, and it is normally combined with Bastion.

prompt: A VM has RDP port 3389 open to the internet and is receiving brute-force sign-in attempts. The team enables just-in-time (JIT) VM access in Defender for Cloud. What does JIT actually change, and what does it not do?

options.text: It replaces the VM administrator password with a one-time code for every sign-in
It encrypts the RDP traffic so brute-force attempts can no longer reach the VM
It permanently closes port 3389 and blocks all future RDP access to the VM
It allows access only when needed, on the ports needed, and for the time needed, with the port closed until an approved time-bound request opens it

explanation: Correct: JIT keeps management ports closed by default and opens them only when an authorised user requests access, for a limited time and from specified source IPs, then restores the block. A is wrong: JIT does not permanently block legitimate access. C is wrong: JIT is a network-access control, not a password replacement. D is wrong: JIT does not encrypt RDP; it controls port exposure, and it requires Defender for Servers Plan 2.

prompt: A company enables Defender for Servers in Defender for Cloud for its Azure VMs. A vendor claims the plan also patches the OS, encrypts the disks and provides remote access. Which capability is actually central to Defender for Servers, and which claims are false?

options.text: It provides RDP and SSH connectivity to VMs that have no public IP address
It replaces the operating system patching service and applies Windows updates automatically
It provides recommendations to improve machine posture and protects against threats, integrating Defender for Endpoint for endpoint detection and response (EDR) and Defender Vulnerability Management
It encrypts all VM disks and manages the encryption keys without any Key Vault

explanation: Correct: Defender for Servers gives posture recommendations and threat protection, integrating Defender for Endpoint for EDR and Defender Vulnerability Management. A is wrong: it does not replace OS patching; update assessment is a separate Plan 2 capability. C is wrong: disk encryption is a separate control. D is wrong: Bastion provides RDP and SSH connectivity, not Defender for Servers. Note the plan matters: JIT, agentless scanning and file integrity monitoring need Plan 2, not Plan 1.

prompt: A company has Windows servers in its own datacentre and wants them covered by Defender for Servers with full functionality, including Azure Policy enforcement, extension management and file integrity monitoring. How should those servers be onboarded, and why does the shortcut fail?

options.text: Open RDP port 3389 on each server so Defender for Cloud can scan it over the internet
Move the servers to Azure; Defender for Servers cannot protect any machine outside Azure
Install only the Defender for Endpoint agent directly; that gives full Defender for Servers Plan 2 functionality
Onboard them as Azure Arc-enabled servers, so they appear as Azure resources and receive full Defender for Servers functionality

explanation: Correct: Learn recommends onboarding non-Azure machines as Azure Arc-enabled VMs so they take full advantage of Defender for Servers features, including Azure Policy and machine configuration. A is wrong: direct Defender for Endpoint install without Arc gives only Plan 1 functionality, plus premium vulnerability-management features in Plan 2, not full functionality. C is wrong: exposing RDP is not an onboarding method. D is wrong: Defender for Servers explicitly protects Azure, AWS, GCP and on-premises machines.

prompt: A security engineer enables Trusted Launch on a new Generation 2 Azure VM. An auditor asks which protections that single setting actually provides against boot kits and rootkits. Which answer is correct?

options.text: Automatic patching, vulnerability scanning, and file integrity monitoring with no agent
Disk encryption, network encryption, and backup encryption in a single setting
Secure Boot, a virtual Trusted Platform Module (vTPM), and integrity monitoring to protect against boot-level malware and rootkits
Just-in-time access, Azure Bastion connectivity, and Defender for Endpoint in one toggle

explanation: Correct: Trusted Launch comprises Secure Boot, a virtual Trusted Platform Module (vTPM) and integrity monitoring, and it is the default for newly created Generation 2 VMs. A is wrong: Trusted Launch is not a disk, network or backup encryption bundle. C is wrong: JIT and Bastion are separate network-access controls. D is wrong: patching, vulnerability scanning and file integrity monitoring are Defender for Servers capabilities, not Trusted Launch itself.

prompt: A security team wants vulnerability scanning of Azure VMs without installing an agent on each VM, and enforcement of secure in-guest settings, for example that a required security setting stays applied. Which two Defender for Cloud capabilities match those needs?

options.text: Scan VMs only during a maintenance window by shutting them down
Agentless scanning and Machine Configuration are the same feature with two names
Install an agent on every VM to scan its disk; that is what agentless scanning means
Use agentless scanning for out-of-band vulnerability scanning of disk snapshots, and Azure Machine Configuration to enforce the in-guest configuration

explanation: Correct: agentless scanning periodically scans disk snapshots out of band without an in-guest agent, and Azure Machine Configuration enforces in-guest settings such as a required secure configuration. A is wrong: agentless scanning does not run inside the guest. C is wrong: shutting VMs down is not how agentless scanning works. D is wrong: they are two distinct capabilities, one for scanning and one for configuration enforcement.

prompt: A regulated workload runs on Windows VMs encrypted with Azure Disk Encryption (BitLocker in the guest, keys in Key Vault). The platform team says encryption is encryption and there is nothing to do. A review notes a retirement date for Azure Disk Encryption. What must actually happen, and why?

options.text: Snapshot the ADE-encrypted disks and restore them onto encryption-at-host VMs
Keep Azure Disk Encryption and renew the Key Vault keys annually; there is no retirement date
Migrate the VMs to encryption at host before 15 September 2028, rebuilding with new upload disks and a new VM, because after that date ADE-encrypted disks fail to unlock on reboot
Switch to platform-managed server-side encryption only and keep the existing VMs untouched; that is a full migration off Azure Disk Encryption

explanation: Correct: Azure Disk Encryption is scheduled for retirement on 15 September 2028, after which encrypted disks will fail to unlock after VM reboots; Learn directs migration to encryption at host, and the migration requires new upload disks and a new VM, not snapshots. A is wrong: waiting is the risk, not a fix. C is wrong: server-side encryption alone does not encrypt the temporary disk and is not a migration off Azure Disk Encryption. D is wrong: snapshots do not migrate an ADE-encrypted VM to encryption at host.

prompt: A company on Defender for Servers Plan 1 enables a JIT policy on a VM, but the policy never takes effect, and the helpdesk, who should only request access, can edit the policy. Two faults are present. Which fix addresses both?

options.text: Open port 3389 in the NSG permanently and call that JIT, because JIT is just an NSG naming convention
Grant every administrator the initiate and action permission, because that single permission both configures policies and requests access
Enable Defender for Servers Plan 1, then grant the admins the Reader role, because Reader alone lets them configure JIT policies

Enable Defender for Servers Plan 2, then grant the admins jitNetworkAccessPolicies write (plus virtualMachines write) to configure policies; the helpdesk only needs initiate and action plus read permissions to request access

explanation: Correct: JIT requires Defender for Servers Plan 2 on the subscription; configuring a policy needs the jitNetworkAccessPolicies write action plus virtualMachines write, while requesting access needs only initiate and action plus read permissions, so a user who can request cannot necessarily configure. A is wrong: Plan 1 does not include JIT, and Reader cannot configure policies. C is wrong: an NSG rule is not the JIT mechanism; JIT temporarily modifies effective access through the policy. D is wrong: the two actions are distinct in the permission model.

prompt: A VM has a public IP and an NSG rule opening 3389 to the internet. The team proposes: keep the public IP because Bastion needs it, open 3389 to the office range for convenience, and enable JIT on Defender for Servers Plan 1. Which response correctly fixes this design?

options.text: Disable Bastion and rely on JIT alone, because JIT encrypts the RDP session
Keep the public IP, because Bastion requires the VM to have a public IP to connect
Deploy Azure Bastion (no public IP on the VM) and enable JIT under Defender for Servers Plan 2; remove the NSG rule opening 3389
Add an NSG rule opening 3389 to the office IP range and enable JIT under Plan 1, because that is equivalent to Bastion

explanation: Correct: Bastion provides RDP and SSH without a public IP on the VM, and JIT under Defender for Servers Plan 2 time-bounds the port; opening 3389 in an NSG, even to a trusted range, reintroduces the exposure both controls exist to remove. A is wrong: Bastion does not require a public IP on the VM. C is wrong: the NSG rule defeats both Bastion and JIT, and JIT is a Plan 2 feature, not Plan 1. D is wrong: JIT does not encrypt the RDP session, and Plan 1 would not enable it.

prompt: A company enables Defender for Servers Plan 2. Its Azure VMs get JIT access and file integrity monitoring, but its on-premises servers, onboarded by installing the Defender for Endpoint agent directly without Azure Arc, do not. Why?

options.text: The Plan 2 toggle was applied at the wrong scope; re-enabling it at the subscription will unlock JIT on those servers
The servers were onboarded by direct Defender for Endpoint agent install instead of Azure Arc, so only Plan 1 functionality is available (plus premium vulnerability management in Plan 2)
Defender for Endpoint was not installed, so no Defender for Servers features work at all
The servers must be migrated to Azure; on-premises machines cannot receive any Defender for Servers protection

explanation: Correct: on-premises machines onboarded by directly installing the Defender for Endpoint agent without Azure Arc get only Plan 1 functionality, and in Plan 2 only the premium Defender Vulnerability Management features are added. A is wrong: the install method determines functionality, not the plan toggle alone. C is wrong: EDR is included in both plans; the gap is the Arc-dependent Plan 2 features. D is wrong: the servers are not unprotected; they get Plan 1 functionality.

prompt: A new workload needs the OS disk, data disks AND the temporary (ephemeral) disk encrypted, with the customer holding the key, on a standard (non-confidential) VM. Azure Disk Encryption is ruled out because it is retiring. Which option fits, and what distinguishes it from the default?

options.text: Azure Disk Encryption, because it encrypts data on the host before it reaches storage
Encryption at host with a customer-managed key in a Disk Encryption Set, because it encrypts on the host including temporary disks, unlike platform-managed server-side encryption alone
Platform-managed server-side encryption alone, because it already encrypts temporary disks and the host layer
Confidential disk encryption, which is available on every VM size and replaces all other encryption options

explanation: Correct: server-side encryption with platform-managed keys encrypts managed disks at rest by default, while encryption at host encrypts data on the host before it reaches storage, including temporary disks, and supports customer-managed keys through a Disk Encryption Set. Azure Disk Encryption is in-guest BitLocker or DM-Crypt and is retiring. A is wrong: it describes Azure Disk Encryption, which is retiring and is not the host-level option. C is wrong: server-side encryption alone does not cover the temporary disk or the host layer. D is wrong: confidential disk encryption applies to confidential VM sizes, not every VM.

prompt: A CISO must choose between Defender for Servers Plan 1 and Plan 2 for a fleet of Azure VMs. The board wants EDR everywhere, but the security team also needs agentless vulnerability scanning, just-in-time access and file integrity monitoring. Which plan statement is correct?

options.text: Plan 1 includes just-in-time VM access and agentless scanning; Plan 2 only adds reporting dashboards
Plan 2 replaces Plan 1 entirely and removes Defender for Endpoint integration
Plan 1 focuses on endpoint detection and response through Defender for Endpoint; Plan 2 adds agentless scanning, just-in-time VM access, file integrity monitoring and OS update assessment
The two plans are identical in capability and differ only in per-machine price

explanation: Correct: Defender for Servers Plan 2 adds agentless scanning for machine posture, vulnerability assessment, threat protection, malware scanning and secrets scanning, plus JIT, file integrity monitoring and OS update assessment. Plan 1 is entry-level EDR only. A is wrong: Plan 1 does not include JIT or agentless scanning. B is wrong: Plan 2 is a superset of Plan 1, not a replacement with different EDR. D is wrong: the plans differ in capability, not merely in price.

prompt: A team enables Defender for Servers Plan 2 and expects file integrity monitoring of OS files and Windows registries to start working immediately. Nothing is monitored. What is the correct enablement sequence, and which assumption is wrong?

options.text: Enable Defender for Servers Plan 2, then explicitly turn file integrity monitoring on, with the Defender for Endpoint agent deployed and agentless machine scanning enabled for extra coverage
Enable Defender for Servers Plan 1, because file integrity monitoring is on by default in every plan
Enable agentless scanning only and assume file integrity monitoring starts automatically
Rely on the Log Analytics agent, because the Defender for Endpoint based file integrity monitoring experience is the legacy one

explanation: Correct: file integrity monitoring is a Plan 2 feature, it is not enabled by default, and it needs the Defender for Endpoint agent plus agentless machine scanning for extra coverage and custom paths, with non-Azure machines connected through Azure Arc. A is wrong: FIM is not on by default. C is wrong: Plan 1 does not include FIM. D is wrong: agentless scanning alone gives 24-hour cadence data; near-real-time change events come from the Defender for Endpoint agent.

prompt: During an incident, a registry change on a server is visible in file integrity monitoring a day after it happened. The SOC asks why the detection was not near real time. Which statement about FIM data collection explains the delay?

options.text: Agentless scanning streams change events in near real time, while the Defender for Endpoint agent reports once a day
Both collection paths stream change events in near real time with identical latency
The Log Analytics agent is the current near-real-time collector and agentless scanning is its backup
The Defender for Endpoint agent streams change events in near real time, while agentless scanning streams them on a 24-hour cadence

explanation: Correct: FIM data collection uses the Defender for Endpoint agent for near-real-time change events and agentless scanning on a 24-hour cadence, so a change found only by agentless scanning can be up to a day old. A is wrong: agentless data is not real-time. B is wrong: the agent path is the near-real-time one, not the 24-hour one. C is wrong: the Log Analytics agent path is the legacy, deprecated collection method.

prompt: A security team wants vulnerability and secrets scanning of VMs without deploying any agent, and a vendor claims agentless scanning is in Plan 1 and replaces EDR. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Agentless scanning is included in Defender for Servers Plan 1 and runs inside the guest operating system
Agentless scanning is a Plan 2 capability that assesses disk snapshots out of band for vulnerabilities, secrets and malware without an in-guest agent
Agentless scanning monitors live guest memory in real time and replaces the Defender for Endpoint agent
Agentless scanning only works on Azure VMs and never on Arc-enabled servers

explanation: Correct: agentless scanning is a Plan 2 capability that scans disk snapshots out of band for software inventory, vulnerabilities, secrets and malware, without an in-guest agent. A is wrong: agentless scanning is not a Plan 1 feature. C is wrong: it scans snapshots, not live guest memory in real time. D is wrong: agentless scanning is in addition to agent-based scanning, not a replacement for the Defender for Endpoint sensor.

prompt: A company runs servers in its own datacentre and in AWS. It wants one Defender for Cloud inventory, Azure Policy enforcement and Sentinel coverage for all of them without migrating any workload. Which Arc design is correct?

options.text: Onboard the servers with the Azure Arc Connected Machine agent, which projects them into Azure Resource Manager over outbound HTTPS on port 443 so Defender for Cloud and Azure Policy can manage them
Migrate the servers into Azure VMs, because Arc cannot manage machines that stay on premises
Open inbound RDP and SSH from the internet so Defender for Cloud can reach each server directly
Install only the Defender for Endpoint sensor, because Arc adds nothing for servers that already have EDR

explanation: Correct: Azure Arc projects on-premises and other-cloud machines into Azure Resource Manager, after which Defender for Cloud, Azure Policy and Sentinel can target them, and the Connected Machine agent connects outbound over port 443. A is wrong: Arc does not move workloads into Azure. C is wrong: inbound RDP is not required; the agent connects outbound. D is wrong: Arc is the prerequisite for full Defender for Servers functionality on non-Azure machines.

prompt: A team must onboard 800 on-premises servers to Azure Arc. The proposed runbook uses one shared global admin account for interactive onboarding and routes agent traffic through the Log Analytics gateway. Which design is correct, and what is wrong with the runbook?

options.text: Onboard every server interactively with one global admin account and leave the agent at default settings
Route the Connected Machine agent through the Log Analytics gateway as a proxy to save firewall rules
Onboard at scale with a dedicated service principal holding the Azure Connected Machine Onboarding role scoped to specific resource groups, and lock down agent settings locally with azcmagent
The Connected Machine agent cannot be locked down locally, so any local administrator can reconfigure it without restriction

explanation: Correct: the Connected Machine agent supports local lockdown through azcmagent, and at-scale onboarding should use a dedicated service principal with the Azure Connected Machine Onboarding role scoped to specific resource groups, not a shared admin account. A is wrong: interactive admin credentials do not scale and are not least privilege. B is wrong: the Log Analytics gateway is not supported as a proxy for the Connected Machine agent. D is wrong: agent settings can be locked down locally; there is no requirement to leave the agent fully open.

prompt: A company runs EC2 instances in AWS and Compute Engine VMs in GCP and wants Defender for Servers coverage with the least operational effort. Which onboarding design is correct?

options.text: The multicloud connector alone gives AWS and GCP servers full Plan 2 features including JIT and file integrity monitoring

Use the Defender for Cloud multicloud connector with automatic Arc agent onboarding: agentless features come through the connector, and Arc-dependent features such as file integrity monitoring arrive once Arc is deployed
Agentless scanning cannot work on AWS or GCP machines at all, even through the connector
Directly install the Defender for Endpoint agent on every EC2 instance instead, because that gives more functionality than Arc

explanation: Correct: the multicloud connector can automatically onboard the Arc agent to AWS and GCP servers, giving agentless features through the connector and Arc-dependent features once Arc is deployed. A is wrong: the connector does not give JIT and file integrity monitoring without Arc. C is wrong: agentless features work through the connector even before Arc is deployed. D is wrong: direct Defender for Endpoint install is a different onboarding path with reduced functionality.

prompt: A regulated bank needs RDP access to production VMs with every session recorded for compliance, and the Bastion host itself must have no public IP address. Which Bastion SKU and design meet both requirements?

options.text: Use the Premium SKU, which includes session recording for compliance and supports private-only deployment without a public IP
Use the Basic SKU, which includes session recording and private-only deployment
Use the Developer SKU in production, because it is free and includes all Standard features
Deploy a self-managed jump VM with a public IP instead, because Bastion cannot record sessions

explanation: Correct: Bastion Premium adds session recording for compliance and private-only deployment without a public IP, while Basic, Standard and Premium require a dedicated AzureBastionSubnet and a public IP. A is wrong: session recording is a Premium feature, not Basic. C is wrong: the Developer SKU is for dev and test, not production session recording. D is wrong: Bastion is a PaaS service, not a self-managed jump VM.

prompt: An architect must design administrative access so that no management port is ever internet-reachable AND no port stays open longer than needed. A colleague argues one control is enough. Which layered design is correct?

options.text: Bastion alone, because Bastion time-bounds management ports automatically
JIT alone, because JIT carries the RDP session over TLS on port 443
Microsoft Entra PIM alone, because PIM opens and closes network ports
Bastion plus JIT: Bastion provides the secure access channel while JIT provides time-bounded port control, and JIT requires Defender for Servers Plan 2

explanation: Correct: JIT and Bastion solve different problems and combine for defence in depth: Bastion provides the secure channel, JIT provides time-bounded port control, and JIT requires Defender for Servers Plan 2. A is wrong: Bastion alone does not time-bound port exposure. B is wrong: JIT alone still needs a connectivity path and does not carry the session. C is wrong: PIM governs role activation, not network port exposure.

prompt: A compliance team requires customer-managed keys for managed disks, with the customer able to revoke access. The team proposes platform-managed keys plus a Disk Encryption Set. What is the correct design, and what is the revocation consequence?

options.text: Use platform-managed keys, because they require a Disk Encryption Set and the customer holds the key
Use a customer-managed key in a Disk Encryption Set backed by Key Vault or Managed HSM, and accept that disabling or deleting the key makes the disks undecryptable
Enable double encryption, because that alone gives the customer control of the key without Key Vault
Use a customer-managed key but store it in the VM, so Key Vault availability never matters

explanation: Correct: a customer-managed key needs a Disk Encryption Set backed by Key Vault or Managed HSM, and if that key is disabled or deleted the disks cannot be decrypted, so key loss is data loss. A is wrong: platform-managed keys need no Disk Encryption Set and Microsoft manages them. C is wrong: double encryption is a second layer, not the mechanism that makes CMK work. D is wrong: key rotation does not remove the dependency on the key vault.

prompt: A team wants Trusted Launch protection against boot kits on an existing Generation 1 VM. The engineer proposes enabling it in place. What is the correct answer, and why?

options.text: Rebuild the workload as a Generation 2 VM, because Trusted Launch is the default for newly created Generation 2 VMs and cannot be added to a Generation 1 VM in place
Install the Trusted Launch agent on the Generation 1 VM and enable it in the guest operating system
Enable Azure Disk Encryption instead, because that provides Secure Boot and a virtual TPM
Enable Defender for Servers Plan 2, because Trusted Launch is included in that plan for any VM generation

explanation: Correct: Trusted Launch is the default for newly created Generation 2 VMs, and it protects the boot chain with Secure Boot, vTPM and integrity monitoring. A Generation 1 VM cannot be converted in place; the workload must be rebuilt as Generation 2. B is wrong: Trusted Launch is not an agent you install. C is wrong: disk encryption does not provide Secure Boot or vTPM. D is wrong: Trusted Launch is a platform feature, not a Defender for Servers plan feature.

prompt: A team must prove that a security baseline stays applied on 200 Azure VMs and drift is corrected, not just reported once. Which mechanism enforces in-guest configuration, and which plan feature assesses the baseline?

options.text: Rely on agentless scanning, because scanning a disk snapshot enforces the in-guest configuration
Use a manual quarterly checklist, because Azure has no mechanism to enforce in-guest VM settings
Use Azure Machine Configuration through the machine configuration extension, with Defender for Servers Plan 2 OS baseline recommendations for Windows and Linux
Use the Log Analytics agent guest configuration, because the machine configuration extension is only for Arc servers

explanation: Correct: Defender for Cloud collects machine information using the Azure machine configuration extension, and Plan 2 OS baseline recommendations cover Linux and Windows compute security baselines. A is wrong: Machine Configuration is the enforcement mechanism, not a manual checklist. B is wrong: agentless scanning assesses snapshots; it does not enforce in-guest settings. D is wrong: the Log Analytics agent path is legacy.

prompt: A VM in a virtual network has no network security group and is not behind Azure Firewall. The team enables a JIT policy, but requests fail. What is the missing prerequisite?

options.text: Enable JIT anyway, because JIT creates its own network security group automatically
Attach a network security group or place the VM behind Azure Firewall first, because JIT works by temporarily adjusting those rules and needs a supported network-control path
Assign a public IP to the VM, because JIT only works on VMs with public IPs
Upgrade to Defender for Servers Plan 2 only, because the plan alone creates the network path JIT needs

explanation: Correct: JIT requires a supported network-control path, an NSG or Azure Firewall, because it works by temporarily adjusting those rules; without one there is nothing for the policy to modify. A is wrong: JIT does not create network controls from nothing. C is wrong: a public IP is not the requirement; the NSG or firewall is. D is wrong: JIT is a Plan 2 feature, but the plan alone does not create the network path.

prompt: An administrator requests JIT access to a VM for two hours from one source IP. What happens automatically when the two hours expire?

options.text: The port stays open until an administrator manually closes it
The VM administrator password is rotated automatically when the window ends
The administrator account is disabled until the next request is approved
Defender for Cloud automatically restores the NSG or Azure Firewall rules to block inbound traffic when the time window expires

explanation: Correct: JIT restores the NSG or firewall rules automatically when the time window expires, so access is time-bound by design. A is wrong: the port does not stay open. B is wrong: JIT does not change the VM password. C is wrong: JIT does not disable the account; it closes the network path.

prompt: A finance team asks whether the default disk encryption on Azure VMs costs extra or slows disks, and a developer claims the default also covers the temporary disk. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Server-side encryption is always enabled, uses 256-bit AES, has no extra cost and no performance effect, but does not encrypt temporary disks or disk caches
Server-side encryption adds significant cost and slows disk performance, so it should be disabled for production VMs
Server-side encryption encrypts network traffic between the VM and the storage cluster only
Server-side encryption is optional and off by default, and must be enabled per disk

explanation: Correct: server-side encryption is always enabled with 256-bit AES, FIPS 140-2 compliant, at no extra cost and with no performance effect, but it does not encrypt temp disks or disk caches. B is wrong: SSE has no extra cost and does not affect disk performance. C is wrong: SSE is at-rest encryption of managed disks, not a network control. D is wrong: SSE is always on; it cannot be disabled to save cost.

prompt: A workload writes sensitive data to the temporary disk and the OS disk cache. Server-side encryption alone leaves both unencrypted. Which option closes that gap, and how does it work?

options.text: Enable BitLocker inside the guest, because that is what encryption at host means
Enable encryption at host in Key Vault, because it is a vault setting not a VM setting
Enable encryption at host on the VM, which encrypts temporary disks, disk caches and the data flow to storage on the host without consuming VM CPU
Use confidential disk encryption, because encryption at host only works on confidential VM sizes

explanation: Correct: encryption at host encrypts data on the host before it reaches storage, covering temporary disks, OS and data disk caches and the data flow to storage, using AES 256 without consuming VM CPU. A is wrong: that describes in-guest Azure Disk Encryption. B is wrong: encryption at host is a VM-level setting, not a Key Vault feature. D is wrong: encryption at host works on standard VMs; confidential disk encryption is the confidential-VM option.

prompt: A team wants Defender for Cloud to assess whether its Azure VMs are missing OS updates, and a vendor claims the plan will also install the patches. Which plan and which correction are right?

options.text: Defender for Servers Plan 1, because update assessment is included in Plan 1 and applies patches automatically
Defender for Servers Plan 2, which provides OS update assessment integrated with Azure Updates, while the patching itself remains a separate update-management action
Defender for Servers Plan 2, because it applies Windows updates automatically with no maintenance window
Azure Arc, because update assessment for Azure VMs requires the Connected Machine agent

explanation: Correct: Defender for Servers Plan 2 OS update assessment is integrated with Azure Updates, and it is a Plan 2 capability, not a patching service that applies updates itself. A is wrong: Defender assesses updates; it does not replace the patching service. C is wrong: update assessment is Plan 2 only. D is wrong: Azure Arc is for non-Azure machines, not the update mechanism for Azure VMs.

prompt: A scan flags a plain-text private key sitting in a backup folder on a VM disk, but no agent ever ran on that VM. Which capability found it, and why is the finding credible?

options.text: Agentless machine secrets scanning in Defender for Servers Plan 2, which scans disk snapshots for plain-text secrets without an in-guest agent
Agentless secrets scanning in Plan 1, because all scanning features are in Plan 1
The Defender for Endpoint agent, because agentless scanning cannot see secrets that are only on disk
A false positive, because secrets at rest on a disk cannot be found without a running agent

explanation: Correct: agentless secrets scanning is a Plan 2 capability that locates plain-text secrets on machines from disk snapshots, which is why it can find a key the running agent never saw. B is wrong: secrets scanning is Plan 2 only. C is wrong: agentless scanning works from snapshots; it does not need the secret to be in a running process. D is wrong: the finding is real; agentless scanning is designed to find secrets at rest on the disk.

prompt: A team still runs file integrity monitoring through the Log Analytics agent (MMA). Microsoft has deprecated that collection method. What must the team do, and what is the current collection model?

options.text: Keep the Log Analytics agent (MMA) collection, because it is the current recommended method
Enable FIM on Plan 1 with any Defender for Endpoint agent version
Enable agentless scanning only, because it fully replaces the Defender for Endpoint agent for FIM
Migrate to the Defender for Endpoint based FIM experience with the minimum agent version, since the MMA and AMA collection methods are deprecated

explanation: Correct: the new FIM experience uses the Defender for Endpoint agent and agentless scanning, requires a minimum agent version, and the MMA and AMA collection methods are deprecated and must be migrated. A is wrong: the MMA path is the legacy one being retired. B is wrong: FIM needs the MDE agent version and Plan 2. C is wrong: agentless scanning adds coverage and custom paths; it does not replace the agent for near-real-time events.

prompt: A firewall team will only allow outbound port 443 from administrator laptops. The team needs RDP to VMs with no public IPs. Which Bastion connectivity statement is correct?

options.text: Open port 3389 to the internet and use Bastion only as a backup path
Connect through Bastion over TLS on port 443 from the portal or native client, with no public IP and no open management port on the VM
Deploy Bastion as a VM in the virtual network and patch it like any other server
Use the Developer SKU for production, because it has the same features as Standard

explanation: Correct: Bastion connects over TLS on port 443 from the portal or native client, and the VM needs no public IP. A is wrong: Bastion does not need 3389 open to the internet. C is wrong: Bastion is a managed PaaS service, not a jump VM you patch. D is wrong: the Developer SKU is for dev and test, not a production replacement for Standard or Premium.

prompt: A company has 300 Azure VMs and 150 datacentre servers. The CISO enables Defender for Servers Plan 2 on the subscription and declares the whole estate covered. What is missing?

options.text: Enable the plan on the subscription; that automatically onboards the datacentre servers too
Enable the plan on the subscription for the Azure VMs and onboard the datacentre servers through Azure Arc for full Plan 2 functionality
Move the datacentre servers to Azure, because Defender for Servers cannot protect on-premises machines
Enable Plan 1 per VM on the datacentre servers, because that is the same as Arc onboarding

explanation: Correct: enabling the plan at the subscription covers Azure VMs, while non-Azure machines need Arc onboarding to get full functionality; direct Defender for Endpoint install gives only Plan 1 functionality. A is wrong: the subscription toggle does not onboard on-premises servers. C is wrong: Defender for Servers protects on-premises and multicloud machines when onboarded correctly. D is wrong: Plan 1 per VM is for Azure VMs, not a substitute for Arc onboarding.

prompt: A defence customer requires two independent layers of encryption at rest on its managed disks, one with a Microsoft-managed key and one with a customer-managed key. Which option meets that requirement?

options.text: Enable double encryption on the managed disks, which layers a platform-managed key and a customer-managed key for two layers of at-rest encryption
Enable encryption at host, because that is the same as double encryption
Use a single customer-managed key, because that already counts as double encryption
Use Azure Disk Encryption, because double encryption is only available in the guest

explanation: Correct: double encryption uses a platform-managed key and a customer-managed key, so it is for customers who need two layers of at-rest encryption, and it is distinct from encryption at host, which covers temp disks. B is wrong: double encryption is not the same as encryption at host. C is wrong: a customer-managed key alone is single encryption with a customer key. D is wrong: double encryption is a managed-disk option, not a replacement for in-guest BitLocker.

prompt: An engineer asks how JIT actually enforces time-bound access at the network layer. Which mechanism is correct?

options.text: JIT authenticates the administrator with MFA and replaces the need for Entra ID
JIT applies a deny rule on management ports and adds a higher-priority temporary allow rule only when access is requested, then removes it
JIT encrypts the RDP session so the open port is safe
JIT removes the public IP from the VM permanently

explanation: Correct: JIT is a Defender for Cloud feature that restricts network access to VMs by applying deny rules and only allowing temporary access when requested, and the temporary allow rule has higher priority than the deny rule. A is wrong: JIT does not authenticate the user; Entra ID and PIM do that. C is wrong: JIT does not encrypt anything. D is wrong: JIT does not remove the public IP; Bastion or removing the IP does that.

prompt: A threat model identifies boot kits and rootkits that load before the operating system as the top VM risk. Which control addresses that threat, and why do the others not?

options.text: Azure Disk Encryption, because encrypting the disk stops a boot kit from running
Just-in-time VM access, because closing port 3389 stops boot-level malware
Defender for Servers vulnerability scanning, because scanning finds boot kits before they run
Trusted Launch with Secure Boot, vTPM and integrity monitoring, because it protects the boot chain against boot kits, rootkits and kernel-level malware

explanation: Correct: Secure Boot, vTPM and integrity monitoring protect the boot chain against boot kits, rootkits and kernel-level malware, which is the Trusted Launch threat model. A is wrong: disk encryption does not stop a boot kit. B is wrong: JIT controls network access, not the boot chain. D is wrong: vulnerability scanning finds known software flaws; it does not prevent boot-level tampering.

prompt: After onboarding datacentre servers through Azure Arc, what does the team actually get in Defender for Cloud, and which common belief about Arc servers is wrong?

options.text: Arc-enabled servers appear in Defender for Cloud inventory alongside Azure VMs, and Defender for Servers then deploys Defender for Endpoint, vulnerability assessment and just-in-time access
Arc-enabled servers are visible in inventory but never receive a Secure Score
Arc-enabled servers require inbound port 3389 from Defender for Cloud to be protected
Arc-enabled servers cannot receive just-in-time access even after Defender for Servers is enabled

explanation: Correct: Arc-enabled servers appear in Defender for Cloud inventory alongside Azure VMs, and enabling Defender for Servers deploys Defender for Endpoint, vulnerability assessment and just-in-time access for them. B is wrong: Arc-enabled servers do get a Secure Score like native resources. C is wrong: the Connected Machine agent connects outbound over 443; no inbound opening is needed. D is wrong: Arc is the recommended path for full functionality.

prompt: A VM shows agent-based vulnerability findings but zero agentless findings, while a sibling VM shows both. What best explains the gap?

options.text: The VM is turned off, so no scanning of any kind can ever run
Agentless scanning runs inside the guest, so it must have failed because the agent crashed
Agentless scanning assesses disk snapshots out of band, so an unreadable or unsupported disk yields no agentless findings even though agent-based scanning still works
The subscription was charged for Plan 1 instead of Plan 2, so all scanning stopped

explanation: Correct: agentless scanning works from disk snapshots, so an encrypted disk it cannot read, or a disk in an unsupported host, produces no agentless findings, while the agent-based path still works. A is wrong: agentless scanning does not run in the guest. B is wrong: agentless findings depend on snapshot readability and host support. D is wrong: Plan 2 includes both paths, and the gap is a coverage limitation, not a billing error.

prompt: A team wants to evaluate Defender for Servers Plan 2 in a trial before committing. What is the trial trap they must plan around?

options.text: The trial can be paused and resumed whenever the team is ready
The trial runs for 30 days from enablement and cannot be stopped, paused or extended, so the team should plan the evaluation before enabling it
The trial lasts 90 days and auto-extends if no alerts fire
The trial only starts when the first threat alert is generated

explanation: Correct: the 30-day trial begins when Defender for Servers is enabled, and there is no way to stop, pause or extend it, so a trial must be planned, not started casually. A is wrong: the trial cannot be paused or extended. C is wrong: the trial is 30 days, not 90. D is wrong: the trial starts on enablement, not on first alert.

prompt: An attacker modifies a system binary and a registry key on a server. The SOC wants a control that detects exactly those changes. Which capability is it, and what does it not do?

options.text: File integrity monitoring in Defender for Servers Plan 2, which scans operating system files, Windows registries, application software and Linux system files for changes that might indicate an attack
File integrity monitoring in Plan 1, which blocks any change to a monitored file automatically
Azure Backup, because FIM restores changed files from backup
Free foundational posture management, because FIM needs no paid plan

explanation: Correct: FIM examines OS files, Windows registries, application software and Linux system files for changes that might indicate an attack, and it is configured after enabling Plan 2. B is wrong: FIM does not block changes; it detects and reports them. C is wrong: FIM is not a backup or restore feature. D is wrong: FIM is a Plan 2 feature, not part of free foundational posture management.

prompt: A team must monitor a custom application folder that is not in the recommended FIM set. How do they add it, and what is the limit?

options.text: FIM only monitors the recommended resources and cannot be extended to custom paths
FIM monitors every file on the disk by default with no configuration
Create a custom FIM rule for the application folder path, because custom rules can monitor specific files or folders, up to 500 rules, and agentless scanning adds custom-path coverage
FIM allows at most five custom rules per subscription

explanation: Correct: a custom FIM rule can monitor a specific folder path, with up to 500 rules, and agentless scanning enables custom paths in addition to recommended resources. A is wrong: FIM does not monitor arbitrary paths by default; custom rules are needed. B is wrong: recommended resources are a starting set, not a hard limit. D is wrong: the limit is 500 rules, not five.

prompt: Administrators need to connect with their native RDP client, use custom ports and transfer files, but the compliance team has not required session recording. Which Bastion SKU is the right fit, and why not the others?

options.text: Basic, because it includes native client access and file transfer
Standard, because it includes native client, IP-based connections, custom ports and file transfer, while session recording stays a Premium feature
Standard, because it includes session recording for compliance
Developer, because it is free and identical to Standard in production

explanation: Correct: Bastion Standard adds native client, shareable links, IP-based connections, custom ports and file transfer over Basic, while Premium adds session recording and private-only deployment. A is wrong: Basic does not include file transfer or native client. C is wrong: session recording is Premium, not Standard. D is wrong: the Developer SKU is free for dev and test, not a production Standard equivalent.

prompt: A compliance report shows OS baseline misconfigurations for some VMs but not others, and the team is on mixed plans. Which plan statement explains the gap?

options.text: OS baseline misconfigurations are assessed under Plan 2 only, using the machine configuration extension, while other Microsoft Cloud Security Benchmark recommendations stay in free foundational posture management
OS baseline misconfigurations are included in Plan 1 and in the free tier
Enabling Plan 2 automatically remediates every OS baseline misconfiguration with no policy needed
OS baselines are assessed by agentless scanning alone, with no machine configuration extension involved
