Moving a subscription breaks the relationship between the role assignment and its definition on the Sandbox management group; the documented fixes are removing the assignment before moving, adding the subscription to the assignable scope, or updating assignable scopes to the root management group. B is wrong — subscriptions with resources can move. A is wrong — management groups can be moved with the right permissions. D is wrong — the error is about the definition-assignment path, not Owner.

prompt: A team designs a custom role with DataActions and wants to assign it at the management group scope to enforce data-plane access across all subscriptions. What will they discover?

options.text: DataActions are automatically converted to Actions at management group scope
DataActions roles can be assigned at any scope including management groups
Only one management group per directory may host a DataActions role
Custom roles with DataActions cannot be assigned at the management group scope

explanation: Correct: D. A documented limitation is that custom roles with DataActions cannot be assigned at the management group scope. B contradicts that limitation. C is wrong — the one-management-group limit applies to assignable scopes in a role definition, not to DataActions. A is wrong — no such conversion exists.

prompt: An enterprise wants new subscriptions to automatically receive governance policies and permissions the moment they are created, with no manual step. Which design delivers this?

options.text: Use the root management group to assign enterprise-wide security elements, since new subscriptions automatically default to the root management group
Assign policies at the subscription level after each creation via a runbook
Create a Blueprint assignment per subscription, which auto-applies to future subscriptions
Rely on Azure Policy's automatic discovery, which assigns policies to new subscriptions without a scope

explanation: Correct: A. Microsoft recommends using the root management group to assign enterprise-wide security elements that apply to all Azure assets, and new subscriptions automatically default to the root management group when created. B is wrong — it requires a manual or runbook step per subscription. C is wrong — Blueprints is retiring and assignments are per-scope. D is wrong — policy assignments require a scope; there is no automatic assignment without one.

prompt: A company has many subscriptions and wants a single pane to assess compliance of all resources against ISO 27001, HIPAA, and PCI DSS. Which Azure Policy capability provides this, and what does it show?

options.text: The activity log, which lists every deployment in the last 24 hours
The compliance dashboard, which provides an aggregated view of the overall state of the environment with drill-down to per-resource, per-policy granularity
Azure Advisor, which only shows cost recommendations
The Blueprint assignment view, which is the only place initiatives appear

explanation: Correct: B. Azure Policy's compliance dashboard provides an aggregated view to evaluate the overall state of the environment, with drill-down to per-resource, per-policy granularity, and built-in initiatives exist for standards including FedRAMP High, HIPAA, HITRUST, PCI DSS, and ISO 27001. A is wrong — the activity log is not a compliance aggregation. C is wrong — Advisor covers more than cost but is not the policy compliance dashboard. D is wrong — initiatives are visible in Policy, not only in Blueprints.

prompt: A healthcare company deploys Azure AI Services and wants to enforce that key-based (local) authentication is disabled so only Microsoft Entra ID can be used. Which governance approach aligns with Microsoft's published regulatory guidance?

options.text: A Conditional Access policy targeting the AI Services data plane, which is the only supported control
An Azure Policy that deletes any AI Services resource found with keys enabled
A FedRAMP Moderate initiative definition that audits or denies AI Services resources with key access enabled, since the built-in guidance says key access is recommended to be disabled for security
A Blueprint lock, because policy cannot evaluate AI Services resources

explanation: Correct: C. The FedRAMP Moderate initiative includes a definition stating Azure AI Services resources should have key access disabled (disable local authentication), noting that after disabling, Microsoft Entra ID becomes the only access method. B is wrong — policy effects remediate or block, they do not delete resources. A is wrong — Conditional Access governs sign-in, not the resource's local-auth setting. D is wrong — policy can evaluate AI Services resources and Blueprints is retiring.

prompt: An AI team wants to use Azure OpenAI Studio for development and testing while the tenant enforces disabled key access on AI Services. What tension must the governance team resolve?

options.text: Policy exemptions are not supported for AI Services resources
OpenAI Studio works without keys, so there is no tension
Key access can only be disabled tenant-wide, so development must move to another tenant
Azure OpenAI Studio requires key access and will not function if key access is disabled, so the policy needs a scoped exemption for the dev environment

explanation: Correct: D. Microsoft's own guidance notes Azure OpenAI Studio, typically used in development/testing, requires key access and will not function if key access is disabled — so a blanket deny breaks dev work and needs scoping or an exemption. B contradicts the published note. C is wrong — policy can be scoped and exemptions exist. A is wrong — policy exemptions are a supported mechanism.

prompt: A governance lead wants to require MFA before any user can create, update, or delete Azure resources. Which mechanism can enforce this at the resource-management layer?

options.text: An Azure Policy identity-based rule blocking resource create, update, and delete requests when initiated by a user who doesn't have MFA enabled
An RBAC role assignment, which natively requires MFA for all write operations
A management group lock, which enforces MFA on all child resources
A Blueprint artifact, which is the only place MFA conditions can be expressed

explanation: Correct: A. Azure Policy can require that all users have MFA enabled, blocking resource create, update, and delete requests when initiated by a user without MFA, using the identity context of the request. B is wrong — RBAC grants permission; it does not itself impose MFA on resource operations. C is wrong — locks prevent deletion/modification, they do not check MFA. D is wrong — Blueprints is retiring and MFA conditions belong in policy or Conditional Access, not only in Blueprints.

prompt: A policy assignment at the management group level is showing resources as non-compliant, but the resources themselves are in a subscription, not in the management group. An engineer claims management group assignments cannot evaluate anything. What is true?

options.text: Management group assignments evaluate the management group object itself, not its resources
Although a policy can be assigned at the management group level, only resources at the subscription or resource group level are evaluated
The assignment is broken; policies must be assigned at the resource level to evaluate anything
Only resources directly in the management group are evaluated, so subscriptions are out of scope

explanation: Correct: B. Microsoft states that although a policy can be assigned at the management group level, only resources at the subscription or resource group level are evaluated — the assignment flows down to the resources. A is wrong — the management group object is not the evaluated target. C is wrong — the assignment is valid. D is wrong — subscriptions are within scope via inheritance.

prompt: A team wants to enforce that every resource carries a cost-center tag, automatically adding a default value when the deployment omits it. Which built-in policy effect and example matches this?

options.text: Deny, using the Allowed Resource Type policy
AuditIfNotExists, which adds the tag automatically
Modify, using the Add a tag to resources policy, which applies a required tag and its default value if the deploy request doesn't specify it
DeployIfNotExists, which only works for Log Analytics workspaces

explanation: Correct: C. The built-in Add a tag to resources policy uses the Modify effect: it applies a required tag and its default value if the deploy request doesn't specify it. A is wrong — Deny blocks, it does not add tags. B is wrong — AuditIfNotExists only records non-compliance. D is wrong — deployIfNotExists deploys related resources; the tagging example is Modify.

prompt: During Blueprint retirement Phase 2 (October 31, 2026), a team tries to create a new Blueprint assignment for a subscription that was onboarded late. What happens?

options.text: Assignments can still be created, but definitions cannot
Only delete is disabled; create and update still work
Everything works normally until January 31, 2027
Assignments cannot be created and definitions cannot be created or updated, though delete remains available

explanation: Correct: D. In Phase 2, assignments cannot be created, definitions cannot be created, and definitions cannot be updated; read and delete remain available through Phase 3. A reverses Phase 1 and Phase 2 (in Phase 1 new definitions stopped but assignments could still be created). C is wrong — the phasedown restricts capabilities before retirement. B is wrong — delete remains available, create/update do not.

prompt: An organization with many subscriptions wants to efficiently manage access, policies, and compliance centrally, and to ensure a policy limiting VM regions cannot be bypassed by a subscription owner. Which structure does Microsoft recommend?

options.text: Organizing subscriptions into management groups and applying governance conditions to the management groups, since all subscriptions within inherit the conditions
Tagging subscriptions by region, because tags enforce inheritance
Creating a separate Microsoft Entra tenant per subscription
Assigning policies at the resource group level in each subscription

explanation: Correct: A. Microsoft states that if an organization has many subscriptions, management groups provide a level of scope above subscriptions, and all subscriptions within a management group automatically inherit the conditions applied to it. B is wrong — tags do not enforce inheritance. C is wrong — management groups require one tenant, and separate tenants fragment governance. D is wrong — resource-group scoping multiplies work and misses new resource groups.

prompt: A CISO wants continuous assessment of resource configuration against compliance controls in applied standards and benchmarks. Which service provides this, and how does Azure Policy relate to it?

options.text: Azure Policy alone performs the assessment; Defender for Cloud only manages firewall rules

Microsoft Defender for Cloud provides continual assessment against compliance controls and best practices in the standards and benchmarks applied; Azure Policy initiatives supply the enforceable definitions
Microsoft Sentinel performs compliance assessment; Policy is unrelated
Azure Monitor assesses compliance; Defender for Cloud only sends alerts

explanation: Correct: B. Microsoft Defender for Cloud provides a continual assessment of the configuration of resources against compliance controls and best practices in the standards and benchmarks applied in subscriptions, and Azure Policy provides the built-in initiatives for those standards. A is wrong — Defender for Cloud is the assessment service. C is wrong — Sentinel is SIEM/SOAR, not the compliance assessor. D is wrong — Monitor collects logs; it is not the compliance dashboard.

prompt: A regulator asks a bank to prove that its Azure Policy compliance posture is not just a point-in-time screenshot. Which combination best answers the regulator?

options.text: A single export of the compliance dashboard
A Blueprint assignment report, which is the only auditable record

Continuous evaluation: create/update triggers, assignment lifecycle triggers, and the 24-hour standard cycle, plus bulk remediation records for existing resources and automatic remediation for new ones
RBAC assignment history, which records resource state

explanation: Correct: C. Policy evaluates on resource create/update, new assignments, policy updates, and the 24-hour cycle, and helps bring resources to compliance through bulk remediation for existing resources and automatic remediation for new resources — a continuous, auditable posture. A is wrong — a single screenshot is point-in-time. B is wrong — Blueprints is retiring and is not the compliance record. D is wrong — RBAC history records who could act, not resource compliance state.

prompt: A team manages Azure Policy as code and wants peer review on every change to definitions, initiatives, and assignments. What does Microsoft recommend, and why does it matter for governance?

options.text: Review only Deny policies; Audit policies cannot cause harm
Edit policies directly in the portal, because code review adds no value for JSON policies
Store policies only in the portal, since exporting them breaks assignments
Manage Azure Policy resources as code with manual reviews on changes to policy definitions, initiatives, and assignments

explanation: Correct: D. Microsoft recommends managing Azure Policy resources as code with manual reviews on changes to definitions, initiatives, and assignments, pointing to Policy-as-Code workflows. B is wrong — portal-only edits bypass review and versioning. C is wrong — policies can be exported and managed as code. A is wrong — even Audit policies shape compliance reporting and later enforcement decisions.

prompt: A multinational wants a governance hierarchy where the European division's subscriptions inherit EU-only region restrictions, while the global root still enforces MFA-based policy. How should the hierarchy be structured?

options.text: A root management group for tenant-wide policy, with a nested Europe management group carrying the region restriction that inherits to its descendant subscriptions
One flat management group containing all subscriptions, with region policy assigned per subscription
Two separate tenants, because a hierarchy cannot nest management groups
Assign the region policy at the resource level in each European subscription

explanation: Correct: A. Hierarchies nest management groups up to six levels deep; the root carries global policy and a child management group carries the regional restriction, which cascades to its subscriptions. B is wrong — a flat structure cannot express regional inheritance. C is wrong — one directory has a single hierarchy and nesting is supported. D is wrong — resource-level assignment does not scale and misses future resources.

prompt: An admin needs to move a management group to a new parent. Which permissions are required on the child management group being moved?

options.text: Only Microsoft.Management/managementGroups/read
Microsoft.Management/managementGroups/write plus Microsoft.Authorization/roleAssignments/write and delete, and Microsoft.Management/register/action
Only Owner on the target parent management group
No permissions are needed; management groups can be moved by any Reader

explanation: Correct: B. Moving a child management group requires Microsoft.Management/managementGroups/write, Microsoft.Authorization/roleAssignments/write, Microsoft.Authorization/roleAssignments/delete, and Microsoft.Management/register/action on the child (plus write on the target and current parents). A is wrong — read is insufficient. C is wrong — the child and current parent also need write. D is wrong — moves are permission-gated.

prompt: A company is deciding between using Azure Policy's built-in regulatory initiatives versus writing custom policies for every control. What is the strongest argument for starting with the built-ins?

options.text: Built-ins automatically grant full regulatory attestation
Custom policies are not supported for regulatory standards
Built-ins are free and already available in the environment for common standards such as FedRAMP High, HIPAA, HITRUST, PCI DSS, and ISO 27001
Built-ins cannot be customized, so they are always faster to deploy

explanation: Correct: C. Policy definitions for common use cases are already available as built-ins, including initiatives for FedRAMP High, HIPAA, HITRUST, PCI DSS, and ISO 27001. B is wrong — custom policies are supported. A is wrong — as established, policy compliance is only a partial view of overall compliance. D is wrong — built-ins support parameters and can be customized via initiatives.

prompt: A policy definition uses parameters for allowed locations so the same definition can be reused for the US and EU. What is the benefit, and where are parameter values supplied?

options.text: Parameter values are fixed at definition time and cannot vary by assignment
Parameters eliminate the need for assignments entirely
Parameters only work for initiative definitions, not single policies
Parameters reduce the number of policy definitions you must create; values are passed in when assigning the policy definition

explanation: Correct: D. Parameters simplify management by reducing the number of definitions; you define a parameter such as location and give it different values such as EastUS or WestUS when assigning. B is wrong — assignments are still required. C is wrong — parameters work in policy definitions. A is wrong — varying values per assignment is the point of parameters.

prompt: A government agency's Blueprint definitions are stored at a management group but not assigned to any subscription. The team uses the View Impacted Blueprints Resources page to find them before migration. What will they observe?

options.text: The view lists impact by subscription, so Blueprint definitions saved at a management group that aren't assigned to any subscription don't appear in it
The view lists all definitions regardless of assignment
The view only lists resources deployed by Blueprints, not definitions
The view is unavailable until after retirement

explanation: Correct: A. The impacted-resources view lists impact by subscription, so Blueprint definitions saved at a management group that are not assigned to any subscription do not appear in it — the team must also check the Blueprints portal, which lists management-group definitions. B contradicts the documented behavior. C is wrong — the view is about impacted Blueprint resources including definitions. D is wrong — the view exists before retirement to support migration.

prompt: A tenant is scheduled for decommissioning in three months, well before the Blueprint retirement date matters for its workloads. What migration approach does Microsoft consider acceptable for this tenant?

options.text: No action is needed at all, because the tenant will be gone

A limited export plus standard Azure resource locks approach is acceptable when the tenant itself is on a near-term decommissioning timeline, though Deployment Stacks remain recommended for workloads that outlive retirement
A full Deployment Stack migration is mandatory even for tenants being decommissioned
The tenant must be migrated to a new tenant first

explanation: Correct: B. Microsoft states a limited export + standard Azure resource locks approach is acceptable when the tenant is on a near-term decommissioning timeline, but recommends Deployment Stacks for any workload that outlives retirement. A is wrong — export is still needed to preserve artifacts. C is wrong — full migration is recommended, not mandatory, for a decommissioning tenant. D is wrong — no tenant migration is required.

prompt: A SOC wants policy enforcement to also block specific actions on resources, not just evaluate their properties — for example, blocking users from deleting critical resources. Which effect and capability provides this?

options.text: The Audit effect, which blocks actions and logs them
The Modify effect, which deletes resources that violate policy
The DenyAction effect, which can block certain actions on resources, combined with identity-aware policy evaluation
RBAC deny assignments, which are part of Azure Policy

explanation: Correct: C. Azure Policy through the DenyAction effect can block certain actions on resources, and policy evaluates identity-based actions via request context. A is wrong — Audit only logs. B is wrong — Modify alters resource properties, it does not block actions. D is wrong — deny assignments are a separate lock mechanism, not a policy effect.

prompt: An organization assigns a Deny policy for disallowed resource types at the management group, but excludes one sandbox subscription. A developer in the sandbox deploys a disallowed resource type and it succeeds. A developer in a production subscription tries the same and is blocked. What explains this?

options.text: The exclusion also removed the policy from production
The sandbox subscription is in a different tenant, so policy cannot reach it
Deny policies only apply to production subscriptions by default
The assignment applies to all resources within the Resource Manager scope of that assignment, and subscopes can be excluded

explanation: Correct: D. An assignment applies to all resources within its Resource Manager scope, and subscopes can be excluded if necessary — the sandbox exclusion is working as designed. B is wrong — all subscriptions in a management group trust the same tenant. C is wrong — there is no production-only default. A is wrong — the production block proves the policy is still active there.

prompt: A company wants governance for AI workloads that covers both the AI service configuration and the data the models can access. Which combination reflects Microsoft's published guidance?

options.text: Disable local authentication on Azure AI Services so Entra ID is the only access method, and use sensitivity labels plus DLP to govern the data
Use only Conditional Access, because policy cannot evaluate AI Services
Store model keys in application code for performance, and rely on network isolation alone
Use Blueprint locks for AI governance, since policy initiatives exclude AI resources

explanation: Correct: A. Published FedRAMP guidance recommends disabling key access on Azure AI Services so Entra ID becomes the only access method, and sensitivity labels with encryption and DLP govern data wherever it lives or travels. B is wrong — policy can evaluate AI Services resources. C is wrong — storing keys in code violates Key Vault centralization guidance. D is wrong — Blueprints is retiring and policy initiatives do include AI Services definitions.

prompt: An auditor notes that a FedRAMP Moderate initiative shows several controls with Manual, Disabled policy definitions. What does this mean for the organization's compliance claim?

options.text: Those controls are automatically compliant because they are listed in the initiative
Those controls are not assessed by policy at all; compliance in Azure Policy is only a partial view and manual controls need separate evidence
Manual definitions are evaluated the same as automated ones
Disabled definitions are still enforced in Audit mode

explanation: Correct: B. The initiative mapping notes many controls are implemented with Manual, Disabled definitions, and the standard includes controls not addressed by any policy definitions — so policy compliance is only a partial view of overall compliance status. A is wrong — listing is not compliance. C is wrong — Manual means human evidence, not automated evaluation. D is wrong — Disabled means the definition is not evaluated.

prompt: A startup with three subscriptions is told to adopt management groups. A skeptic says management groups are only for enterprises with hundreds of subscriptions. What is the correct response?

options.text: Management groups are only available with an Enterprise Agreement
Management groups require at least 100 subscriptions to activate
Management groups give enterprise-grade management at scale no matter what type of subscriptions you might have, and they provide a governance scope above subscriptions
Three subscriptions cannot be placed in a management group

explanation: Correct: C. Management groups give enterprise-grade management at scale no matter what type of subscriptions you might have, and they provide a governance scope above subscriptions. B is wrong — there is no minimum subscription count. A is wrong — all Azure customers can see the root management group. D is wrong — any subscriptions can be organized under management groups.

prompt: A team wants to migrate Blueprints to the recommended replacement while keeping definition storage and versioning. Which pairing does Microsoft describe?

options.text: Resource locks for assignment and Azure DevOps for versioning only
Policy initiatives for assignment and Blueprints for versioning
ARM templates alone, which provide deny assignments natively
Deployment Stacks for assignment and lifecycle management, plus template specs or a Git repository for definition storage and versioning

explanation: Correct: D. Microsoft recommends Deployment Stacks as the replacement, providing grouping, lifecycle management, and deny assignments, and notes you can publish definitions as template specs or store them in a Git repository to take advantage of versioning. B is wrong — Blueprints is retiring, not a versioning store. C is wrong — plain ARM templates do not provide deny assignments. A is wrong — resource locks do not group or lifecycle-manage deployments.

prompt: A ransomware attack is spreading laterally across Azure VMs. An analyst manually isolates one VM at a time while the SOC manager asks why containment is not keeping up. What does Microsoft's incident guidance say about this approach?

options.text: Manual containment is preferred because automation causes false positives
Manual containment is faster than playbooks because playbooks need approval
Manual containment takes hours while automated attacks complete objectives in minutes, so Sentinel playbooks should automate containment actions
Containment should wait until the full forensic image is complete

explanation: Correct: C. Microsoft states manual containment takes hours while automated attacks complete objectives in minutes, and recommends deploying Sentinel playbooks for user, network, device, and malware response. A is wrong — automation is recommended, with approval workflows for high-impact actions. B is wrong — playbooks act at machine speed once triggered. D is wrong — evidence preservation happens in parallel, not as a precondition for containment.

prompt: A compromised VM must be remediated, but the forensics team needs the evidence preserved first. Which sequence does Microsoft recommend?

options.text: Delete the VM immediately, then restore from backup
Disable the VM's network, then delete its disks to stop the attacker
Reimage the VM first, then collect logs from the new image
Create point-in-time VM snapshots before remediation, export logs to immutable storage with legal hold, and maintain chain of custody with cryptographic hashing and access logging

explanation: Correct: D. Microsoft recommends creating point-in-time snapshots for compromised VMs before remediation, exporting logs and evidence to Azure Storage with immutable storage policies and legal hold, and maintaining chain of custody with cryptographic hashing and access logging. A is wrong — deletion destroys evidence. C is wrong — reimaging destroys volatile and disk evidence. B is wrong — deleting disks destroys evidence.

prompt: An incident timeline is incomplete: the team has Entra sign-in logs but cannot trace lateral movement or control-plane changes. Which log sources are missing?

options.text: NSG flow logs for network traffic with source/destination mapping, and Azure Activity Logs for control plane operations including resource modifications
Only Defender for Cloud alerts, which replace all logs
Only the Microsoft 365 audit log, which covers Azure lateral movement
No logs are missing; sign-in logs alone are sufficient for timelines

explanation: Correct: A. Comprehensive logging requires Entra ID logs, Azure Activity Logs for control plane operations, NSG flow logs for lateral movement detection, and resource diagnostic logs, sent to a Log Analytics workspace. B is wrong — alerts do not replace logs. C is wrong — the M365 audit log does not cover Azure network lateral movement. D is wrong — timelines need multiple log sources.

prompt: A company writes its first Azure incident response plan by copying its datacenter plan verbatim. What gap does Microsoft warn about?

options.text: Datacenter plans are superior and need no changes
Traditional plans often fail in cloud environments where the shared responsibility model, API-based evidence collection, and service provider collaboration differ from datacenter incident handling
Cloud plans must not mention Microsoft Support or MSRC
Azure plans must omit VM snapshots because they are not supported

explanation: Correct: B. Microsoft warns traditional plans often fail in cloud environments where the shared responsibility model, API-based evidence collection, and service provider collaboration differ from datacenter incident handling. A is wrong — adaptation is required. C is wrong — plans should include Microsoft Support and MSRC collaboration processes. D is wrong — VM snapshots are a recommended evidence step.

prompt: During a ransomware incident, the SOC wants to isolate VMs, block attacker IPs, and revoke a compromised admin's privileges — all without losing investigation access. Which Azure-native isolation combination achieves this?

options.text: Delete the VMs, delete the admin account, and shut down the firewall
Only Defender for Endpoint isolation, which handles network, identity, and privilege revocation alone

NSG deny rules to isolate VMs while preserving investigation access, Azure Firewall rules blocking malicious IPs, Conditional Access blocking the compromised account, and PIM revoking privileged assignments
Disable all Conditional Access policies so the admin can be investigated

explanation: Correct: C. Microsoft lists NSG deny rules to isolate VMs while preserving investigation access, Azure Firewall rules blocking malicious IPs/domains, Conditional Access to block compromised accounts or locations, and PIM to revoke privileged access assignments. A is wrong — deletion destroys evidence and access. B is wrong — Endpoint isolation covers devices, not identity or privilege revocation. D is wrong — disabling Conditional Access removes a containment control.

prompt: After an incident, the team updates its playbooks and detection rules. Which post-incident practice does Microsoft recommend for identifying defense gaps?

options.text: Delete all logs older than 30 days to start fresh
Skip the lessons-learned review if containment succeeded
Disable the analytics rules that fired, since they are now known to be noisy
Add detection rules for attack techniques observed, and map detected activities to MITRE ATT&CK techniques to identify defense gaps

explanation: Correct: D. Post-incident activities include updating detection capabilities by adding rules for observed techniques and mapping detected activities to MITRE ATT&CK to identify defense gaps, plus documenting lessons learned and updating playbooks. A is wrong — evidence must be retained per regulatory requirements. C is wrong — rules that fired correctly should be kept and tuned, not disabled. B is wrong — lessons-learned documentation is required regardless of outcome.

prompt: A Defender XDR incident shows a yellow bar and an Attack Disruption tag. A junior analyst asks whether the SOC still needs to investigate. What is the correct answer?

options.text: Yes, automatic attack disruption limits lateral movement and gives the team time, but leaves security operations teams in complete control of investigating, remediating, and bringing assets back online
No, attack disruption fully remediates the incident automatically
No, the incident is auto-closed once disruption acts
Yes, but only to approve the disruption, which cannot be undone

explanation: Correct: A. Automatic attack disruption limits lateral movement and reduces impact while leaving security operations teams in complete control of investigating, remediating, and bringing assets back online; all automatic actions can be undone. B is wrong — disruption contains, it does not fully remediate. C is wrong — incidents are not auto-closed by disruption. D is wrong — actions can be undone by the security team.

prompt: An attacker is moving laterally using a compromised user account and an unrecognized device. Which automatic attack disruption actions contain each element?

options.text: Disable user only, which also blocks unknown devices automatically
Contain user, which blocks communication from that user on onboarded devices, and contain IP, which blocks communication from an IP associated with undiscovered devices
Isolate device only, which contains users as a side effect
Revoke session only, which contains both the user and the device

explanation: Correct: B. Contain user applies a policy on all Defender for Endpoint onboarded devices to block communication from that user; contain IP contains an IP associated with undiscovered or not onboarded devices by blocking communication from that IP. A is wrong — disabling the user does not contain the unknown device's IP. C is wrong — device isolation does not contain the user identity elsewhere. D is wrong — session revocation interrupts access but does not contain the device or IP.

prompt: A CISO worries that automatic containment will act on weak signals and disrupt business operations. What confidence standard does Microsoft cite for attack disruption containment actions?

options.text: 50% confidence is sufficient for containment
Confidence is not measured; all high-severity alerts trigger disruption
Defender maintains a confidence level of 99% or higher based on real production data for containment actions, with detectors validated in audit mode before broad release
Containment requires human approval in every case, so confidence is irrelevant

explanation: Correct: C. Confidence refers to detector precision measured by signal-to-noise ratio, and for containment actions Defender maintains 99% or higher based on real production data, validating detectors in audit mode before broad release. A is wrong — 50% would be far too low. B is wrong — confidence is measured and gated. D is wrong — disruption is automatic by design.

prompt: A domain controller is a critical asset that must never be automatically isolated. A ransomware incident triggers attack disruption. How can the SOC protect this asset in advance?

options.text: It cannot be protected; disruption applies to all assets
Disable automatic attack disruption tenant-wide
Remove the domain controller from Defender for Endpoint onboarding permanently
Configure exclusions for supported users, devices, and IP addresses from automated response actions

explanation: Correct: D. Microsoft states that if you have critical assets that should not be automatically contained, you can configure exclusions for supported users, devices, and IP addresses. A is wrong — exclusions exist. C is wrong — removing onboarding loses protection and visibility. B is wrong — tenant-wide disablement removes protection everywhere.

prompt: A synced Active Directory account is compromised and attack disruption disables it. What happens in Microsoft Entra ID, and why?

options.text: Attack disruption also disables the user account in Microsoft Entra ID, because the account is synced and the disruption must stop cloud access too
Nothing in Entra ID; the disable only affects on-premises AD
The Entra account is deleted automatically
The Entra account is suspended only if the admin approves within 24 hours

explanation: Correct: A. For an account hosted in AD and synced to Entra ID, Defender for Identity triggers the disable via onboarded domain controllers and attack disruption also disables the user account in Microsoft Entra ID. B is wrong — the synced cloud account is also disabled. C is wrong — the account is disabled/suspended, not deleted. D is wrong — disruption is automatic, not approval-gated.

prompt: An analyst wants to understand how automatic attack disruption differs from blocking a single malicious IP. What is the key distinction?

options.text: There is no difference; both block one indicator

Attack disruption evaluates the entire attack at the incident level using XDR signals from endpoints, identities, email, and apps, and contains attacker-controlled assets in real time, rather than acting on a single indicator of compromise
Disruption only works on email threats, while IP blocking works everywhere
Disruption requires a playbook; IP blocking does not

explanation: Correct: B. Attack disruption uses XDR signals and evaluates the entire attack to take action at the incident level, which differs from prevention and blocking based on a single indicator of compromise. A is wrong — the incident-level scope is the distinction. C is wrong — disruption spans endpoints, identity, email, and apps. D is wrong — disruption is built in, not playbook-dependent.

prompt: A SOC is drowning in alerts: many are ignored and incidents go uninvestigated. Which Sentinel capability is designed for this problem, and what does it automate?

options.text: Workbooks, which automate alert triage
Threat intelligence feeds, which close incidents automatically
Sentinel as a SOAR platform: automating recurring and predictable enrichment, response, and remediation tasks so analysts can focus on in-depth investigation and hunting for advanced threats
KQL hunting queries, which auto-remediate

explanation: Correct: C. Sentinel is a SIEM and a SOAR platform whose primary purpose is automating recurring and predictable enrichment, response, and remediation tasks, freeing time for in-depth investigation and hunting. A is wrong — workbooks visualize, they do not automate response. B is wrong — threat intelligence enriches, it does not close incidents. D is wrong — hunting queries find threats; they do not remediate.

prompt: A Sentinel automation rule should tag, assign, and close low-risk incidents without calling a Logic App, and trigger a playbook for high-risk ones. Which mechanism supports both in one place?

options.text: Playbooks alone, which can tag and close incidents without an automation rule
Watchlists, which trigger playbooks
Analytics rules, which perform the tagging directly
Automation rules, which centrally manage incident handling: automatically tag, assign, or close incidents without a playbook, and assign advanced automation using playbooks

explanation: Correct: D. Automation rules let users manage incident handling automation centrally: assign advanced automation using playbooks, automatically tag, assign, or close incidents without a playbook, automate responses for multiple analytics rules at once, and control action order. A is wrong — playbooks are invoked via automation rules. C is wrong — analytics rules create alerts/incidents, not handling automation. B is wrong — watchlists are reference data, not triggers.

prompt: A playbook must block a malicious IP in the firewall, create a ServiceNow ticket, and notify the SOC in Teams when a Sentinel incident is created. What is a Sentinel playbook built on?

options.text: Workflows built in Azure Logic Apps, which provide integration, orchestration, scalability, and reliability as a Tier 1 Azure service
Azure Functions only, with no workflow engine
Sentinel notebooks, which execute response actions
Defender for Endpoint live response scripts only

explanation: Correct: A. Playbooks are based on workflows built in Azure Logic Apps, a cloud service for scheduling, automating, and orchestrating tasks across systems, giving playbooks Logic Apps integration, orchestration, and Tier 1 scalability and reliability. B is wrong — Logic Apps is the foundation. C is wrong — notebooks are for advanced investigation, not response. D is wrong — live response is an Endpoint capability, not a Sentinel playbook.

prompt: A Sentinel workspace is onboarded to the Defender portal. An analyst notices incident-triggered automation now runs on Defender XDR incidents too, and a rule that used the Incident provider condition behaves differently. What changed?

options.text: Nothing changes; the Incident provider condition still filters providers separately

After onboarding, all incidents have Microsoft XDR as the incident provider, so existing automation rules run on both Sentinel and Defender XDR incidents, including those where the condition was set to only Sentinel or Microsoft 365 Defender
Automation stops working entirely in the Defender portal
Only Microsoft incident creation rules run now

explanation: Correct: B. In the Defender portal the Incident provider condition property is removed because all incidents have Microsoft XDR as provider, so existing automation rules run on both Sentinel and Defender XDR incidents. A is wrong — the condition is removed. C is wrong — automation continues with documented differences. D is wrong — Microsoft incident creation rules are not supported in the Defender portal.

prompt: An analytics rule is configured with incident creation disabled. The SOC still wants a playbook to run when its alerts fire. Which automation trigger should they use, and what is its limitation in the Defender portal?

options.text: Incident trigger, which works for alerts without incidents
No trigger can run a playbook for an alert without an incident

Alert-triggered automation, which runs a playbook in response to an alert not associated with an incident; in the Defender portal, alert-triggered automation for alerts created by Defender XDR isn't available, so use the Enhanced Alert Trigger
Watchlist trigger, which replaces alert triggers

explanation: Correct: C. Automation rules can run a playbook in response to an alert not associated with an incident, which is the main reason to use alert-triggered automation; in the Defender portal, alert-triggered automation for Defender XDR alerts is unavailable and the Enhanced Alert Trigger should be used. A is wrong — incident triggers need incidents. B is wrong — alert triggers exist for this case. D is wrong — watchlists are not triggers.

prompt: A playbook that isolates devices is delayed by several minutes after an incident appears in the Defender portal. The SOC blames the playbook. What is the more likely cause?

options.text: Playbooks always take 30 minutes to start
The playbook is blocked by the incident's severity
Automation rules only run once per day
It might take up to 5 minutes for Microsoft Defender incidents to appear in Microsoft Sentinel, so playbook triggering is delayed too

explanation: Correct: D. Microsoft documents latency in playbook triggers: it might take up to 5 minutes for Defender incidents to appear in Sentinel, and if this delay is present, playbook triggering is delayed too. A is wrong — there is no 30-minute baseline. C is wrong — automation runs on incident create/update, not daily. B is wrong — severity does not block playbook triggering.

prompt: A SOC builds automation that processes each incident status change in sequence. After onboarding to the Defender portal, intermediate status changes are sometimes lost. What explains this?

options.text: The automation batching window: if multiple changes are made to the same incident in a 5-10 minute period, a single update is sent with only the most recent change, and intermediate updates are lost
Automation rules delete intermediate updates by design in both portals
The incident queue drops updates when severity is low
Playbooks overwrite the incident history

explanation: Correct: A. The automation batching window means if multiple changes are made to the same incident in a 5-10 minute period, a single update is sent to Sentinel with only the most recent change, and intermediate updates are lost, which can impact workflows depending on sequential state changes. B is wrong — batching is a Defender-portal behavior, not a universal rule. C is wrong — severity does not drop updates. D is wrong — playbooks do not overwrite history.

prompt: An analyst opens a 120-alert incident and asks Copilot in Defender to summarize it. What will Copilot do?

options.text: Summarize all 120 alerts into one summary
Summarize only up to 100 alerts; incidents containing up to 100 alerts can be summarized into one incident summary
Refuse, because summaries require fewer than 10 alerts
Summarize the first 10 alerts and ignore the rest silently

explanation: Correct: B. Incidents containing up to 100 alerts can be summarized into one incident summary; a 120-alert incident exceeds that limit. A is wrong — the cap is 100. C is wrong — there is no 10-alert minimum. D is wrong — Copilot does not silently truncate to 10.

prompt: A SOC lead wants Copilot incident summaries generated only for high-severity incidents to control Security Copilot capacity consumption. How can this be configured?

options.text: It cannot be configured; summaries always generate for every incident
Disable Copilot in Defender entirely
Change the incident summary setting to auto-generate based on incident severity, choosing the minimum severity level, with an estimate of SCU consumption shown
Delete low-severity incidents so they never generate summaries

explanation: Correct: C. By default Copilot generates a summary for each incident opened, but you can change the setting to generate based on severity level, choosing the minimum severity, with an estimate of incidents per severity and SCU consumption displayed. A is wrong — the setting is configurable. B is wrong — disabling Copilot removes the capability entirely. D is wrong — deleting incidents destroys the record.

prompt: An analyst reopens an unchanged incident a day later and the Copilot summary appears instantly at no additional cost. Why?

options.text: The analyst has unlimited SCU capacity
Copilot regenerates every summary for free
Summaries are stored permanently in the incident record
Copilot caches summaries for a week; if the incident didn't change significantly, the summary is redisplayed at no cost

explanation: Correct: D. Copilot saves generated incident summaries for a week; if the incident has a cached summary and did not change significantly, the summary is automatically redisplayed at no cost regardless of the setting. B is wrong — regeneration consumes capacity; the cache avoids it. C is wrong — the cache lasts a week, not permanently. A is wrong — capacity is not unlimited.

prompt: A junior analyst opens an incident and sees a Copilot summary with the attack start time, the asset where it started, a timeline, assets involved, indicators of compromise, and threat actor names. Where did this summary come from, and what else does it offer?

options.text: Copilot automatically creates the incident summary in the Tasks pane when the incident is opened, including suggested prompts for follow-up investigation
It was written manually by the previous shift
It is generated only after the analyst clicks Regenerate three times
It comes from the Sentinel workbook, not Copilot

explanation: Correct: A. Copilot automatically creates an incident summary in the Tasks pane when an incident page is opened; the summary includes start time, origin asset, timeline, assets, IoCs, threat actor names, and suggested Copilot prompts for next steps. B is wrong — it is AI-generated. C is wrong — it is automatic on open. D is wrong — workbooks visualize data; they do not generate Copilot summaries.

prompt: An analyst wants Copilot in Defender to summarize a device's posture, vulnerable software, and unusual behavior during an investigation. Which capability is this, and what does it require?

options.text: Incident summary, which requires no Copilot access
Device summary, available in the Defender portal for customers with provisioned access to Security Copilot, also available via the Defender XDR plugin in the standalone experience
Advanced hunting, which summarizes devices automatically
The Action Center, which generates device summaries

explanation: Correct: B. The device summary capability of Copilot in Defender gives a device's security posture, vulnerable software, and unusual behaviors, and is available for customers with provisioned access to Security Copilot, including via the Defender XDR plugin standalone. A is wrong — incident summary covers incidents, not device posture. C is wrong — advanced hunting is query-based threat hunting. D is wrong — the Action Center handles pending remediation actions.

prompt: A company still manages Sentinel in the Azure portal in late 2026. What deadline must the SOC plan for, and what happens after it?

options.text: No deadline; the Azure portal remains supported indefinitely
Sentinel will be retired entirely on March 31, 2027
After March 31, 2027, Microsoft Sentinel will no longer be supported in the Azure portal and will be available only in the Microsoft Defender portal
The Azure portal loses only playbooks, not the rest of Sentinel

explanation: Correct: C. After March 31, 2027, Microsoft Sentinel will no longer be supported in the Azure portal and will be available only in the Microsoft Defender portal, with Azure-portal customers redirected. A is wrong — the retirement of Azure-portal support is announced. B is wrong — Sentinel continues in the Defender portal. D is wrong — all of Sentinel moves, not just playbooks.

prompt: A Defender XDR incident contains alerts from endpoints, identities, email, and cloud apps. An analyst asks what an incident represents and how it was formed. What is the correct explanation?

options.text: An incident is a single alert from one product
Incidents group alerts only from the same device
Incidents are manually created by analysts only
Microsoft Defender XDR automatically correlates alerts into incidents, providing end-to-end attack chain visibility and AI-powered automation for faster detection and response

explanation: Correct: D. Defender XDR automatically correlates alerts into incidents, providing end-to-end attack chain visibility and AI-powered automation. A is wrong — an incident is a collection of correlated alerts. C is wrong — correlation is automatic. B is wrong — correlation spans endpoints, identities, email, and apps.

prompt: A SOC must choose between XDR and SIEM for a new program. An architect says they are substitutes and only one is needed. What is the correct design guidance?

options.text: XDR and SIEM are complementary: XDR integrates detection, investigation, and response across endpoints, identities, email, and apps, while SIEM provides centralized analytics, long-term retention, and orchestration across multicloud sources
SIEM replaces XDR entirely
XDR replaces SIEM entirely
Neither is needed if EDR is deployed

explanation: Correct: A. XDR and SIEM are complementary solutions that together provide comprehensive threat detection and response; Defender XDR correlates across domains while Sentinel as SIEM delivers AI-driven security across multicloud environments with hunting, investigation, and response. B and C are wrong — each covers gaps the other does not. D is wrong — EDR is one signal source, not a detection and response program.

prompt: A phishing campaign leads to a token theft incident. Which Microsoft incident response playbook should the SOC follow, and what is its focus?

options.text: The password spray playbook, which covers token theft
The token theft playbook, one of Microsoft's detailed playbooks for common attack scenarios alongside phishing, password spray, app consent grant, and compromised applications
The ransomware playbook, which is the only playbook covering identity attacks
There is no token theft playbook; analysts must improvise

explanation: Correct: B. Microsoft provides detailed playbooks for phishing investigation, password spray investigation, app consent grant investigation, compromised and malicious applications, and token theft. A is wrong — password spray is a different scenario. C is wrong — ransomware is not the identity playbook. D is wrong — the token theft playbook exists.

prompt: A malicious OAuth app was granted consent by a user and is now exfiltrating mail. Which investigation path and which attack disruption action apply?

options.text: The phishing playbook only, with no disruption action available
The password spray playbook and device isolation
The app consent grant investigation playbook, and the OAuth app compromise disruption action in Defender for Cloud Apps
Delete the user account and ignore the app

explanation: Correct: C. Microsoft provides an app consent grant investigation playbook, and automatic attack disruption includes an OAuth app compromise action executed by Defender for Cloud Apps for potentially compromised OAuth applications. B is wrong — password spray does not cover consent grants. A is wrong — a disruption action exists for OAuth apps. D is wrong — the app itself must be investigated and contained.

prompt: A DLP alert fires for a user emailing sensitive files externally. The SOC wants to investigate it in the Defender portal. Where do DLP alerts appear, and what is required?

options.text: DLP alerts appear only in the Purview portal and cannot be investigated in Defender
DLP alerts are emailed to the SOC and never appear in any queue
DLP alerts appear as Sentinel watchlists
DLP alerts are grouped under incidents in the Defender XDR incident queue, and investigating them requires a license from an eligible subscription

explanation: Correct: D. DLP alerts can be viewed grouped under incidents in the Defender XDR incident queue, and investigating Purview DLP incidents in the Defender portal requires a license from an eligible subscription. A is wrong — Defender portal investigation is supported. C is wrong — watchlists are reference data. B is wrong — alerts appear in the incident queue.

prompt: An analyst investigates a DLP alert in Defender and clicks Summarize for a Copilot alert summary. What information does the summary contain?

options.text: Alert severity, alert title, the name of the policy that was matched, the name of the file involved with a link, alert status, and the email address of the user who performed the action
Only the file name
Only the user's email address
The full file contents

explanation: Correct: A. The Security Copilot-generated alert summary contains alert severity, alert title, the name of the policy that was matched, the name of the file involved and a link to it, alert status, and the email address of the user who performed the action. B and C are wrong — the summary is richer than a single field. D is wrong — the summary does not include full file contents.

prompt: A critical incident is unacknowledged for two hours because nobody was notified. What notification practice does Microsoft recommend to prevent this?

options.text: Rely on analysts checking the portal queue periodically

Use Azure Logic Apps and Sentinel playbooks to automatically route alerts to appropriate stakeholders based on severity, regulatory requirements, and affected resources, with time-based escalation for unacknowledged critical incidents
Send all alerts to a single shared mailbox with no routing
Disable notifications for low-severity alerts only

explanation: Correct: B. Microsoft recommends automated notification workflows using Logic Apps and Sentinel playbooks to route alerts by severity, regulatory requirements, and affected resources, with escalation procedures and time-based triggers for unacknowledged critical incidents. A is wrong — manual checking introduces critical delays. C is wrong — unrouted mailboxes delay response. D is wrong — it does not fix notification of critical incidents.

prompt: A company discovers gaps in its response only during real incidents. What testing practice does Microsoft recommend, and how often?

options.text: Test once a year with a single scenario
Never test; testing disrupts operations
Conduct quarterly tabletop exercises using attack scenarios like ransomware, data exfiltration, and insider threats
Test only after a major incident occurs

explanation: Correct: C. Microsoft recommends testing response procedures regularly and conducting quarterly tabletop exercises using attack scenarios like ransomware, data exfiltration, and insider threats. A is wrong — annual testing is too infrequent. B is wrong — untested procedures fail during real incidents. D is wrong — testing should be proactive, not only post-incident.

prompt: An incident involves regulatory-protected health data on a critical business system. How should the SOC prioritize and escalate it?

options.text: Treat it like any other incident; all incidents have equal priority
Deprioritize it because health data is covered by DLP
Escalate only if the attacker is still active

Tag resources with criticality levels based on business impact, revenue dependency, and regulatory scope, and automatically escalate incidents involving regulatory-protected data or critical business systems

explanation: Correct: D. Microsoft recommends tagging Azure resources with criticality levels based on business impact, revenue dependency, and regulatory scope, and automatically escalating incidents involving regulatory-protected data or critical business systems. A is wrong — prioritization is based on business impact. C is wrong — regulatory scope alone warrants escalation. B is wrong — DLP is a control, not a reason to deprioritize.

prompt: A SOC wants to configure Defender for Cloud alerting so known false positives do not flood the queue, without losing threat coverage. What does Microsoft recommend?

options.text: Tune alert thresholds and create suppression rules for known false positives, while maintaining threat coverage
Disable all Defender plans for the affected workloads
Delete the alerts as they arrive
Turn off Defender for Cloud and rely on Sentinel alone

explanation: Correct: A. Microsoft recommends configuring Defender for Cloud with appropriate Defender plans for workloads, tuning alert thresholds, and creating suppression rules for known false positives while maintaining threat coverage. B is wrong — disabling plans removes coverage. C is wrong — deleting alerts destroys the record. D is wrong — Defender for Cloud provides workload alerts Sentinel consumes.

prompt: An attacker uses Safe Mode reboots to tamper with endpoint protection during an incident. Which attack disruption capability counters this, and what is it classified as?

options.text: Contain device, classified as attack disruption
Safeboot hardening, classified as predictive shielding, which applies preventive hardening to block tampering through Safe Mode reboots
Disable user, classified as predictive shielding
Revoke session, classified as attack disruption

explanation: Correct: B. Safeboot hardening is a predictive shielding action that applies preventive hardening to block potential tampering through Safe Mode reboots. A is wrong — contain device blocks communication, it does not harden Safe Mode. C is wrong — disable user affects accounts, not boot tampering. D is wrong — session revocation interrupts access, it does not harden boot.

prompt: A high-risk user is identified by prediction logic before an incident escalates. Which action proactively contains them, and how does it differ from the attack disruption contain user action?

options.text: Contain device, which targets users
Disable user, which is identical in both contexts
Proactive user containment under predictive shielding, which applies restrictions more selectively and prevents new sessions rather than terminating existing ones
Suspend user in Okta, which is the only proactive action

explanation: Correct: C. Proactive user containment is a predictive shielding action that proactively contains a user to prevent misuse before an incident escalates, focusing on high-risk users; in predictive shielding the contain user action applies restrictions more selectively and prevents new sessions rather than terminating existing ones. B is wrong — disable user is a different, stronger action. A is wrong — contain device targets devices. D is wrong — Okta suspension is a Sentinel disruption action for Okta users, not the predictive shielding mechanism.

prompt: A company uses Okta for identity and AWS for infrastructure alongside Azure. Can automatic attack disruption act in those environments?

options.text: No, disruption only works in Microsoft Entra ID and Active Directory
Yes, but only for Okta, not AWS
Yes, but only for AWS, not Okta
Yes, in preview: suspend a user in Okta via the Sentinel Okta connector, and attach a deny policy to a compromised AWS IAM user via the Sentinel AWS connector

explanation: Correct: D. Attack disruption supports actions in Entra ID and AD generally, with preview support for Okta and AWS: suspending an Okta user via the Sentinel Okta connector and attaching a deny policy to a compromised AWS IAM user via the Sentinel AWS connector. A is wrong — Okta and AWS preview support exists. C and B are each half right and therefore wrong.

prompt: An analyst needs to run a playbook manually on a specific alert in the Defender portal. What will they find?

options.text: Running a playbook manually on an alert, and running a playbook manually on an entity, are not currently supported in the Defender portal
Manual playbook runs on alerts are fully supported in the Defender portal
Manual runs work only for incidents, not alerts or entities
Manual runs require the Azure portal but work identically there

explanation: Correct: A. Microsoft states the following procedures are not currently supported in the Defender portal: run a playbook manually on an alert, and run a playbook manually on an entity. B is wrong — they are unsupported. C is wrong — manual runs on incidents are supported once synced, but the question is about alerts. D is wrong — the Azure portal supports manual runs on alerts and entities, so behavior differs.

prompt: An analyst tries to run a playbook on an incident from the Defender portal and sees: Can't access data related to this action. Refresh the screen in a few minutes. What does this mean?

options.text: The playbook is broken and must be rebuilt
The incident isn't yet synchronized to Microsoft Sentinel; refresh the incident page after synchronization to run the playbook successfully
The analyst lacks permission to run any playbook
Playbooks cannot run on incidents from the Defender portal at all

explanation: Correct: B. Running playbooks on incidents requires Sentinel sync; this message means the incident is not yet synchronized to Sentinel, and refreshing after sync allows the playbook to run. A is wrong — the playbook is fine. C is wrong — the message indicates sync timing, not permissions. D is wrong — playbooks can run on incidents from the Defender portal once synced.

prompt: A SOC's automation rules use incident titles as condition criteria. After onboarding to the Defender portal, some rules stop matching. What should they use instead?

options.text: Keep using titles; the correlation engine preserves them
Use the incident ID, which never changes
Avoid incident titles as condition criteria; use the name of an analytics rule that created alerts in the incident, and tags if more specificity is required
Use the alert severity only

explanation: Correct: C. The Defender portal uses a unique correlation engine that may change existing incident names on onboarding, so Microsoft recommends avoiding incident titles as condition criteria and using the analytics rule name and tags instead. A is wrong — titles may change. B is wrong — IDs are not the recommended condition property. D is wrong — severity alone is too coarse.

prompt: A Defender XDR alert fires and automated investigation starts. What verdict and remediation actions can result, and where are pending actions handled?

options.text: No verdict is produced; analysts must decide everything manually
Remediation is limited to blocking URLs
The verdict is always malicious and devices are wiped automatically

Automated investigations produce a verdict on whether a threat was found; when malicious threats are identified, remediation includes sending a file to quarantine, stopping a process, blocking a URL, or isolating a device, with pending actions handled in the Action Center

explanation: Correct: D. As alerts create incidents, automated investigations produce a verdict determining whether a threat was found; remediation actions include quarantining a file, stopping a process, blocking a URL, or isolating a device, and pending remediation actions are handled in the portal Action Center. A is wrong — AIR produces verdicts. C is wrong — verdicts vary and wiping is not automatic. B is wrong — remediation covers files, processes, URLs, and devices.

prompt: An analyst uses advanced hunting to proactively search for indicators of compromise. How much raw data can they explore, and what is the tool's purpose?

options.text: Up to 30 days of raw data, to proactively inspect events and locate threat indicators
Up to 7 days, for compliance reporting only
Unlimited retention, for forensic archiving
Up to 90 days, but only for email events

explanation: Correct: A. Advanced hunting is a query-based threat hunting tool that lets analysts explore up to 30 days of raw data to proactively inspect events and locate threat indicators. B is wrong — the window is 30 days. C is wrong — hunting is not archival storage. D is wrong — it covers events across the environment, not only email.

prompt: A company integrates Defender XDR data with two Sentinel workspaces in one tenant, then onboards to the Defender portal. Where does XDR data go now, and what must the SOC do about automation?

options.text: Data continues to both workspaces unchanged
Data is now only ingested into the primary workspace; transfer automation rules to the relevant workspace to keep them running
Data stops flowing to both workspaces
A new workspace is created automatically for each incident

explanation: Correct: B. If XDR data was integrated with more than one workspace in a single tenant, data will now only be ingested into the primary workspace in the Defender portal, and automation rules must be transferred to the relevant workspace to keep them running. A is wrong — ingestion consolidates to the primary workspace. C is wrong — data still flows, to the primary workspace. D is wrong — no per-incident workspaces are created.

prompt: An incident involves a compromised account used to access an AWS-hosted workload from an Azure identity. The SOC wants a single pane for SIEM, SOAR, XDR, exposure management, and Copilot. Which portal provides this unified experience?

options.text: The Azure portal only
The Microsoft Purview portal
The Microsoft Defender portal, which combines Defender XDR, Sentinel, Security Exposure Management, and Security Copilot in a single location to monitor, detect, investigate, remediate, and respond
The Entra admin center

explanation: Correct: C. The Defender portal provides unified security operations integrating SIEM, SOAR, and XDR, combining Defender XDR, Sentinel, Exposure Management, and Security Copilot in a single location. A is wrong — Sentinel leaves the Azure portal after March 31, 2027. B is wrong — Purview covers data governance and compliance. D is wrong — Entra covers identity, not unified SecOps.

prompt: After an incident is contained, evidence must be retained to meet regulatory requirements for different incident types. How should it be stored?

options.text: In the analyst's local drive for quick access
Evidence retention is not required once containment succeeds
In a public blob container so auditors can access it
In immutable Azure Storage with retention policies meeting regulatory requirements for different incident types

explanation: Correct: D. Post-incident guidance says to store evidence in immutable Azure Storage with retention policies meeting regulatory requirements for different incident types. A is wrong — local storage breaks chain of custody. C is wrong — public containers expose evidence. B is wrong — retention is a post-incident requirement.
